    A historical encyclopedia · Edition 4 (fact-checked, with footnotes and source links)

    The Complete History of Christianity and the Christian Church

    Fifteen volumes, from the world into which Christianity was born to the Churches of 2026, with a comparative guide to today's traditions and specialised studies on worship, Mary, Islam, Judaism, violence, church and state, and the transmission of texts.

    c. 1200 BC – AD 2026 · Volumes I–XV · Parts III–IV · Updated November 2026

    What this edition is

    This edition contains all fifteen planned volumes:

    • Volumes I–III: the background to Christianity, Jesus and the apostolic age, and the Church before Constantine.
    • Volumes IV–IX: the imperial Church, the councils and the East–West schism. These are the most detailed volumes, with each council analysed under eleven headings.
    • Volumes X–XV: the medieval Church, the Protestant and Catholic Reformations, Eastern Christianity beyond Constantinople (with a dedicated chapter on the Antiochian and Maronite Churches), the modern world, and the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

    Part III profiles fifteen Christian traditions and compares twelve of them on twenty-four topics. Part IV gathers specialised studies. Volumes X–XV cover very long periods and are written at survey depth. The editorial report explains what has been verified and what remains to deepen.

    The aim is historical understanding supported by evidence, not religious advocacy. The text tries throughout to separate three things that popular accounts often blur together:

    • What the surviving sources show: documents, council acts, letters, inscriptions.
    • What historians infer, including where they agree and where they disagree.
    • What particular Churches teach about these events. These teachings are reported accurately and in their own terms, but they are not presented as historical findings.

    How to read the evidence labels

    Important claims carry a small label showing what kind of claim they are. Tap or hover a label for its definition.

    Supported by contemporary or near-contemporary sources whose authenticity is not seriously disputed.
    An inference accepted by a clear majority of specialists, even though the sources leave room for argument.
    A question on which qualified historians actively disagree. Both or all positions are summarised.
    An account preserved within a Church's own tradition that cannot be independently confirmed from early sources. This is not a judgement that it is false.
    A doctrinal position officially taught by a Church. It is reported as that Church's teaching, not as a historical finding.
    A story first attested long after the events it describes.
    The evidence is too thin to support a confident conclusion either way.

    Finding your way

    • Contents (left sidebar, or the ☰ button on phones) lists every volume and chapter and marks where you are.
    • Search (top bar, or press /) searches the full text, the glossary, the people directory and the councils.
    • Eras jumps to a historical period. Topics gathers chapters on councils, schisms, authority, Christology and the Trinity.
    • Underlined terms such as open a glossary definition without leaving the page. Superscript numbers open the footnote in place; each chapter also lists its notes at the end.
    • Grey boxes marked Scholarly debate expand to give the more technical arguments.
    • The Atlas, Timeline and Council table are interactive reference tools, reached from the Reference section of the contents.
    • Use ☆ to bookmark a chapter in this browser. Printing from your browser gives a clean, print-formatted copy of the current chapter, or of everything if you choose “Show all chapters” first.

    A note on quotations and translations

    Primary sources are quoted from public-domain translations, chiefly the Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885–96) and the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (1886–1900). Their English is old-fashioned and occasionally loose, but their texts are freely available, so every quotation here can be checked against them. Each quotation panel names the translator and volume. Where a modern critical translation differs significantly, the note says so. Modern church documents still under copyright are quoted only in short phrases and otherwise summarised. Every quotation is listed in the Verification register with its verification status.

    Honest limits of this edition

    • Quotations marked “checked” were compared word for word against an edition during preparation. Other factual claims rest on the standard scholarship listed in the bibliography, but not every claim was individually re-checked. The editorial report gives the exact figures.
    • Secondary works are cited by author, title and chapter or section rather than page number. No page numbers have been supplied that could not be checked.
    • This hosting environment cannot display remotely hosted photographs. The maps and diagrams are original drawings made for this edition, and the Visual sources page directs readers to museum and archive images of the objects discussed.

    Method and sources

    The problem of sources for this period

    The history of the councils is unusually well documented for antiquity. For Ephesus (431), Chalcedon (451), Constantinople II (553), Constantinople III (680–81) and Nicaea II (787), large parts of the minutes (acta) survive. They record speeches, acclamations, the reading of documents and lists of signatories. The standard critical edition is Eduard Schwartz's Acta Conciliorum Oecumenicorum (from 1914), and Richard Price and his collaborators have produced annotated English translations in the Translated Texts for Historians series.1 For Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), no minutes survive. Historians rely on the creed, the canons, a synodal letter, and the accounts of participants such as Eusebius of Caesarea and Athanasius and of fifth-century church historians: Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret.

    These sources share three limitations that the reader should keep in mind:

    • The winners kept the records. Most surviving texts were copied by communities that accepted a council's outcome. The writings of Arius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and the opponents of icons survive mainly as hostile quotations, though important exceptions exist, such as Nestorius' own Book of Heracleides, preserved in Syriac.
    • The acta are edited documents. They were compiled, sometimes revised, and transmitted in Greek, Latin, Syriac and other versions that do not always agree.
    • Later tradition shaped earlier memory. Round numbers (318 fathers at Nicaea, 150 at Constantinople, 630 at Chalcedon) and tidy narratives grew up after the events. They tell us how a council was remembered, which is itself historically important, but they are not always reliable records.

    Approach

    Each chapter starts from the primary evidence, gives the range of current scholarly interpretation, and reports separately how Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Church of the East traditions understand the events, along with Protestant traditions where relevant. Terms that later became party labels ("Arian", "Nestorian", "Monophysite") are used with care: they are often names opponents used, and modern scholarship has shown they can misdescribe the people they label. The glossary explains each one.

    Dates are AD/CE. Where a date is disputed, the range is given and the dispute is noted.

    Source standards (Edition 4)

    Every footnote and reference in this edition points to one of five kinds of source. Each bibliography entry is labelled with its kind:

    • Primary sources and official texts: Scripture; ancient and medieval authors cited by book and chapter; council acts and canons (Tanner's Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils); papal and curial documents (cited by Denzinger–Hünermann number, DH, where possible); confessions of faith (the Book of Concord, Schaff's Creeds of Christendom); and joint declarations and statistics published by the Churches themselves.
    • University-press monographs (Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Chicago, California and others).
    • Peer-reviewed articles and reference works, including the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
    • Academic publishers (Brill, de Gruyter, Eerdmans, Fortress, Blackwell and similar).
    • Trade books by recognised specialists. A few standard works by leading scholars appeared with general publishers. They are labelled as such and are never the only support for a contested claim.

    News reports are not used as authorities. They were used only to find official texts. For a few events of 2024–2026 in Volume XV, news reporting is still the only available record. Those statements are kept brief and general. Secondary works are cited as whole works or by volume, never by invented page numbers. The editorial report lists what was verified and what was corrected.

    Notes

    1. Price & Gaddis 2005; Price 2009; Price 2018; Price & Graumann 2020. ↩

    Volume I · c. 1000 BC – AD 30

    The World before Christianity

    Christianity began as a movement within Second Temple Judaism, in a province of the Roman Empire, in a Mediterranean world whose shared language was Greek. This volume sketches that world. It does not try to be a full history of ancient Israel or of Rome. It aims to set out what a reader needs in order to understand Jesus, the first Christians and the Church that followed.

    In this volume

    1. Ancient Israel and the First Temple
    2. Exile, the Persian period and the Second Temple
    3. Hellenism, the Maccabees and Roman conquest
    4. Second Temple Judaism: groups, scriptures, hopes
    5. The Greco-Roman world
    6. Judea and Galilee in the time of Jesus

    The Hebrew Bible is both a historical source and Scripture for Jews and Christians. This volume treats it as a source. It reports where historians and archaeologists find its narratives corroborated, where they do not, and where they disagree. These are historical judgements and are not meant to pass judgement on the texts' religious meaning.

    Volume I · Chapter 1

    Ancient Israel and the First Temple

    Origins: what the evidence allows

    The biblical narrative runs from the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob), through the exodus from Egypt and the conquest of Canaan, to the united monarchy of Saul, David and Solomon. Historians and archaeologists generally conclude that this narrative was shaped centuries after the periods it describes.1

    • The patriarchs and the exodus cannot be confirmed from sources outside the Bible. No archaeological evidence matches the exodus as narrated, a migration of hundreds of thousands. Many scholars think that memories of smaller groups, perhaps including people who had been in Egypt, were woven into a national epic.
    • Israel as a people is first named outside the Bible on the Merneptah Stele (Egypt, c. 1208 BC). In the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC, small villages spread across the central hill country. Most archaeologists interpret these as the emergence of Israel largely from within Canaanite society, not by conquest from outside.2
    • David and Solomon. The Tel Dan inscription (9th century BC) refers to the "House of David", strong evidence that a dynasty traced itself to David. How large and powerful David's and Solomon's kingdom was is one of the most debated questions in biblical archaeology. "Minimalists" see a modest chiefdom. Others, citing finds such as Khirbet Qeiyafa, argue for a substantial early state.

    Two kingdoms

    From the ninth century the evidence becomes firmer. There were two kingdoms. In the north was Israel, with its capital at Samaria. Its kings Omri and Ahab appear in Assyrian and Moabite inscriptions; the Mesha Stele, c. 840 BC, refers to Omri. In the south was Judah, ruled from Jerusalem by the house of David. Assyria destroyed Israel in 722/720 BC and deported much of its elite. Judah survived as an Assyrian vassal. Under King Josiah (c. 640–609 BC), a reform centralised worship in the Jerusalem Temple. Many scholars connect this reform with a form of Deuteronomy.3

    Religion

    Inscriptions and archaeology show that religion in Israel and Judah was more varied than the biblical writers approved of. Inscriptions from Kuntillet 'Ajrud (c. 800 BC) invoke "Yahweh and his Asherah". Most scholars hold that strict monotheism, the belief that only one God exists, emerged gradually. It was articulated most clearly during and after the exile (e.g. Isaiah 40–55). This is a scholarly reconstruction. Traditional Jewish and Christian readings see the biblical faith as revealed from the beginning.

    The fall of Jerusalem

    Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem in 597 BC. After a revolt, it destroyed the city and the Temple Solomon was said to have built, in 587 or 586 BC. The exact year is disputed because ancient chronologies conflict. Babylonian administrative tablets (the "Jehoiachin ration tablets") confirm that Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, received rations in Babylon.4

    Why this matters for Christian history

    • Christianity inherited Israel's scriptures, its worship of one God, and its hope in a coming king of David's line ("messiah", the anointed one).
    • The idea of a covenant people, the Temple and its sacrifices, and the prophetic critique of injustice all shaped how the first Christians understood Jesus.

    Notes

    1. The classic statement of the documentary approach is Julius Wellhausen, Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1878; Eng. trans. 1885). On the period, see Dever 2003 and Finkelstein & Silberman 2001. ↩
    2. Finkelstein & Silberman 2001, chs. 2–4; Dever 2003. Both argue for indigenous origins, from different perspectives. ↩
    3. The reform is narrated in 2 Kings 22–23. W. M. L. de Wette (1805) first connected the book found in the Temple with Deuteronomy. A survey is in Collins 2016. ↩
    4. These are the Babylonian ration lists from Nebuchadnezzar II's palace, first published by E. F. Weidner (1939). English translation in Pritchard 1969. ↩

    Volume I · Chapter 2

    Exile, the Persian period and the Second Temple

    The Babylonian exile (587/6–539 BC) was the formative crisis of ancient Judaism. Without land, king or Temple, the exiles preserved their identity through law, Sabbath, circumcision and the collection and editing of their traditions. Many scholars date much of the editing of the Torah, the historical books and the prophets to the exile and the Persian period that followed.

    • 539 BC. Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylon. His policy of allowing deported peoples to return and restore their cults is reflected in the Cyrus Cylinder, which does not mention the Jews specifically, and in the Bible (Ezra 1; Isaiah 45:1, which calls Cyrus God's "anointed").1
    • c. 515 BC. The Second Temple was completed in Jerusalem. Judah became the small Persian province of Yehud.
    • 5th century BC. Ezra and Nehemiah carried out reforms, enforcing the law and separating from neighbouring peoples. The dates and the order of their missions are debated.
    • The diaspora. Many Jews stayed in Babylonia, the origin of a great centre of Jewish learning. Others settled in Egypt. The Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, a garrison on the Nile (5th century BC), show a Jewish community with its own temple, in correspondence with Jerusalem.2
    • The Samaritans worshipped the same God, held to the Torah, and had their own sanctuary on Mount Gerizim. The tension between them and Judeans forms the background to Gospel stories such as the parable of the Good Samaritan.3

    By the end of the Persian period, the Torah (the Pentateuch) was very probably authoritative in Jerusalem. The collection of "Prophets" was taking shape. Other writings, the later "Writings", circulated without a fixed list. How the Hebrew canon was closed is discussed in Vol. II ch. 9.

    Notes

    1. The Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum, 1880,0617.1) records Cyrus' policy of restoring cults and peoples, though it does not mention Judah. English translation in Pritchard 1969. ↩
    2. The Elephantine papyri: Cowley 1923; Porten 1968. They include a petition of 407 BC to the governor of Judah about rebuilding the temple of YHW. ↩
    3. On Samaritans and Jews, see Schurer 1973, vol. 2, and Cohen 2014. ↩

    Volume I · Chapter 3

    Hellenism, the Maccabees and Roman conquest

    Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire (334–323 BC). Judea passed first to the Ptolemies of Egypt (to c. 200 BC) and then to the Seleucids of Syria. Greek became the language of government and culture across the eastern Mediterranean. Jews everywhere had to decide how far to adopt Greek ways, and they decided differently.

    The Septuagint

    In Alexandria, the largest Jewish community outside Judea translated its scriptures into Greek. The Letter of Aristeas tells how seventy-two elders translated the Law for Ptolemy II (283–246 BC). Its details are legendary.1 Scholars agree, however, that the Pentateuch was translated in Alexandria in the third century BC, and the other books over the next two centuries. This Greek Bible, the Septuagint (LXX), became the Old Testament of the early Church. The New Testament usually quotes it. Its contents, including books not later in the Hebrew canon such as Wisdom, Sirach and 1–2 Maccabees, underlie the difference between Catholic/Orthodox and Protestant Old Testaments (Vol. II ch. 9).

    The Maccabean crisis

    In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, amid conflicts between Jerusalem factions, banned Jewish practices and set up a pagan cult in the Temple. A revolt led by the priestly family of Mattathias and his son Judas Maccabeus retook the Temple and rededicated it in 164 BC, the origin of the festival of Hanukkah. The main sources are 1 and 2 Maccabees and Josephus.2 The crisis produced two lasting ideas:

    • Martyrdom, as in the story of the mother and seven sons in 2 Maccabees 7, which later Christians read as a model.
    • Apocalyptic hope. The book of Daniel, which most scholars date in its final form to c. 167–164 BC, promises the resurrection of the dead (Daniel 12:2) and a coming kingdom of God.

    Hasmoneans, Romans and Herod

    The Maccabees' descendants, the Hasmoneans, ruled an independent kingdom (c. 140–63 BC). They combined the offices of king and high priest, which offended some pious Jews. In 63 BC the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem. In 37 BC Rome installed Herod ("the Great") as client king. Herod ruled until 4 BC and rebuilt the Temple on a vast scale, as well as Caesarea Maritima, Masada and other fortresses.3 Jesus' birth "in the days of Herod the king" (Matthew 2:1) is therefore dated before 4 BC. See ch. 6.

    Notes

    1. Letter of Aristeas; English translation in Charles 1913, vol. 2. ↩
    2. 1 Maccabees 1–4; 2 Maccabees 4–10; Josephus, Antiquities 12.5–7 (Josephus (Whiston)). For analysis, see Hengel 1974 and Schurer 1973, vol. 1. ↩
    3. Josephus, Antiquities 15–17 and Jewish War 1.401–428 (Josephus (Whiston)); Schurer 1973, vol. 1. ↩

    Volume I · Chapter 4

    Second Temple Judaism: groups, scriptures, hopes

    Judaism in the late Second Temple period (c. 200 BC – AD 70) was diverse. Historians sometimes speak of "Judaisms". What united Jews was worship of the one God, the Temple in Jerusalem, the Torah, and practices such as Sabbath, circumcision and food laws. They disagreed about how to interpret all of these.

    The Jews had, for a great while, had three sects of philosophy peculiar to themselves…

    Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.1.2 (c. AD 93–94). Trans. William Whiston (1737), as online at LacusCurtius/Penelope. Q42 · checked

    Josephus, writing for Greek and Roman readers, described the parties as "philosophies":

    GroupWhat the sources sayRelevance to the Gospels
    PhariseesA lay movement devoted to precise interpretation of the Torah and to "traditions of the elders". They believed in resurrection and angels. Josephus says they were popular with the people. The rabbis who reshaped Judaism after AD 70 stood partly in their tradition.Jesus' most frequent debating partners. The Gospels' hostile portrait reflects later conflicts, and modern scholarship warns against reading it as a fair description of Pharisaism.
    SadduceesAssociated with the priestly aristocracy and the Temple. They accepted only the written Torah as binding and rejected resurrection.Challenge Jesus over resurrection (Mark 12:18–27). The high priests involved in his arrest were of this milieu.
    EssenesCommunal, ascetic groups described by Josephus, Philo and Pliny the Elder.Not mentioned in the New Testament.
    "Fourth philosophy"Josephus' term for those who held that God alone was Israel's ruler and resisted Roman taxation (from AD 6, under Judas the Galilean). Later revolutionary groups (Zealots, Sicarii) are often connected with it.One of Jesus' disciples was "Simon the Zealot". The precise meaning of the label is debated.

    The Dead Sea Scrolls

    Between 1947 and 1956, about 900 manuscripts were found in caves near Qumran on the Dead Sea. They include the oldest surviving copies of the Hebrew Bible, every book except Esther being represented, and the rules and writings of a separatist community that called itself the Yahad ("the Union"). Most scholars identify that community with the Essenes, or a branch of them. A minority dispute both the identification and the link between the caves and the settlement. The Scrolls show that the scriptural text was still fluid. They also show a community expecting the end of the age, using a calendar opposed to the Temple's, and expecting more than one messianic figure (a royal and a priestly messiah).1

    Messianic and apocalyptic hopes

    There was no single "Jewish expectation of the Messiah". Texts of the period hope variously for:

    • a Davidic king who would defeat Israel's enemies (Psalms of Solomon 17);
    • a priestly messiah;
    • a prophet like Moses or a returning Elijah;
    • a heavenly "Son of Man" figure (Daniel 7; the Parables of Enoch, whose date is debated);
    • God's direct intervention without any messiah.

    Apocalyptic literature, such as 1 Enoch, Daniel and later 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, spoke of revealed secrets, cosmic conflict, judgement and the resurrection of the dead. The early Christians used this language to interpret Jesus.

    Synagogue and diaspora

    Far more Jews lived outside Judea than in it: in Alexandria, Antioch, Asia Minor, Rome and Babylonia. Their gatherings2 (synagōgai, proseuchai) for reading and interpreting Scripture are attested by inscriptions, such as the Theodotus inscription from pre-70 Jerusalem, and by Philo and Josephus. Some Gentiles were attracted to Jewish worship and ethics without converting. Acts calls them "God-fearers". They were among the first hearers of the Christian mission. Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – c. AD 50) interpreted the Torah through Platonic philosophy and spoke of the divine Logos ("Word") as God's agent in creation. His method deeply influenced later Christian theology in Alexandria (Vol. III ch. 6).

    Notes

    1. VanderKam 2010, chs. 4–6; Collins 2016, ch. 6. ↩
    2. Cohen 2014, chs. 4–5; Schurer 1973, vol. 2. ↩

    Volume I · Chapter 5

    The Greco-Roman world

    Augustus' victory at Actium (31 BC) brought the whole Mediterranean under one ruler. The early Christian mission depended on what followed: the "Roman peace", roads and sea lanes, cities linked by trade, and Greek as a common language (the koinē) from Rome to Syria.1

    Religion in the Roman world

    • Civic cult. Each city honoured its gods with sacrifices and festivals, believed to secure the community's well-being. Religion was a matter of practice more than belief. Refusing to take part could appear antisocial and dangerous, which is why Christians were called "atheists" (Vol. III ch. 2).
    • The imperial cult. Honours to Rome and the emperor, living or deified, especially in the eastern provinces. Its titles (saviour, son of god, lord, the "good news" of an emperor's birth) overlap with Christian language. Scholars debate how far early Christian texts deliberately contrasted Christ with the emperor.
    • Voluntary cults and "mysteries". Isis, Mithras, the Eleusinian and Dionysiac rites offered initiation and personal relationship with a deity. Older scholarship (the "History of Religions school") claimed that Christianity borrowed its sacraments from them. Modern scholars generally reject direct borrowing. Most Mithraic evidence, for example, is later than the New Testament.2
    • Toleration with limits. Judaism was generally tolerated as an ancestral religion. New cults could be suppressed if they seemed to threaten public order, as with the Bacchanalia in 186 BC.

    Philosophy

    Educated people looked to philosophy for answers about God, the soul and the good life. Each school left a mark on Christian thought:

    • Platonism taught a transcendent, unchanging First Principle, an intelligible world above the material one, and the immortality of the soul. "Middle Platonism" (1st c. BC – 2nd c. AD) shaped Philo, Justin, Clement and Origen. It also shaped the vocabulary of the fourth-century debates (Key terms).
    • Stoicism taught a rational order (logos) pervading the cosmos, natural law and the brotherhood of humanity. It influenced Paul's environment and later Christian ethics.
    • Epicureanism taught that the gods are indifferent, and that the soul dies with the body. It was the philosophy the early Christians most opposed.
    • Aristotle's logic and categories became important in theology later, from the fourth century.

    How much Christianity was "Hellenised" was a famous question in older scholarship (Adolf von Harnack). It is now usually reframed: Judaism itself was already Hellenised by this period, and Christian writers used Greek philosophy critically, not passively.3

    Notes

    1. Ferguson 2003; Beard, North & Price 1998, vol. 1. ↩
    2. Beard, North & Price 1998, vol. 1, chs. 6–8; Ferguson 2003, ch. 3. ↩
    3. Justin Martyr, 2 Apology 13; Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 1.5 (ANF, vols. 1–2). See Pelikan 1971, vol. 1. ↩

    Volume I · Chapter 6

    Judea and Galilee in the time of Jesus

    On Herod's death (4 BC), Augustus divided his kingdom among three sons.1

    • Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea. He was deposed in AD 6, and Judea became a Roman province governed by a prefect of equestrian rank.
    • Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea (4 BC – AD 39). This is the "Herod" of Jesus' ministry, who executed John the Baptist.
    • Philip received the north-eastern territories.

    Pontius Pilate and the high priests

    Pontius Pilate was prefect of Judea from c. AD 26 to 36. A dedicatory inscription found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 confirms his name and title (praefectus Iudaeae). Philo and Josephus portray him as harsh and provocative.2 The high priest Caiaphas held office c. AD 18–36, an unusually long tenure suggesting close cooperation with Rome. An ossuary inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas", found in Jerusalem in 1990, is widely but not universally thought to be his. Under the prefects, the Jerusalem priestly aristocracy ran local affairs. Rome kept the power of execution.

    The census of Quirinius: a dating problem

    Luke 2:1–2 connects Jesus' birth with a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria". Josephus dates Quirinius' census of Judea to AD 6, ten years after Herod's death. Matthew and Luke both place the birth under Herod, so before 4 BC. Proposed harmonisations include an earlier governorship of Quirinius or a different translation of Luke's Greek. None has won general acceptance. Most historians conclude that Luke's chronology is confused at this point.3 Jesus' birth is usually placed c. 6–4 BC. The AD/BC era itself was calculated by Dionysius Exiguus in the sixth century and is a few years off.

    Galilee

    Galilee was a largely Jewish region of villages and two new cities built by Antipas, Sepphoris and Tiberias, which the Gospels never mention Jesus visiting. Archaeology at Nazareth, Capernaum and Magdala (including a first-century synagogue found in 2009) shows observant Jewish village life: stone vessels for ritual purity and immersion pools. Scholars debate the economic situation of Galilean peasants and how far urbanisation strained it.

    Key takeaways

    • Jesus lived in a Jewish world under indirect and then direct Roman rule, in which the Temple, the Torah and hope of God's intervention were live issues.
    • The figures in the Passion story (Pilate, Caiaphas, Antipas) are historically attested.
    • Exact dates for Jesus' birth cannot be fixed. The evidence points to c. 6–4 BC.

    Notes

    1. Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.4 (Josephus (Whiston)); Schurer 1973, vol. 1. ↩
    2. Philo, Embassy to Gaius 299–305; Josephus, Antiquities 18.3.1–2 and Jewish War 2.169–177. A 1961 inscription from Caesarea Maritima confirms his title as praefectus Iudaeae. ↩
    3. Luke 2:1–2; Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.1 dates Quirinius' census to AD 6. See Schurer 1973, vol. 1, and Brown 1994. ↩

    Volume II · c. 6 BC – AD 135

    Jesus, the Apostles and the Apostolic Age

    This volume covers the life of Jesus, the emergence of belief in his resurrection, the first communities in Jerusalem and Antioch, Paul's mission, the deaths of the leading apostles, the war with Rome, and the writing and gathering of the New Testament. In this period, more than any other, the line between historical reconstruction and Christian faith must be kept visible. Historians can establish what the sources report and what probably happened. They cannot, as historians, decide claims about God's action, such as the incarnation or the resurrection, which Christians affirm by faith.

    In this volume

    1. The sources for Jesus
    2. Jesus of Nazareth: what historians can say
    3. Crucifixion and resurrection belief
    4. Jerusalem, Antioch and the Gentile question
    5. Paul: mission and letters
    6. The deaths of James, Peter and Paul
    7. War, the Temple and the parting of the ways
    8. Worship and ministry in the earliest communities
    9. The New Testament: writing, transmission and canon

    Volume II · Chapter 1

    The sources for Jesus

    Christian sources

    • Paul's letters (c. 50–60) are the earliest surviving Christian writings. They say little about Jesus' life, but confirm his Jewish descent, his brother James, the Twelve, the Last Supper, his crucifixion, and early belief in his resurrection (1 Cor. 11:23–26; 15:3–8; Gal. 1:19).
    • The Gospels. Most scholars date Mark c. 65–75, Matthew and Luke c. 80–90, and John c. 90–110.1 All four were anonymous; the titles "according to Matthew" and so on are attested from the second century. The early tradition recorded by Papias (c. 110–130) links Mark to Peter:

      Mark having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.

      Papias, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.39.15. Trans. A. C. McGiffert, NPNF II/1 (1890). Q46 · checked
      How much weight this tradition bears is debated.2
    • The Synoptic problem. Matthew, Mark and Luke share much material, often word for word. The majority explanation is the "Two-Source Hypothesis": Matthew and Luke independently used Mark and a lost collection of sayings ("Q"). Alternatives include the Farrer hypothesis (no Q; Luke used Matthew) and the Griesbach hypothesis (Mark is last).
    • John differs in chronology (a ministry of two to three years, a Temple action at the start), style and theology. Scholars debate how far it preserves independent historical tradition.
    • Non-canonical gospels, such as the Gospel of Thomas, a sayings collection preserved complete in Coptic and in Greek fragments, are occasionally argued to preserve early material. Most scholars date them later than, or dependent on, the canonical Gospels.

    Non-Christian sources

    Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man… [And when] Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men among us, had condemned him to the cross…

    Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.3.3 (18.63–64), c. AD 93–94. Trans. Whiston. Segments checked; ellipsis omits disputed lines. Q43 · checked

    The "Testimonium Flavianum" survives in all Greek manuscripts in a form that a Jewish writer is unlikely to have written ("he was the Christ"; he "appeared to them alive again the third day"). The majority view is that Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral notice that Christian copyists later expanded. A tenth-century Arabic version quoted by Agapius has been cited in support of this view. A minority regard the whole passage as interpolated.3 A second, almost universally accepted passage mentions "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James" (ch. 6).

    Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus…

    Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. AD 116). Trans. A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb (1876). Checked in segments (Wikisource text). Tacitus calls Pilate “procurator”; his actual title was prefect. Q45 · checked

    Pliny the Younger (c. 112) describes Christians in Bithynia meeting before dawn on a fixed day and singing "a hymn to Christ as to a god" (carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere, Ep. 10.96.7). Suetonius (c. 120) reports that Claudius expelled Jews from Rome for disturbances "at the instigation of Chrestus" (impulsore Chresto, Claudius 25.4). This is probably a garbled reference to disputes about Christ (compare Acts 18:2).4

    Assessment

    Virtually all historians of antiquity, whatever their religious views, agree that Jesus existed. They agree that he was a Jewish teacher from Galilee, baptised by John, with a following, and crucified under Pilate. The "Christ myth" theory, which denies his existence, has very little support among specialists.5

    Volume II · Chapter 2

    Jesus of Nazareth: what historians can say

    Historical reconstruction of Jesus uses criteria to weigh the Gospel material. The best-known criteria are multiple attestation, embarrassment (what the early Church would not have invented), dissimilarity, coherence, and plausibility in a first-century Jewish setting. In recent decades several scholars have criticised these criteria as too mechanical and proposed approaches based on social memory. Three successive "quests" for the historical Jesus have produced very different portraits: an apocalyptic prophet (Albert Schweitzer; E. P. Sanders; Dale Allison), a wisdom teacher and social critic (the Jesus Seminar; J. D. Crossan), a prophet of Israel's restoration (N. T. Wright). There is nevertheless a wide area of agreement.1

    ClaimStatus among historians
    Born c. 6–4 BC; grew up in Nazareth in Galilee; family members included his mother Mary and brothers including James2 Birth in Bethlehem and the virginal conception are Christian affirmations () that historical method cannot test. Their historicity is debated.
    Baptised by John the Baptist3 An "embarrassing" fact, since it seems to subordinate Jesus to John. Josephus independently mentions John (Ant. 18.5.2).
    Preached the coming "kingdom (reign) of God", often in parables
    Was known as a healer and exorcist Historians accept that contemporaries saw him so. Whether miracles occurred is not a question historical method can settle.
    Called disciples and a group of "the Twelve", symbolising Israel's twelve tribes4
    Associated with outsiders ("tax collectors and sinners"); included women among his followers
    Debated Torah interpretation with other Jews The details reflect later controversies in places.
    Performed a provocative action in the Temple in Jerusalem Widely held to have precipitated his arrest.
    Shared a last meal with his disciples Attested by Paul (1 Cor. 11) and the Gospels.
    Was crucified on Pilate's authority, around Passover, c. AD 30 or 335 One of the most secure facts of ancient history.
    Claimed to be the Messiah or Son of God, and in what sense Debated. Most agree he spoke with distinctive authority and was executed as "King of the Jews", a political charge.
    Scholarly debate: the date of the crucifixion

    All four Gospels place the crucifixion on a Friday at Passover. The Synoptics make the Last Supper a Passover meal (15 Nisan). John places the death on the day of preparation (14 Nisan), when the Passover lambs were slain. Astronomical calculations of the Jewish calendar allow 7 April AD 30 or 3 April AD 33 as the most likely dates, given Pilate's term (26–36) and Caiaphas' (18–36). Scholars are divided.

    Christian doctrine affirms more than history can show: that Jesus was the eternal Son of God made flesh, without sin, and that his death was a sacrifice for the world. These doctrinal affirmations () and their development are the subject of Volumes III–VI.

    Notes

    1. Sanders 1993; Allison 2010, ch. 1 (critique of the criteria); Meier 1991. ↩
    2. Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19; Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1. ↩
    3. Mark 1:9–11 and parallels; on John the Baptist, Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2 (Josephus (Whiston)). See Meier 1991, vol. 2. ↩
    4. 1 Corinthians 15:5; Mark 3:13–19 and parallels; Sanders 1993. ↩

    Volume II · Chapter 3

    Crucifixion and resurrection belief

    Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and provincials, intended as public humiliation. The remains of a crucified man named Yehohanan, found in Jerusalem in 1968, with a nail still through the heel bone, show that a crucified Jew could receive burial. Jesus' execution under the charge "King of the Jews" indicates that Pilate treated him as a political threat. The Gospels1 assign varying degrees of responsibility to the Temple leadership. Their emphasis on Jewish guilt, especially Matthew 27:25, was later used to justify Christian hostility to Jews. Modern Catholic teaching explicitly rejects collective Jewish guilt (Nostra aetate 4, 1965), as do most other Churches.

    The earliest resurrection testimony

    For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: and that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: after that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once … After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles.

    Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 (written c. AD 53–55). King James Version (1611). Standard text. Q61 · not re-checked

    Paul calls this a tradition he had "received". Most scholars date the formula to within a few years of the crucifixion, probably the 30s. Historians generally agree on three points: shortly after Jesus' death, several of his followers, and also his brother James and the persecutor Paul, became convinced that they had seen him alive. This conviction, expressed as "God raised him from the dead", was the founding claim of the movement. And the claim, in a Jewish context, implied the bodily raising of a person, not the survival of a soul.2

    Beyond this, positions diverge. Questions include:

    • Whether the tomb was found empty. The Gospels, but not Paul explicitly, say it was. Many historians, though not all, think an empty-tomb tradition is early.
    • How to explain the experiences. Explanations range from the Christian belief in an actual resurrection to psychological, visionary or social explanations.

    The resurrection as an act of God is a faith claim. Historical method can document the belief and its early date, but cannot confirm or exclude its truth.

    Notes

    1. Brown 1994 is the standard detailed study of the Passion narratives. ↩
    2. Wright 2003 argues for the historicity of the empty tomb and appearances; Allison 2005 surveys the evidence and the range of explanations. ↩

    Volume II · Chapter 4

    Jerusalem, Antioch and the Gentile question

    The Jerusalem community

    Our main narrative source is Acts, written by the author of Luke, probably c. 80–90, though some scholars date it into the early second century. Where Acts can be compared with Paul's letters, it is broadly accurate on places and people but sometimes differs on details and emphasis. Acts tells of the Spirit's outpouring at Pentecost (Acts 2), a community in Jerusalem that shared goods and attended the Temple, and leadership by the Twelve, with Peter as spokesman. Paul independently names three "pillars" in Jerusalem: James the brother of the Lord, Cephas (Peter) and John (Gal. 2:9). By the 40s James was the leading figure.1

    Acts distinguishes "Hebrews" from "Hellenists", Greek-speaking Jewish believers. The Seven, among them Stephen and Philip, led the Hellenists. Stephen's criticism of the Temple led to his death (Acts 7), and to a persecution that scattered the Hellenists to Samaria, Damascus and Antioch. Paul, a Pharisee from Tarsus, was among the persecutors before his conversion (c. 33–36).

    Antioch

    At Antioch, the third city of the empire, believers began preaching to non-Jews, and the disciples were first called "Christians" (Acts 11:26). Antioch became the base for missions by Barnabas and Paul.2

    The Jerusalem meeting (c. 48–49)

    Should Gentile converts be circumcised and keep the whole Torah? Two accounts survive. They agree in substance and differ in details.

    Galatians 2:1–10 (Paul, c. 50s)

    A private meeting with the pillars. Titus, a Gentile, was not compelled to be circumcised. The pillars recognised Paul's mission to the Gentiles and asked only that he "remember the poor".

    Acts 15 (c. 80–90)

    A public assembly. Peter and James speak. A decree requires Gentile believers to abstain from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled animals and from sexual immorality (porneia).

    Scholars debate whether these describe the same meeting and whether Paul knew the "apostolic decree". Later Christian tradition saw Acts 15 as the model of a church council (Vol. VI).

    The "Antioch incident" (Gal. 2:11–14) shows that the issue was not settled. Peter withdrew from table fellowship with Gentiles under pressure from "men from James", and Paul publicly opposed him. How the dispute ended is unknown.3

    Why it matters

    • Accepting Gentiles without circumcision made Christianity a separate, mainly Gentile movement within a few generations.
    • The tension between "Jewish Christianity" and "Gentile Christianity" shaped the New Testament itself.

    Notes

    1. Galatians 1:18–2:10; Acts 12:17, 15:13–21, 21:18. ↩
    2. Acts 11:19–26; 13:1–3. ↩
    3. Galatians 2:11–14. See Dunn 1998 and Becker & Reed 2003. ↩

    Volume II · Chapter 5

    Paul: mission and letters

    Paul's letters are the earliest Christian documents, and an inscription allows his career to be partly dated. A letter of Claudius found at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, dating his term to c. 51–52. Acts 18:12 places Paul in Corinth before Gallio.1

    Approximate dateEvent
    c. 33–36Conversion near Damascus; time in "Arabia" (Nabataea)
    c. 36–47Visit to Jerusalem; work in Syria and Cilicia; Antioch
    c. 48–49Jerusalem meeting; Antioch incident
    c. 49–52Mission in Galatia, Macedonia (Philippi, Thessalonica) and Greece (Corinth); 1 Thessalonians, the earliest surviving Christian text (c. 50)
    c. 52–56Ephesus; Corinthian correspondence; Galatians; Philippians (date debated)
    c. 56–57Romans, from Corinth; collection for Jerusalem
    c. 57–60Arrest in Jerusalem; custody at Caesarea
    c. 60–62Voyage to Rome; house arrest (end of Acts)
    c. 62–67Death in Rome under Nero (tradition; see ch. 6)

    Which letters did Paul write?

    • Undisputed (seven): Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon.
    • Disputed: 2 Thessalonians, Colossians and Ephesians. Scholars are divided, with Ephesians most often judged pseudonymous.2
    • The Pastorals (1–2 Timothy, Titus) are judged by a majority of critical scholars to be by a later follower. They are defended as Pauline by others, and taught as such in much traditional Christian teaching.
    • Hebrews is anonymous. Its Pauline attribution was doubted in antiquity (Origen, quoted in Eusebius, HE 6.25).

    Paul's theology centred on the crucified and risen Christ; justification by faith, not by "works of the law"; the Church as the "body of Christ"; the Spirit; and the expectation of Christ's coming. It became central for every later tradition. It was read in very different ways: by Augustine, by Luther, and by the "New Perspective on Paul" (from E. P. Sanders, 1977), which re-examined what Paul meant by "works of the law".3

    Notes

    Volume II · Chapter 6

    The deaths of James, Peter and Paul

    • James son of Zebedee was executed by Herod Agrippa I c. 44 (Acts 12:2).
    • James the brother of Jesus was killed in 62, during an interregnum between Roman governors, on the initiative of the high priest Ananus:

      …[he] brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others; and when he had formed an accusation against them as breakers of the law, he delivered them to be stoned…

      Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 20.9.1 (20.200). Trans. Whiston. The central phrase was checked; the remainder follows the same translation. Q44 · partly checked
      Hegesippus (2nd century, in Eusebius HE 2.23) gives a later, more legendary account.1
    • Peter and Paul in Rome. The evidence and its assessment are given in Vol. VII ch. 1. The earliest text, 1 Clement 5 (c. 96), commemorates them as martyrs:

      Peter, through unrighteous envy, endured not one or two, but numerous labours and when he had at length suffered martyrdom, departed to the place of glory due to him.

      1 Clement 5.4. ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q48 · checked
      The tradition that Peter was crucified (upside down, in the later Acts of Peter) and Paul beheaded is later. The crucifixion is perhaps alluded to in John 21:18–19.2
    • Nero's persecution (64). After the great fire of Rome, Nero blamed Christians, whom Tacitus calls "a class hated for their abominations". Many were put to death cruelly in the imperial gardens (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). This is the first documented persecution by the Roman state. It was confined to Rome.3
    • John. Tradition, attested by Irenaeus, places John "the disciple of the Lord" at Ephesus until the reign of Trajan. Whether this John is the son of Zebedee, the author of the Gospel, the author of Revelation, or the "presbyter John" mentioned by Papias was already debated in antiquity (Eusebius, HE 3.39).
    • Other apostles. Traditions associate Thomas with India, Andrew with Scythia and Greece, Mark with Alexandria, and others with Ethiopia, Armenia and Persia. These traditions are mostly late and cannot be verified. They matter as foundation narratives of particular Churches (Vol. V ch. 1; VII.3).

    Notes

    Volume II · Chapter 7

    War, the Temple and the parting of the ways

    The Jewish revolt against Rome (66–73/74) ended with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple by Titus in AD 70. Josephus, who changed sides during the war, is the principal source.1 Later tradition (Eusebius, HE 3.5) says the Jerusalem Christians fled to Pella beyond the Jordan. Some scholars doubt this account.2

    Without the Temple, Judaism was reorganised around Torah study and the synagogue, under sages traditionally associated with Yavneh (Jamnia). This became rabbinic Judaism. A second revolt under Simon bar Kosiba ("Bar Kokhba", 132–135) led Hadrian to refound Jerusalem as the pagan colony Aelia Capitolina, which Jews were forbidden to enter.3 The Jerusalem Church thereafter had Gentile bishops (Eusebius, HE 4.6).

    How and when did Christianity and Judaism separate?

    Older accounts dated a decisive break to c. 85–90, citing a supposed "Council of Jamnia" that fixed the Hebrew canon, and the "Benediction against heretics" (Birkat ha-Minim) in the synagogue prayer, said to target Christians. Both points have been substantially revised.

    • There was no "Council of Jamnia" in the sense of a canonising council. The idea is a nineteenth-century construction.
    • The early form, date and targets of the Birkat ha-Minim are uncertain.
    • Recent scholarship (e.g. Daniel Boyarin, and the volume The Ways that Never Parted, 2003) stresses a long, regionally variable process. Boundaries were drawn by Christian and rabbinic authorities over the second to fourth centuries, and groups of "Jewish Christians" (Ebionites, Nazoraeans) persisted for centuries.4

    Christian polemic against Jews developed early: the "Adversus Iudaeos" tradition of the Epistle of Barnabas, Justin's Dialogue with Trypho, and Melito's Peri Pascha, with its charge that Israel killed God. This legacy is treated in Part IV, study H.

    Notes

    3. Cassius Dio, Roman History 69.12–14; Eusebius, Church History 4.6. ↩
    4. Boyarin 2004; Becker & Reed 2003. ↩

    Volume II · Chapter 8

    Worship and ministry in the earliest communities

    Worship

    Early Christians met in households (Rom. 16:5; 1 Cor. 16:19).1 Their worship included:

    • Baptism "in the name of Jesus" or in the threefold name (Matt. 28:19). The Didache prescribes it:

      …baptize into the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in living water. But if thou have not living water, baptize into other water; and if thou canst not in cold, in warm.

      Didache 7.1–2 (late 1st or early 2nd century; date debated). ANF 7 (1886). Checked. Q51 · checked
    • The Lord's Supper / Eucharist, linked to a community meal (1 Cor. 11:17–34). The Didache gives the oldest surviving Eucharistic prayers (Vol. III ch. 8).
    • Meeting on "the first day of the week", the "Lord's day" (1 Cor. 16:2; Rev. 1:10). Jewish believers probably continued to keep the Sabbath.
    • Prayer, Scripture, hymns and prophecy. Possible hymn fragments in Phil. 2:6–11 and Col. 1:15–20 show Christ honoured in worship within two decades of his death. Scholars such as Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham argue this "Christ-devotion" was an early development within Jewish monotheism.2

    Ministry

    The New Testament shows several kinds of leadership, without a single fixed structure.3

    • Paul lists "apostles, prophets, teachers" and gifts of healing and administration (1 Cor. 12:28).
    • Philippians greets "bishops (episkopoi) and deacons (diakonoi)" (Phil. 1:1).
    • Acts and the Pastorals speak of "elders" (presbyteroi), apparently overlapping with episkopoi (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7).
    • Women exercised leadership roles. Phoebe is a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Rom. 16:1). Prisca is Paul's co-worker. Junia is "of note among the apostles" (Rom. 16:7). Most scholars now read Junia as a woman's name, though the meaning of the phrase is debated.4

    How this plural pattern became a single bishop presiding over presbyters and deacons, the "threefold ministry", is traced in Vol. III ch. 8. The Catholic and Orthodox Churches teach that the episcopate is of apostolic institution, received through succession (). Many Protestant traditions regard church order as more flexible.

    Notes

    1. Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Philemon 2. On worship, see Bradshaw 2002. ↩
    2. Hurtado 2003; Bauckham 2008. ↩
    3. 1 Corinthians 12:28; Philippians 1:1; Acts 14:23 and 20:17–28; 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1:5–7. ↩
    4. Romans 16:7. See Dunn 1998, and the textual discussion in Metzger & Ehrman 2005. ↩

    Volume II · Chapter 9

    The New Testament: writing, transmission and canon

    Writing

    The 27 books of the New Testament were written between about 50 (1 Thessalonians) and the early second century. 2 Peter is often dated c. 100–130 and is the most widely judged pseudonymous. Other early Christian writings, such as 1 Clement, the Didache, Ignatius and the Shepherd of Hermas, were contemporary with the later New Testament books. Some of them were read in churches.

    Formation of the canon

    No single council created the Bible. Recognition of a fixed list of authoritative books was a process lasting several centuries.

    1. Early second century. Paul's letters circulated as a collection. 2 Peter 3:16 already refers to them alongside "the other scriptures".
    2. c. 140s. Marcion of Sinope rejected the Jewish scriptures and accepted only an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters. His challenge is often credited with prompting others to define the canon, a claim some scholars now consider overstated.
    3. c. 180. Irenaeus argued that there must be exactly four Gospels:

      It is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are. For, since there are four zones of the world in which we live, and four principal winds…

      Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.11.8. ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q57 · checked
    4. The Muratorian Fragment. A Latin list of New Testament books. It is traditionally dated to late second-century Rome, but some scholars (A. C. Sundberg, G. M. Hahneman) argue for the fourth-century East.1
    5. Early fourth century. Eusebius sorted books into "acknowledged", "disputed" (James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John) and "spurious", with Revelation placed uncertainly (HE 3.25). On 2 Peter, he reports that it was not considered canonical but "has appeared profitable to many" (HE 3.3.1).
    6. 367. Athanasius' Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter is the first known list of exactly the 27 books now accepted:

      These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone is proclaimed the doctrine of godliness. Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.

      Athanasius, Festal Letter 39.6 (367). NPNF II/4 (1892). Checked. Q58 · checked
    7. Late fourth and early fifth centuries. Western regional councils (Hippo 393; Carthage 397 and 419) and Roman lists confirmed the 27 books. In the East, Revelation remained disputed for centuries. The Syriac Peshitta has 22 books, omitting 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation. The Ethiopian Church has a broader canon.

    The Council of Nicaea (325) did not discuss the canon (Misconceptions).

    The Old Testament canons

    Early Christians used the Septuagint, which included books not in the later rabbinic Hebrew canon: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees, and additions to Esther and Daniel. Jerome preferred the Hebrew canon and called the rest "apocrypha". Augustine and the African councils accepted them. The divergence was formalised in the sixteenth century. The Council of Trent (1546) defined the Catholic list, including the "deuterocanonical" books. Protestant Churches adopted the Hebrew canon, with Luther placing the other books in a separate section. Orthodox Churches accept a broader list with some variation between them. The Ethiopian canon is the broadest. Volume XI covers the Reformation debate in full.

    Manuscripts and textual variants

    The New Testament survives in more than 5,000 Greek manuscripts, along with early translations (Latin, Syriac, Coptic) and quotations by Church Fathers. The earliest are papyrus fragments:

    • P52 (a fragment of John) was traditionally dated c. 125–150. Recent palaeographers allow a later second- or even third-century date.2
    • Substantial papyri such as P46 (Pauline letters) and P66 and P75 (John, Luke) are usually dated c. 200–250.
    • The first complete New Testaments are the fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.

    Most textual variants are minor. A few affect whole passages:

    • The "longer ending" of Mark (16:9–20) is absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.
    • The story of the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest manuscripts.
    • The Trinitarian "Johannine Comma" (1 John 5:7–8) is a late Latin addition.

    Modern critical editions (Nestle-Aland, UBS) reconstruct the earliest attainable text.

    Non-canonical writings

    Many other gospels, acts and apocalypses circulated. They include the Protevangelium of James (2nd century, the source of the names of Mary's parents), the Gospel of Peter, the Acts of Paul and Thecla, and the texts found at Nag Hammadi in 1945, such as the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of Truth. The Gospel of Judas (Codex Tchacos) was published in 2006. Some apocryphal texts shaped later piety and art. Others were associated with groups the emerging mainstream rejected (Vol. III ch. 4).

    Notes

    1. Hahneman 1992; for the canon process generally, Metzger 1987. ↩
    2. Nongbri 2005; Metzger & Ehrman 2005. ↩

    Volume III · c. 100–313

    Early Christianity and the Church Fathers

    Between the death of the apostles and Constantine, Christianity grew from scattered house-churches into an empire-wide network of communities. They were led by bishops, read a recognisable body of scriptures, defined themselves against rival interpretations, and had produced a learned literature in Greek, Latin and Syriac. They did all this without state support, and at times under state persecution. This volume traces how.

    In this volume

    1. The Apostolic Fathers
    2. Persecution and martyrdom (c. 100–311)
    3. The Apologists
    4. Marcion, “Gnosticism” and Montanism
    5. Irenaeus: rule of faith, Scripture and succession
    6. Tertullian, Clement and Origen
    7. Monarchianism and the Logos
    8. Ministry and worship: from Ignatius to Cyprian
    9. The beginnings of asceticism
    10. Beyond the Greco-Roman centres
    11. How the Church was organised before 313

    Volume III · Chapter 1

    The Apostolic Fathers

    "Apostolic Fathers" is a seventeenth-century label for the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, whose authors were thought to have known the apostles. The collection is conventional, not ancient.1

    TextDate (approx.)Content and significance
    1 Clementc. 96 (some argue c. 70)Letter from the Roman church to Corinth about deposed presbyters. Cites Peter and Paul's martyrdom. Speaks of apostles appointing "bishops and deacons" and arranging for succession (chs. 42–44). See VII.1.
    Ignatius of Antioch, seven lettersc. 105–115 (some argue later)Written on the way to martyrdom in Rome. The first clear evidence of a single bishop with presbyters and deacons in each church, and the first use of "catholic Church". Authenticity of the "middle recension" is accepted by most scholars and challenged by a minority.2
    Polycarp, To the Philippiansc. 110–140Bishop of Smyrna and, per Irenaeus, a disciple of John.
    Martyrdom of Polycarpc. 155–160 (date of death debated, c. 155–167)Earliest Christian martyr-account outside the New Testament; earliest evidence for annual commemoration at a martyr's tomb.
    Didachelate 1st – early 2nd c.Church manual: "two ways" ethics, baptism, fasting, Eucharistic prayers, itinerant prophets, local bishops and deacons. Rediscovered in 1873.
    Shepherd of Hermasc. 100–150, RomeVisions about repentance after baptism. Read as Scripture in some churches.
    Epistle of Barnabasc. 96–135Allegorical reading of the Old Testament against Jewish interpretation.
    Papias, fragmentsc. 110–130Traditions about the origins of Mark and Matthew (II.1).
    Epistle to Diognetus2nd–3rd c.Apologetic. Christians are like the soul in the body of the world.

    Ignatius' letters are crucial for the history of church order. He urges unity around the bishop:

    Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.

    Ignatius, To the Smyrnaeans 8.2 (c. 110). Trans. Roberts and Donaldson, ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q49 · checked

    "Catholic" (katholikē) here means "whole" or "universal", not yet a denominational name (Glossary: catholic). Ignatius' strong episcopal language may reflect his ideal more than the universal reality. His letter to Rome, notably, mentions no bishop there (VII.1).3

    Notes

    1. Texts and translations: Holmes 2007; public-domain translations in ANF, vols. 1 and 7. ↩
    2. The classic defence is Lightfoot 1885; Theodor Zahn's edition (1873) reached the same conclusion. Texts and introduction in Holmes 2007. ↩
    3. Ignatius, Romans, inscription and 3.1 (Holmes 2007). See Lampe 2003 and Brent 1995. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 2

    Persecution and martyrdom (c. 100–311)

    Popular imagination pictures the early Christians in hiding, under constant persecution. The evidence shows something different: long periods of local tolerance, broken by local outbreaks of violence and, after 250, by a few empire-wide campaigns.

    The legal position

    Around 112, Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia-Pontus, asked the emperor Trajan how to treat people accused of being Christians. Trajan's reply set the pattern for over a century. Christians were not to be hunted out, and anonymous accusations were to be ignored. Those formally accused who refused to sacrifice to the gods and the emperor's image were to be punished, but those who recanted were to be pardoned (Pliny, Ep. 10.96–97). Being a Christian was thus punishable "for the name" itself, yet not actively pursued.1 Why Christians were hated is a separate question. They refused to honour the gods on whom civic welfare depended, which made them "atheists". Rumours spread of incest and cannibalism, distortions of the "love-feast" and the Eucharist. They were also a new, unregistered association.

    Principal episodes

    • c. 155–167: Polycarp at Smyrna.

      Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?

      Martyrdom of Polycarp 9.3. ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q54 · checked
    • c. 165: Justin Martyr and companions at Rome. Their trial record (Acta Iustini) survives in several recensions.
    • 177: Lyons and Vienne, in a letter preserved in Eusebius, HE 5.1.
    • 180: The Scillitan martyrs of North Africa. Their trial record is the earliest dated Christian document in Latin.
    • 203: Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage, whose Passion contains Perpetua's own prison diary. This is one of the earliest surviving texts by a Christian woman.
    • 250–251, Decius. The first empire-wide requirement for all inhabitants to sacrifice. Certificates (libelli) on papyrus survive from Egypt. Many Christians complied or bought certificates. Bishop Fabian of Rome was executed.2
    • 257–260, Valerian. Measures targeting clergy and Christian property. Cyprian of Carthage (258) and Sixtus II of Rome were executed. Gallienus ended the persecution in 260.
    • 303–311, the Great Persecution. See IV.1.

    The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.

    Tertullian, Apology 50.13 (197). Trans. S. Thelwall, ANF 3 (1885). Checked. The popular form “the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church” is a later paraphrase. Q55 · checked
    Scholarly debate: how many martyrs?

    No reliable total exists. Later martyrologies multiplied numbers and invented stories. Modern estimates for the whole pre-Constantinian period range from the low thousands to a few tens of thousands. Candida Moss (2013) argued that many martyr narratives were later inventions and that systematic persecution was rarer than often supposed. Her critics accept the source-critical point but stress the reality and trauma of the persecutions under Decius, Valerian and Diocletian.3

    Persecution shaped Christianity beyond the deaths it caused. It produced the cult of martyrs, their tombs and their anniversaries. It made "confessors" who had survived torture into authorities. And it raised the divisive question of how to treat the "lapsed", which produced the Novatianist (251) and Donatist schisms (ch. 8; IV.4).

    Notes

    1. Pliny, Letters 10.96–97 (Trajan's reply). See Frend 1965. ↩
    2. The surviving Egyptian libelli are collected in Knipfing 1923. On the decree, see Rives 1999; Cyprian, On the Lapsed (ANF, vol. 5). ↩
    3. Moss 2013; Frend 1965; Lane Fox 1986, chs. 9–10. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 3

    The Apologists

    From the reign of Hadrian, educated Christians addressed "apologies" (defences) to emperors and the public.1 Major writers include:

    • Quadratus and Aristides (c. 125–140), in Athens;
    • Justin Martyr (First and Second Apology, c. 150–155; Dialogue with Trypho), a convert from Platonism teaching in Rome;
    • Tatian (Oration to the Greeks; and the Diatessaron, a harmony of the four Gospels, influential in Syriac Christianity);
    • Athenagoras of Athens (c. 177);
    • Theophilus of Antioch (c. 180), who first used the Greek trias of God, his Word and his Wisdom;
    • Minucius Felix and Tertullian in Latin.

    The apologists answered the charges of atheism, immorality and disloyalty. They argued that Christianity was the true philosophy and the fulfilment of Hebrew prophecy, older than the Greek thinkers. Justin developed the idea of the Logos spermatikos, the "seed-bearing Word": whatever truth the philosophers had spoken came from the Logos who became incarnate in Christ (2 Apology 13).

    Justin also gives the earliest detailed description of Christian Sunday worship:

    And on the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things.

    Justin Martyr, First Apology 67.3–4 (c. 155). ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q52 · checked

    Note "the president" (proestōs), the person who presides, as opposed to the reader. Scholars debate whether Justin means a bishop in the later sense.2

    Notes

    1. Justin Martyr, 1 Apology 1 (address to Antoninus Pius) (ANF, vol. 1). ↩
    2. Justin, 1 Apology 65–67, which describes the president (proestōs) of the assembly. See Lampe 2003 and Bradshaw 2002. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 4

    Marcion, “Gnosticism” and Montanism

    Second-century Christianity was diverse. Several movements offered interpretations that the majority of churches eventually rejected. Their rejection helped define what became "orthodoxy". Walter Bauer's influential thesis (1934) held that "heresy" often preceded "orthodoxy" in particular regions. It has been heavily criticised in its details, but it changed the way historians approach the question.1

    Marcion

    Marcion, a shipowner from Sinope, broke with the Roman church c. 144. He taught that the God of the Old Testament, a just but harsh creator, was a different being from the good Father revealed by Jesus. He rejected the Jewish scriptures and accepted a single Gospel, an edited Luke, and ten Pauline letters. His church spread widely and lasted for centuries in the East. Our knowledge comes mainly from opponents, above all Tertullian's five books Against Marcion.

    “Gnosticism”

    Church writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus described many teachers: Basilides, Valentinus (in Rome c. 140–160) and his followers Ptolemy and Heracleon, the "Sethians", and others. These teachers offered secret knowledge (gnōsis) of the soul's divine origin and its escape from a material world made by an ignorant or hostile lesser god (the demiurge). The discovery in 1945 of the Nag Hammadi codices, thirteen Coptic books of the fourth century, allowed these traditions to be read in their own words for the first time.

    Recent scholarship questions whether "Gnosticism" names a coherent religion. Michael A. Williams argued it should be "dismantled" as a category (1996). Karen King argued that the term is a construction of modern and ancient polemic (2003). Others, such as David Brakke, prefer to speak of a specific "Gnostic school".2 This edition therefore uses the term cautiously.

    Montanism (“the New Prophecy”)

    Beginning in Phrygia c. 160s–170s, the prophet Montanus and the prophetesses Prisca (Priscilla) and Maximilla proclaimed new revelations of the Paraclete (the Holy Spirit). They called for rigorous fasting and discipline and for readiness for martyrdom. Asian synods condemned the movement. It was probably among the first occasions for synods of bishops (ch. 11). Tertullian joined a rigorist party sympathetic to the New Prophecy later in life, though whether he formally left the Catholic church is debated. The movement raised a question that would recur: is the Spirit's authority found in prophecy, or in Scripture and the episcopal office?

    Notes

    1. Bauer 1971. ↩
    2. Williams 1996; King 2003; Brakke 2010. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 5

    Irenaeus: rule of faith, Scripture and succession

    Irenaeus came from Asia Minor and in his youth heard Polycarp. He became bishop of Lyons after the persecution of 177. His Against Heresies (c. 180) is the first comprehensive refutation of Valentinian and other teachers. It set out three criteria that became fundamental to later Christianity.

    1. The rule of faith (regula fidei, Greek kanōn tēs alētheias): a summary of belief in one God the Creator, in Christ incarnate for our salvation, and in the Holy Spirit, held by the churches everywhere (AH 1.10.1). It is a forerunner of the creeds.1
    2. The Scriptures of both Testaments, including exactly four Gospels (Q57).
    3. Apostolic succession. The public succession of bishops in churches founded by apostles guarantees that their teaching is the apostles' teaching, in contrast to teachers who claimed secret traditions. Rome serves as his model example (Q28; see VII.1).

    Irenaeus' theology of "recapitulation" held that Christ sums up and restores the whole of human history in himself. This became a lasting resource for Eastern and Western theology. In the Quartodeciman dispute he also mediated against Victor of Rome (VII.1).2

    Notes

    1. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.10.1 and 3.3–4 (ANF, vol. 1). See Kelly 1972. ↩
    2. Eusebius, Church History 5.23–24 (NPNF II/1). ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 6

    Tertullian, Clement and Origen

    Tertullian and Latin theology

    Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160–c. 225) was the first major Christian author in Latin. He coined or popularised much of the West's theological vocabulary: trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum. In Against Praxeas (c. 213) he answered a teacher who identified the Father and Son:

    …which distributes the Unity into a Trinity, placing in their order the three Persons — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power, inasmuch as He is one God…

    Tertullian, Against Praxeas 2. Trans. Peter Holmes, ANF 3 (1885). Checked. Q56 · checked

    The formula "one substance, three persons" anticipates later orthodoxy. However, Tertullian's thought also contains subordinationist elements, which judged by fourth-century standards would be inadequate. This shows that the doctrine of the Trinity developed over time, without being "invented" at any single moment (Misconceptions).

    Alexandria: Clement and Origen

    Alexandria had a tradition of Christian teaching that came under episcopal supervision by about 200. Its relation to the bishop is debated.1 Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215) presented Christianity as the true gnōsis and philosophy as a preparation for the Gospel.

    Origen (c. 185–c. 254) was the greatest scholar of the early Church. His works include:

    • the Hexapla, a six-column comparison of the Hebrew Old Testament and its Greek translations;
    • commentaries and homilies on most of Scripture;
    • On First Principles, the first systematic theology;
    • Against Celsus, a reply to a pagan critic.

    His preface to On First Principles distinguishes the "apostolic teaching" held by the Churches from questions left open to inquiry. He then explores speculative answers: the pre-existence of souls, and the possible final restoration of all things (apokatastasis).

    Origen fell out with Bishop Demetrius of Alexandria, who objected to his ordination as presbyter in Palestine. He moved to Caesarea (c. 231–234) and died after torture under Decius. His legacy was immense: both Arius and Athanasius, and the Cappadocians, drew on him. But some of his ideas, or those of later "Origenists", were condemned in 400, 543 and 553 (VI.5). Modern scholarship stresses the gap between Origen's exploratory theology and the later Origenism that was condemned.2

    Notes

    1. Eusebius, Church History 6.3 and 6.19 (NPNF II/1). ↩
    2. The fifteen anathemas against Origenism (543 and 553) are translated in Price 2009. See Kelly 1977. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 7

    Monarchianism and the Logos

    How can there be one God, the "monarchy" (single rule), if the Son is also God? Two "monarchian" answers, later rejected, prepared the ground for the fourth-century debates.1

    • Modalism ("Sabellianism", "Patripassianism"): Father, Son and Spirit are names or modes of one divine person, so that "the Father suffered". Noetus of Smyrna, Praxeas and Sabellius taught versions of this in Rome c. 190–220.

      He alleged that Christ was the Father Himself, and that the Father Himself was born, and suffered, and died.

      Hippolytus, Against Noetus 1 (early 3rd century; attribution debated). ANF 5 (1886). Opening of the sentence checked; its continuation is quoted from the same text. Q59 · checked
    • Adoptionism ("dynamic monarchianism"): Jesus was a man empowered by God. It was taught by Theodotus "the cobbler" in Rome (c. 190). Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, was deposed in 268 by a synod for teaching a related view. The synod also reportedly rejected the term homoousios in his sense, which later complicated its use at Nicaea (IV.6).

    Against both, theologians developed a "Logos theology". The Word, distinct from the Father, was generated for creation and revelation. This affirmed distinction, but often ranked the Son below the Father. In Rome, Hippolytus accused bishops Zephyrinus and Callistus of modalism and appears to have led a rival community. The authorship of the works under his name, including the Apostolic Tradition, is now much debated.2 In the 260s the "affair of the two Dionysii", bishops of Rome and Alexandria, showed that East and West already had different worries: Rome feared tritheism, Alexandria feared modalism.3

    Notes

    1. Tertullian, Against Praxeas; Hippolytus, Against Noetus (ANF, vols. 3 and 5). See Kelly 1977. ↩
    2. Brent 1995; Bradshaw, Johnson & Phillips 2002. ↩
    3. Athanasius, On the Opinion of Dionysius (NPNF II/4). See Hanson 1988. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 8

    Ministry and worship: from Ignatius to Cyprian

    The threefold ministry

    By the late second century, almost every church known to us had a single bishop, with presbyters and deacons. How this happened is debated. Three explanations have been offered:

    • Bishops emerged as presidents of presbyteral colleges, at different speeds in different places. Ignatius' Asia was early, Rome and perhaps Alexandria later.
    • The apostles directly appointed single bishops.
    • The pattern was a response to the need for unity against division.

    Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the episcopate is of apostolic and divine institution (). Historians agree that by Irenaeus (c. 180) the churches understood their bishops as successors of the apostles.

    Other ministries developed alongside. Readers and subdeacons are listed at Rome c. 251, when Bishop Cornelius counted 46 presbyters, 7 deacons, 7 subdeacons, 42 acolytes and 52 exorcists, readers and doorkeepers, with over 1,500 widows and poor supported (Eusebius, HE 6.43.11). There was also an order of widows, and in the East deaconesses (the Didascalia, 3rd century).

    Cyprian and the unity of the episcopate

    Cyprian, bishop of Carthage (248/9–258), faced two crises: how to readmit those who lapsed under Decius, and the rival Roman bishop Novatian, who refused readmission and founded a rigorist church. Cyprian's On the Unity of the Church (251) taught that "the episcopate is one, each part of which is held by each one for the whole" (De unit. 5)1. There is no salvation outside the Church: "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother" (De unit. 6, ANF 5; register Q62). His conflict with Stephen of Rome over heretical baptism is discussed in VII.1.

    Worship

    The Didache preserves early Eucharistic prayers:

    Now concerning the Thanksgiving (Eucharist), thus give thanks. First, concerning the cup: We thank thee, our Father, for the holy vine of David Thy servant, which Thou madest known to us through Jesus Thy Servant; to Thee be the glory for ever.

    Didache 9.1–2. ANF 7 (1886). Checked. Q50 · checked

    Justin (c. 155) describes the Eucharist as something received "not as common bread and common drink", but as "the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh" (1 Apol. 66; Q53). The text is quoted in Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran arguments for Christ's real presence, and read differently by some Reformed scholars.

    For not as common bread and common drink do we receive these; but in like manner as Jesus Christ our Saviour, having been made flesh by the Word of God, had both flesh and blood for our salvation, so likewise have we been taught that the food which is blessed by the prayer of His word … is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh.

    Justin Martyr, First Apology 66.2 (c. 155). ANF 1 (1885). Checked; the ellipsis omits a clause. Q53 · checked

    Other developments in this period :

    • Infant baptism is attested by c. 200. Tertullian argued against it (On Baptism 18); Origen called it apostolic tradition.
    • Initiation came to involve a long catechumenate, renunciation of Satan, threefold immersion with a creedal questioning, anointing and laying on of hands. Its fullest description is in the Apostolic Tradition, whose date, origin and attribution to Hippolytus are debated.2
    • The earliest securely identified church building is the house-church at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates. It was adapted c. 232/233, with a baptistery decorated with paintings, and buried in 256.
    • Easter was the great feast. Its date was disputed (the Quartodeciman controversy), and it became the main time for baptism.

    Notes

    1. Cyprian, De unitate 5–6; ANF 5. On the two versions of ch. 4, see Bevenot 1938 and VII.1. ↩
    2. Bradshaw 2002, chs. 4–5. ↩
