    Volume III · Chapter 9

    The beginnings of asceticism

    Celibacy "for the kingdom" and voluntary poverty were present from the beginning (Matt. 19:12; 1 Cor. 7). By the second and third centuries the following forms are attested :

    • Consecrated virgins and widows living in their families or communities, addressed by Tertullian and Cyprian.1
    • In Syria, the "Encratites" made celibacy a condition of baptism, a view associated with Tatian. The bnay and bnāt qyāmā (sons and daughters of the covenant), described in the fourth century by Aphrahat, had probably earlier roots.2
    • Origen's demanding asceticism, and the Acts of Thomas and Acts of Paul and Thecla, which celebrate renunciation of marriage.
    • By the 270s, individuals were withdrawing to the edges of Egyptian villages and then to the desert. Antony's withdrawal (c. 270–285) is the best-known example (IV.10).3

    Peter Brown's The Body and Society (1988) remains the classic account4 of how sexual renunciation became a defining Christian ideal and a source of authority.

    Notes

    1. Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins; Cyprian, On the Dress of Virgins (ANF, vols. 4–5). ↩
    2. Aphrahat, Demonstrations 6 (NPNF II/13). See Brown 1988. ↩
    3. Athanasius, Life of Antony (NPNF II/4); Harmless 2004. ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 10

    Beyond the Greco-Roman centres

    Syria and Edessa

    Edessa (Urhay) became the centre of Syriac-speaking Christianity. The legend of King Abgar's correspondence with Jesus (Eusebius, HE 1.13; the Doctrine of Addai) is legendary. A Christian church at Edessa is recorded in a flood of 201, and the philosopher Bardaisan (d. 222) wrote at the royal court. Tatian's Diatessaron was the Syriac churches' gospel until the fifth century. Early Syriac poetry (Odes of Solomon) shows a distinctive, Semitic Christianity.

    Mesopotamia and Persia

    Christian communities in Adiabene and Mesopotamia by the late second or third century; Roman captives deported by Shapur I. Mani (216–274/277), founder of Manichaeism, grew up in a Jewish-Christian baptist sect (the Elchasaites). See V.1.

    Egypt

    Early evidence is scanty until Bishop Demetrius (189–231/2), though Christian papyri from Oxyrhynchus and elsewhere attest to Christians from the 2nd century. Coptic translations of Scripture had appeared by the 3rd century.1

    North Africa

    Latin Christianity's first centre: the Scillitan martyrs (180), Tertullian and Cyprian. Councils at Carthage gathered dozens of bishops; in 256, 87 bishops were present.2 The density of African sees, several hundred by 300, was unique.

    Armenia and the Caucasus

    Royal conversion under Tiridates III through Gregory the Illuminator, traditionally 301, often dated c. 314 by historians. Georgia followed in the 330s (V.2).

    Gaul, Spain and Britain

    Lyons and Vienne (177). Spanish bishops at the Council of Elvira (date debated, c. 300–314). Three British bishops at Arles (314).3

    Notes

    1. On Demetrius, Eusebius, Church History 6.2–8 (NPNF II/1); Davis 2004. ↩
    2. Cyprian, Sententiae episcoporum (ANF, vol. 5). See Shaw 2011. ↩
    3. The subscriptions of Arles are edited in Charles Munier, Concilia Galliae A. 314–A. 506, CCSL 148 (Turnhout: Brepols, 1963). ↩

    Volume III · Chapter 11

    How the Church was organised before 313

    By Constantine's time the Church already had a recognisable institutional structure, developed without state support.1

    • Synods. Bishops met in councils to handle common problems: the New Prophecy (Asia, 170s), the date of Easter (c. 190, across several regions, Eusebius HE 5.23), the lapsed (Carthage and Rome, 251), rebaptism (Carthage, 255–256), and Paul of Samosata (Antioch, 268). These meetings are the direct ancestors of the councils of Volume VI.
    • Regional hierarchy. Bishops of major cities (Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Carthage) exercised informal leadership over wider regions. Nicaea canon 6 later called this "ancient custom" (VII.2).
    • Communication. Letters of communion and peace allowed Christians to travel and be received. Bishops informed each other of their election.
    • Property. Churches owned cemeteries and buildings. Gallienus' restitution (260) and Aurelian's ruling in the Paul of Samosata case (272) show that the state recognised Christian corporate property. Aurelian ordered the church building "to be given to those to whom the bishops of Italy and of the city of Rome should adjudge it" (Eusebius, HE 7.30.19, NPNF II/1).
    • Charity. Organised care for widows, orphans, the sick, prisoners and the dead, as in Rome in 251 (ch. 8). Pagan observers, including the emperor Julian a century later, remarked on it.
    • Size. Christians were perhaps a tenth of the empire's population by 300, unevenly distributed. This is an estimate, not a count (IV.1).2

    This is the Church Constantine encountered in 312: organised, divided by its own disputes, and practised in settling them through bishops in council. Volume IV continues the story.

    Notes

    1. Lampe 2003; Hopkins 1998. ↩
    2. Hopkins 1998; Stark 1996, ch. 1, whose model is debated. ↩

    Volume IV · c. 303–451

    Constantine and the Imperial Church

    In 303 the Roman state launched its most systematic attempt to suppress Christianity. Within ten years an emperor had declared himself the Christians' patron. Within eighty, a law required his subjects to follow the faith defined at Nicaea. This volume traces that transformation and the theological controversies it produced and shaped: over the divinity of the Son, the status of the Holy Spirit, and the unity of God and humanity in Christ.

    In this volume

    1. The Great Persecution and its end (303–311)
    2. Constantine’s conversion
    3. The so-called Edict of Milan (313)
    4. The Donatist controversy
    5. Arius and the outbreak of the controversy
    6. The road to Nicaea and the Creed of 325
    7. After Nicaea: Athanasius and the parties (325–361)
    8. The Cappadocians and the language of the Trinity
    9. Theodosius, 380–381, and the Nicene settlement
    10. The rise of monasticism
    11. Nestorius, Cyril, and Ephesus (428–433)
    12. From Eutyches to Chalcedon (448–451)
    13. Key Greek terms: ousia, hypostasis, physis, prosopon, homoousios, Theotokos

    The councils of this period are treated narratively here. The full eleven-point analysis of each ecumenical council (context, participants, politics, theology, arguments, decisions, reception, consequences, sources, controversies, legacy) is in Volume VI.

    Volume IV · Chapter 1

    The Great Persecution and its end (303–311)

    By 300, Christians were a substantial minority in the Roman Empire, more numerous in the Greek-speaking East and North Africa than in the Latin West. Precise figures are impossible. Estimates that are often cited (around 10 per cent of the population, perhaps five to six million people) come from modelling rather than counts, and should be treated as orders of magnitude.1

    Persecution before 303 had been intermittent and mostly local. The empire-wide measures of Decius (250) and Valerian (257–260) were the main exceptions. After Valerian's capture by the Persians, his son Gallienus restored confiscated property, and the Church enjoyed some forty years of de facto toleration. In this period churches were built openly, Christians served at court and in the army, and bishops held property recognised by the state.2

    The four edicts

    Beginning in February 303, the tetrarchic government of Diocletian and his co-emperors issued a series of measures:

    1. February 303: churches were to be destroyed, scriptures surrendered and burned, and Christians of rank stripped of privileges. The church at Nicomedia, visible from the palace, was demolished on 23 February.
    2. Later in 303: clergy were to be imprisoned.
    3. Late 303: imprisoned clergy were to be released if they sacrificed, and compelled to if they refused.
    4. Early 304: a general order for all inhabitants to sacrifice, attested mainly for the East.

    Our main narrative sources are Lactantius, a Christian rhetorician at Nicomedia, and Eusebius of Caesarea, who witnessed the persecution in Palestine. Both wrote as partisans, after the persecutors had fallen.3 Enforcement was uneven. In the West, where Constantius (Constantine's father) governed Gaul and Britain, it seems to have gone little further than destroying some buildings. In Egypt, Palestine and the eastern provinces under Galerius and later Maximinus Daia, it was severe and prolonged.

    The persecution left lasting divisions inside the Church as well as martyrs. Christians who had handed over scriptures (traditores) or sacrificed (lapsi) had to be dealt with when it ended. In North Africa this question produced the Donatist schism, and in Egypt the Melitian schism, which the Council of Nicaea later addressed.

    Galerius’ edict of toleration (311)

    The persecution was ended not by Constantine but by its chief architect. Mortally ill, Galerius issued an edict in April 311, in his own name and those of his co-emperors. It conceded that the attempt to bring Christians back to ancestral religion had failed. It permitted them to "exist again" and rebuild their meeting places, provided they did nothing contrary to public order, and asked them to pray for the emperors' safety.4 Galerius died days later. In the East, Maximinus Daia resumed pressure on Christians until his defeat by Licinius in 313.

    Key takeaways

    • Legal toleration of Christianity (311) came before Constantine's patronage and was not his invention.
    • How severe the "Great Persecution" was depended greatly on region and ruler.
    • Its aftermath (what to do with those who had lapsed) shaped church divisions for a century.

    Notes

    1. For the method and its limits, see Stark 1996, ch. 1, and the critical discussion in Hopkins 1998. These figures are estimates, not data. ↩
    2. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 7.13 (Gallienus' rescript) and 8.1 (the prosperity before 303). ↩
    3. Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 10–15; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 8.2–6 and Martyrs of Palestine. On the edicts and their uneven enforcement, see Barnes 1981, chs. 2 and 9. ↩
    4. Text in Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 34, and in Greek translation in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 8.17. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 2

    Constantine’s conversion

    Constantine was acclaimed emperor by his father's army at York in 306. In 312 he invaded Italy against Maxentius, who held Rome, and defeated him at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October.1 Two Christian authors, both close to the events, describe a divine sign before the battle. Their accounts differ in ways that matter.

    Constantine was directed in a dream to cause the heavenly sign to be delineated on the shields of his soldiers, and so to proceed to battle. He did as he had been commanded, and he marked on their shields the letter X, with a perpendicular line drawn through it and turned round thus at the top, being the cipher of Christ.

    Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 44.5, written c. 314–315. Trans. William Fletcher, ANF 7 (1886). Q01 · checked

    He said that about noon, when the day was already beginning to decline, he saw with his own eyes the trophy of a cross of light in the heavens, above the sun, and bearing the inscription, Conquer by this.

    Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.28, written after Constantine’s death in 337. Trans. E. C. Richardson, NPNF II/1 (1890). Q02 · checked

    Lactantius, writing within about three years, describes a dream on the eve of battle and a monogram painted on shields. Eusebius, writing a quarter-century later, describes a daytime vision seen by the whole army, followed by a dream and the making of the labarum standard. He says Constantine told him this himself "long after" and confirmed it with oaths. Notably, Eusebius did not mention the vision in his Ecclesiastical History, which he revised in the 310s and 320s.2

    Scholarly debate: what happened in 312?

    Historians broadly agree that by late 312 Constantine publicly identified his victory with the Christian God. They disagree about the nature and timing of his personal religious change.

    • Early, sincere conversion. Timothy Barnes argues that Constantine was a committed Christian from 312 and pursued an increasingly Christian policy, including restrictions on sacrifice.3
    • Gradual or syncretic development. Others stress continued solar imagery (Sol Invictus on coins until the early 320s) and the ambiguous wording of the Arch of Constantine (315), which credits victory to "the prompting of the divinity" (instinctu divinitatis). They see a monotheist who moved towards Christianity over time.4
    • Policy of consensus. H. A. Drake reads Constantine's policy as aiming at a broad, inclusive monotheism that left room for non-Christians, with harsher measures mostly coming later.5
    • Natural phenomena. Some have proposed that a solar halo explains the vision Eusebius describes. This is a speculative attempt to explain a later account, not established fact.

    Constantine was baptised only on his deathbed in May 337, by Eusebius of Nicomedia. Deferring baptism was common at the time and does not by itself show insincerity.

    Imperial patronage

    Constantine's practical support for the Church is well documented:

    • restoration of confiscated property;
    • exemption of clergy from burdensome civic duties (from 313);
    • the right of bishops to arbitrate civil cases (episcopalis audientia);
    • Sunday as a legal day of rest (321);
    • lavish building programmes: the Lateran basilica in Rome, St Peter's on the Vatican hill, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem (dedicated 335).6

    Above all, Constantine treated church unity as a concern of the state. When Christians disputed, he summoned bishops to councils, paid their travel through the public post, and enforced their decisions with exile. This model of the emperor as convener and enforcer, though not formally the judge of doctrine, shaped every council in this volume.

    The idea that Constantine "made Christianity the state religion" or "decided the content of the Bible" is a modern misconception. See Common misconceptions. Christianity became the official religion only under Theodosius I, half a century later (ch. 9).

    Notes

    1. The date is given by Lactantius as the anniversary of Maxentius' accession, "the sixth of the kalends of November" (De mort. pers. 44.4). ↩
    2. Eusebius, Life of Constantine 1.28–31; compare Ecclesiastical History 9.9, which describes the battle without any vision. ↩
    3. Barnes 1981, chs. 3 and 13; Barnes 2011, chs. 4–6. ↩
    4. See the essays in Lenski 2006, especially those on religious policy and coinage. ↩
    5. Drake 2000, esp. chs. 5–7. ↩
    6. Codex Theodosianus 16.2.1–2 (clerical immunities); 2.8.1 (Sunday, 321); Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.25–40 (Holy Sepulchre). ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 3

    The so-called Edict of Milan (313)

    In February 313 Constantine and Licinius, who ruled the Balkans and would soon take the East, met at Milan. Licinius married Constantine's half-sister, and the two agreed a common religious policy. What is called the "Edict of Milan" was not an edict and was not issued at Milan. The surviving text is a letter of instruction to provincial governors that Licinius published in the East after defeating Maximinus Daia. Lactantius gives the Latin version as posted at Nicomedia in June 313; Eusebius gives a Greek version.1

    [We resolved] that the Christians and all others should have liberty to follow that mode of religion which to each of them appeared best.

    Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 48.2. Trans. William Fletcher, ANF 7 (1886). Opening words supplied in brackets. Q03 · checked

    The document is notable for its general principle of religious freedom, which extends explicitly to "all others", and for ordering that confiscated church property be restored to the Christian communities at state expense where necessary. It did not establish Christianity, end pagan worship or privilege the Church over other cults. Those developments came gradually over the next eighty years.

    Key takeaways

    • Not an edict, not from Milan: a Licinian letter of 313 recording a policy agreed at Milan.2
    • It granted toleration to all religions and restitution to Christians. It did not make Christianity the state religion.

    Notes

    1. Lactantius, De mort. pers. 48 (dated "the ides of June"); Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 10.5.2–14. The point that the "edict" is a Licinian rescript was made influentially by Otto Seeck (1891); see Barnes 1981, ch. 4, and Lenski 2006. ↩
    2. Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors 48 (Creed 1984); a Greek version in Eusebius, Church History 10.5. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 4

    The Donatist controversy

    The first church dispute that Constantine was asked to settle was not about the Trinity but about holiness and authority. In 311 or 312, Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage. His opponents claimed that one of his consecrators, Felix of Abthugni, had been a traditor who surrendered scriptures in the persecution. They argued that sacraments administered by such men were invalid, and that a Church tolerating them had ceased to be the true Church. A council of Numidian bishops elected a rival bishop, Maiorinus. He was soon succeeded by Donatus, whose name the movement took.1

    Both sides appealed to the emperor. Constantine referred the case to a synod under Bishop Miltiades of Rome (October 313), then to a larger council at Arles (1 August 314). Both found for Caecilian. Felix was later cleared by a civil inquiry. Arles also ruled that baptism given in the name of the Trinity was not to be repeated, even if given by heretics. This marked a divergence from the earlier African practice associated with Cyprian. After further appeals Constantine tried coercion (317–321), failed, and settled for toleration.

    The schism lasted more than a century. For much of the fourth century Donatists were probably the majority Church in Numidia. Augustine of Hippo became their most important opponent, developing a theology in which the Church is a "mixed body" of saints and sinners. In this theology the validity of a sacrament depends on Christ, not on the holiness of the minister. After an imperial conference at Carthage in 411 the Donatists were outlawed, and Augustine came, with misgivings, to justify state coercion against them. Recent scholarship stresses the violence on both sides and the deep regional roots of the dispute.2

    Why it matters

    • It set the pattern of rival Christian parties appealing to the emperor, and of the emperor acting through councils.
    • Augustine's answers on the Church and the sacraments became foundational in Western theology, and were invoked again at the Reformation.
    • It showed that "schism" (a break over order and communion) could be as divisive as "heresy" (a dispute over doctrine). See the glossary entries and .

    Notes

    1. The main sources are Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists (c. 365–385), and the documents Augustine collected; see Frend 1952 and Shaw 2011. ↩
    2. Shaw 2011, esp. chs. 1, 6 and 11. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 5

    Arius and the outbreak of the controversy

    Arius was a respected presbyter in charge of the Baucalis church in Alexandria. Around 318–321 (the exact date is disputed) he came into conflict with his bishop, Alexander, over how to describe the relation of the Son (the divine Word, Logos) to God the Father.1

    Arius' own words survive only in a few letters and in fragments of his poem Thalia quoted by hostile writers. His letter to Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, his most powerful supporter, preserves his position in his own voice:

    We are persecuted, because we say that the Son has a beginning, but that God is without beginning. This is the cause of our persecution, and likewise, because we say that He is of the non-existent.

    Arius, Letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, preserved in Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History 1.4. Trans. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF II/3 (1892). Q04 · checked

    Arius' concern was to protect the uniqueness and indivisibility of God the Father. For him the Son was the first and highest of God's works, the agent of creation, and "perfect God" in a derived sense. But he was brought into being by the Father's will. There was a time "when he was not", and he was not eternal in the way the Father is. Alexander, and later Athanasius, held that this made the Son a creature. A creature, they argued, could not reveal God or save humanity. If the Father is eternally Father, he must eternally have a Son.

    Scholarly debate: what was “Arianism”?

    Since the 1970s, scholarship has substantially revised the traditional picture.

    • Not a single system. R. P. C. Hanson and others showed that "Arianism" as a coherent party is largely a construction of its opponents, especially Athanasius. Arius was not the founder of a school, and most later "Arians" did not regard him as their teacher.2
    • A widespread theology. Rowan Williams situates Arius within Alexandrian philosophical theology. He argues that many bishops shared a broadly "subordinationist" view in which the Son is divine but ranked below the Father. To them Arius' clear-cut statements appeared not shocking but over-precise.3
    • A dispute about method. Lewis Ayres describes the century after 318 as a search for adequate terms. In that search, positions were refined and sometimes reversed, and the eventual "pro-Nicene" consensus of the 360s–380s was not simply a return to 325.4

    Hence modern specialists often avoid "Arian" as an umbrella term. Where they use it, it is shorthand for a range of non-Nicene theologies. This edition follows that practice.

    Alexander condemned Arius at an Egyptian synod. Arius found support from Eusebius of Nicomedia and from Eusebius of Caesarea, among others, and the dispute spread through the eastern episcopate. When Constantine defeated Licinius and took control of the East in 324, he found the Church there divided. He first sent his adviser Ossius (Hosius) of Córdoba with a letter treating the question as a trivial dispute over words. Ossius found otherwise. A synod at Antioch in early 325 condemned Arius' position and provisionally excommunicated Eusebius of Caesarea. The emperor then summoned a general council.5

    Notes

    1. For the chronology, see Williams 1987, part I, and Hanson 1988, ch. 5. Older accounts date the outbreak to 318; several modern scholars prefer c. 321. ↩
    2. Hanson 1988, chs. 1 and 4; Ayres 2004, introduction and chs. 1–4. ↩
    3. Williams 1987, parts II–III. ↩
    4. Ayres 2004, esp. chs. 4–6 and 11. ↩
    5. Constantine's letter to Alexander and Arius is in Eusebius, Life of Constantine 2.64–72. The Antioch synod of 325 is known from a Syriac letter first published by Eduard Schwartz in 1905, whose authenticity is now generally accepted; see Hanson 1988, ch. 6. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 6

    The road to Nicaea and the Creed of 325

    The council met at Nicaea in Bithynia (modern İznik), near the imperial residence at Nicomedia. It opened in early summer 325, traditionally 20 May, with Constantine presiding over at least the opening sessions. No minutes survive. What we know comes from the creed, twenty canons, a synodal letter to the Egyptian Church, letters of Constantine, and accounts by participants (Eusebius of Caesarea, Eustathius of Antioch, Athanasius) and by later historians.

    How many bishops?

    Eusebius, who was there, wrote that "the number of bishops exceeded two hundred and fifty".1 Athanasius later spoke of about 300. The figure of 318, which became canonical, appears from the 360s onwards (in Hilary of Poitiers and others) and was linked to the 318 servants of Abraham in Genesis 14:14. Socrates repeats it in the fifth century.2 Modern estimates usually fall between 250 and 300. Only a handful came from the Latin West: Ossius, two Roman presbyters representing Bishop Silvester, and a few others.

    The Creed

    We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten of his Father, of the substance of the Father, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance (ὁμοούσιον, consubstantialem) with the Father. By whom all things were made, both which be in heaven and in earth. Who for us men and for our salvation came down [from heaven] and was incarnate and was made man. He suffered and the third day he rose again, and ascended into heaven. And he shall come again to judge both the quick and the dead. And [we believe] in the Holy Ghost. And whosoever shall say that there was a time when the Son of God was not, or that before he was begotten he was not, or that he was made of things that were not, or that he is of a different substance or essence [from the Father] or that he is a creature, or subject to change or conversion — all that so say, the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes them.

    The Creed of Nicaea (325), as preserved in the acts of Ephesus and Chalcedon and in Eusebius, Athanasius, Socrates and Theodoret. Trans. H. R. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q05 · checked

    Three features deserve attention:

    • It is not the creed most Christians recite today. The "Nicene Creed" used in liturgy is the longer text associated with Constantinople (381) (ch. 9). The 325 creed ends abruptly with "and in the Holy Spirit", followed by anathemas.
    • "Of the substance (ousia) of the Father" and "of one substance" (homoousios) were the decisive additions. was not a biblical word, had been associated with Gnostic and modalist theologies, and had been rejected at Antioch in 268 in the case of Paul of Samosata. Its adoption was controversial from the start. Eusebius of Caesarea's letter to his church shows him accepting it only after it was explained in a sense he could live with.3
    • The anathemas equate and ("of a different substance or essence"; Greek ex heteras hypostaseōs ē ousias). This was a source of later confusion. When the Cappadocians later distinguished the two terms (ch. 8), they had to explain away this wording.

    Only two bishops, Theonas of Marmarica and Secundus of Ptolemais, refused to sign and were exiled with Arius. Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea signed the creed but not the condemnation of Arius, and were exiled shortly afterwards. Accounts of this differ. Socrates names five initial objectors.4

    Other business

    The council also:

    • decided to celebrate Easter on a common Sunday independent of the Jewish calendar. The detailed method of calculation was not fixed by the council, and the Alexandrian and Roman reckonings continued to differ for centuries.
    • settled the Melitian schism in Egypt.
    • issued twenty canons. Canon 6, recognising the authority of Alexandria, Rome and Antioch over their regions, became the founding text for later arguments about church authority (Vol. VII ch. 2).

    It did not discuss or decide the canon of Scripture. That widespread modern claim has no basis in any ancient source (Misconceptions).

    Full council analysis: Volume VI, Nicaea I.

    Volume IV · Chapter 7

    After Nicaea: Athanasius and the parties (325–361)

    Nicaea did not end the controversy. For a generation afterwards, its creed was rarely invoked. The struggle that followed was as much about people, councils and imperial favour as about doctrine.

    Athanasius

    Athanasius had attended Nicaea as Alexander's deacon and became bishop of Alexandria in 328. He was exiled five times: by Constantine in 335, after the Council of Tyre found against him on disciplinary charges; and again in 339, 356, 362 and 365. He spent about seventeen of his forty-five years as bishop away from his see.1 His theological case rested on salvation. Only one who is truly God can unite humanity to God:

    For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father.

    Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54.3, c. 330s (date disputed). Trans. Archibald Robertson, NPNF II/4 (1892). Q08 · checked

    This theme of , salvation as participation in divine life, remained central to Eastern Christian theology (Vol. IX ch. 6).

    The theological parties

    After Constantine's death (337) the empire was divided among his sons. Constantius II, sole ruler from 350 to 361, favoured a broad, non-Nicene settlement. The positions that emerged are conventionally grouped as follows. These labels are modern simplifications.

    GroupFormulaMain figures
    Niceneshomoousios, "of the same substance"Athanasius, Marcellus of Ancyra (whose own views were suspect to many), Western bishops
    "Homoiousians"homoiousios, "of like substance"Basil of Ancyra, George of Laodicea
    Homoianshomoios, "like [the Father]", with substance language bannedAcacius of Caesarea; the imperial creeds of 359–360
    "Anomoeans" / Heterousiansanomoios, "unlike"Aetius, Eunomius

    The Councils of Antioch (341) and Serdica (c. 343) showed the developing East–West divide. Western bishops, led by Julius of Rome, defended Athanasius and Marcellus. Many Eastern bishops saw Marcellus as a modalist who denied the Son's distinct existence, and saw Western support for him as proof that "Nicene" meant "Sabellian". At Serdica the two delegations met separately and excommunicated each other (Vol. VI, other councils).

    Under Constantius, the twin councils of Ariminum (Rimini) and Seleucia (359), followed by Constantinople (360), imposed a Homoian creed on almost the whole episcopate. Jerome, looking back, wrote that the world "groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian".2 For a time, Homoian Christianity was the empire's official faith. Through the mission of Ulfila, it became the faith of the Goths and later of the Vandals, Burgundians and Lombards. That fact shaped Western politics until the conversion of the Visigothic king Reccared in 589 (Vol. VIII ch. 5).

    Notes

    1. The chronology of the five exiles is reconstructed chiefly from Athanasius' Festal Index and Apologia contra Arianos; see Barnes 1993. ↩
    2. Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 19. Paraphrased; this passage is not quoted here because it was not checked against an edition. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 8

    The Cappadocians and the language of the Trinity

    The resolution of the fourth-century debates owed most to three theologians from Cappadocia in central Anatolia: Basil of Caesarea (d. 378 or 379), his brother Gregory of Nyssa (d. c. 395), and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus (d. c. 390). Their writings are extensive and survive well.

    The Council of Alexandria (362) and the problem of words

    After Julian's accession (361), exiled bishops returned. Athanasius held a synod at Alexandria in 362 whose Tome to the Antiochenes made a crucial concession. It accepted that those who spoke of three could be orthodox, provided they did not mean three different substances, and that those who spoke of one hypostasis could be orthodox, provided they did not mean to deny the distinction of persons.1 The dispute had partly been about vocabulary. In Greek, ousia and hypostasis could both mean "reality" or "substance". In Latin, substantia was the natural translation of hypostasis, so Latins heard "three hypostases" as "three substances", that is, three gods.

    The Cappadocian distinction

    Basil and the Gregories established the formula that became standard in the East:

    one ousia (essence, substance) · three hypostaseis (concrete subsistences, "persons")

    The Father, Son and Spirit share one divine nature completely. They are distinguished not by degree of divinity but by their relations of origin: the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding. For a detailed comparison of terms, see Key Greek terms. Latin theology came to express the same structure as una substantia, tres personae. The overlap and mismatch between hypostasis and persona (originally a "role" or "face") remained a source of misunderstanding.

    The Holy Spirit

    By the 360s a new question had emerged. Some who accepted the Son's full divinity denied it to the Holy Spirit; opponents called them Pneumatomachoi, "Spirit-fighters", later identified with "Macedonians". Basil's On the Holy Spirit (c. 375) argued from the Church's worship, specifically the doxology giving glory to the Father "with the Son together with the Holy Spirit", that the Spirit shares the same honour. Characteristically, he avoided calling the Spirit "God" or homoousios outright. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Fifth Theological Oration (380), did both.2 Basil's treatise also contains an image argument that the iconophiles of the eighth century would later quote:

    …because the honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype.

    Basil, On the Holy Spirit 18.45. Trans. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF II/8 (1895). In context Basil refers to the emperor’s image and, by analogy, to the Son as image of the Father; he is not discussing religious pictures. Q10 · checked

    Apollinarius and the humanity of Christ

    Apollinarius of Laodicea, a staunch Nicene, taught that in Christ the divine Word took the place of the human mind (nous). Gregory of Nazianzus' reply gave the classic soteriological principle that would govern all later Christology:

    For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.

    Gregory of Nazianzus, Letter 101 (to Cledonius), c. 382. Trans. C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, NPNF II/7 (1894). Q09 · checked

    Apollinarianism was condemned in Rome and at Constantinople in 381. The question it raised, how to affirm one subject in Christ without diminishing either his divinity or his humanity, opened the controversies of the next century (ch. 11).

    Notes

    1. Athanasius, Tomus ad Antiochenos 5–6; NPNF II/4. ↩
    2. Basil, De Spiritu Sancto 1.3, 25.58–29.75; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 31.10, NPNF II/7. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 9

    Theodosius, 380–381, and the Nicene settlement

    The Homoian emperor Valens died at the battle of Adrianople against the Goths (9 August 378). Gratian appointed Theodosius, a Nicene Christian from Spain, to rule the East.

    Cunctos populos (380)

    On 27 or 28 February 380, at Thessalonica, Theodosius, with his co-emperors Gratian and Valentinian II, issued the law later placed at the head of the religious book of the Theodosian Code. It commanded all peoples under imperial rule to follow the religion that "the divine apostle Peter transmitted to the Romans". It identified that faith by naming two living bishops, Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria, as its exemplars, and declared that only those who held it might be called "Catholic Christians"; others were "demented and insane" heretics, liable to divine and imperial punishment.1

    This law, not anything done by Constantine, is the best candidate for the moment Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the Roman state. Later laws excluded non-Nicenes from church buildings (381) and prohibited public pagan sacrifice and temple cult (391–392).2 Enforcement was uneven. Pagan cults, Jewish communities and dissident Christian groups persisted, but the legal framework of a Christian empire was in place.

    The Council of Constantinople (381)

    Theodosius summoned about 150 Eastern bishops to his capital in May 381. No Western bishop attended, and Rome was not represented. The council was presided over first by Meletius of Antioch, who died during it, then by Gregory of Nazianzus. Gregory resigned amid disputes over the Antiochene succession and over his own appointment as bishop of Constantinople. Nectarius, an unbaptised senator, was elected in his place.

    The council reaffirmed Nicaea and condemned the Homoians, Anomoeans, Pneumatomachians and Apollinarians. It is associated with an expanded creed, the "Niceno-Constantinopolitan" Creed, whose article on the Spirit reads:

    And we believe in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, who spoke by the prophets.

    The Creed of Constantinople (381). Trans. H. R. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Q11 · checked
    Scholarly debate: did the council of 381 compose this creed?

    The text is first attested in the acts of Chalcedon (451), where it was read as the creed "of the 150 fathers". No document from 381 itself preserves it. J. N. D. Kelly reviewed the theories. One is that the council endorsed an existing local creed, perhaps from Jerusalem or Constantinople; another is that the creed formed part of the council's lost "tome". He concluded that the council probably did adopt it, in connection with the baptism and installation of Nectarius.

    What is certain is that from 451 this creed became the common creed of the Greek and Latin Churches. With the later Western addition of the , it is the creed recited in most churches today. The Oriental Orthodox Churches also use it. The Church of the East has its own historic creed, but it too recognises the councils of 325 and 381.3

    The council's canon 3 had long-term consequences for church politics:

    The bishop of Constantinople however shall have the prerogative of honour next after the bishop of Rome, because Constantinople is new Rome.

    Constantinople I, canon 3 (381), in the form read into the record at Chalcedon, Session 16. Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Socrates (HE 5.8) paraphrases it in the same sense. Q12 · checked

    Rome did not accept the canons of 381 for centuries. Its objection was to the principle that a see's rank depended on its city's political status rather than its apostolic foundation. See Vol. VII ch. 3.

    Notes

    1. Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2. Paraphrased here; a quoted English translation was not checked during preparation. See the translation by Clyde Pharr, The Theodosian Code (Princeton, 1952), and the discussion in Errington 2006. ↩
    2. CTh 16.5.6 (381); 16.10.10–12 (391–392). ↩
    3. Kelly 1972, ch. 10. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 10

    The rise of monasticism

    As Christianity became the religion of the powerful, a movement of ascetic withdrawal grew up at its edges. It became one of its defining institutions. Monasticism had antecedents: celibate "sons and daughters of the covenant" (bnay qyāmā) in Syriac Christianity, ascetic virgins and widows in cities, and the Jewish Therapeutae described by Philo. But the fourth century saw it take recognisable forms.

    • Anchoritic (solitary) life. The Life of Antony, attributed to Athanasius and written c. 357–362, presented Antony of Egypt (c. 251–356) as the model hermit. Its Latin translations spread the ideal to the West and helped prompt Augustine's conversion (Confessions 8.6). How much the Life reflects Athanasius' own agenda, for example by showing Antony as a loyal ally of the bishop, is debated.1
    • Coenobitic (communal) life. Pachomius (c. 292–348) founded communal monasteries in Upper Egypt from the 320s, with a written rule, common work and obedience to a superior. By his death they formed a federation of several thousand monks and nuns.2
    • Semi-anchoritic settlements at Nitria, Kellia and Scetis (Wadi al-Natrun), whose sayings were collected in the Apophthegmata Patrum.
    • Basil of Caesarea integrated ascetic communities with the life of the local Church, including care for the poor and sick, through his Asketikon. It remains the basis of Byzantine-rite monasticism.
    • Syrian asceticism developed spectacular forms, such as Symeon the Stylite (d. 459) on his pillar near Antioch, and strong links with Syriac poetry and theology (Ephrem, d. 373).
    • In the West, Martin of Tours, John Cassian (Marseille, c. 415), Lérins and later Benedict of Nursia (6th c.) adapted Eastern models.

    Monks became a force in church politics. Egyptian monks under Shenoute and others were active against pagan temples. The archimandrite Eutyches in Constantinople, the Syrian monk Barsauma at Ephesus in 449, and Palestinian monastic resistance after 451 all show that the controversies of the fifth century were fought in monasteries as well as councils. Canon 4 of Chalcedon accordingly placed monks under the supervision of the local bishop.3

    Notes

    1. Harmless 2004, chs. 3–4. ↩
    2. Rousseau 1985. ↩
    3. Gaddis 2005, chs. 5–8. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 11

    Nestorius, Cyril, and Ephesus (428–433)

    Two traditions

    Once the full divinity of the Son was settled, the question became how God and a full human being are united in the one Christ. Two broad traditions had developed. Modern textbooks call them "Alexandrian" and "Antiochene", labels that oversimplify real diversity within each.1

    “Alexandrian” emphasis“Antiochene” emphasis
    Starting pointThe divine Word is the single subject of everything Christ does and suffersThe full integrity of Christ's humanity, including human growth, will and suffering
    Typical model"The Word became flesh" (John 1:14)The Word "dwelling" in the "temple" of his humanity (John 2:21)
    Main danger fearedSplitting Christ into two subjectsConfusing the natures, making God suffer or change
    RepresentativesAthanasius, Cyril of AlexandriaDiodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Nestorius, Theodoret

    The Theotokos dispute

    Nestorius, a monk-preacher from Antioch, became bishop of Constantinople in April 428. Socrates, a lay historian in the capital who was not hostile to him, records how the controversy began:

    This Anastasius preaching one day in the church said, ‘Let no one call Mary Theotocos: for Mary was but a woman; and it is impossible that God should be born of a woman.’ These words created a great sensation…

    Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 7.32. Trans. A. C. Zenos, NPNF II/2 (1890). Q13 · checked

    Nestorius backed his chaplain. He proposed Christotokos ("bearer of Christ") as more accurate, or accepted only if paired with anthropotokos ("bearer of a human being"). For his opponents, this implied that the one born of Mary was not God the Word himself but a man joined to him: in effect, two sons.

    Cyril's campaign

    Cyril of Alexandria (bishop 412–444) responded in letters to Egyptian monks, to Nestorius and to the imperial court, and secured the support of Celestine of Rome. A Roman synod in August 430 condemned Nestorius. Cyril's Third Letter to Nestorius (November 430) attached twelve anathemas for Nestorius to sign:

    If anyone will not confess that the Emmanuel is very God, and that therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Theotokos), inasmuch as in the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh [as it is written, “The Word was made flesh”]: let him be anathema.

    Cyril of Alexandria, Twelve Anathemas, no. 1, appended to his Third Letter to Nestorius (430). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Q14 · checked

    The anathemas, with their language of "natural" or "hypostatic union" and the claim that "the Word of God suffered in the flesh", alarmed Antiochene theologians, including John of Antioch and Theodoret. To them, they seemed Apollinarian.2

    Ephesus, 431

    Theodosius II summoned a council to Ephesus for Pentecost 431. What followed was less a single council than rival assemblies:

    • 22 June. Cyril opened the council before John of Antioch and the Syrian bishops arrived, despite the protests of the imperial commissioner Candidian and of some 68 bishops. Nestorius refused to attend. In one day the assembly examined his teaching and deposed him.

      …we have come, with many tears, to this sorrowful sentence against him, namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has blasphemed, decrees by the holy Synod that Nestorius be excluded from the episcopal dignity, and from all priestly communion.

      Council of Ephesus, Decree against Nestorius (22 June 431). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14. Q15 · checked
    • 26 June. John of Antioch arrived and held a counter-synod of some 43 bishops that deposed Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus.
    • July. The Roman legates arrived and endorsed Cyril's council.
    • Afterwards. The emperor at first confirmed both sets of depositions and arrested Cyril, Memnon and Nestorius. Eventually he accepted Cyril's council. Contemporary sources suggest Cyril's agents were active at court and gave generous "blessings" (gifts). Nestorius was sent back to his monastery near Antioch and later exiled to Egypt, where he died after 450.3

    Canon 7 of the council (passed at a later session) forbade composing "a different faith" from that of Nicaea. It would be cited against every subsequent attempt at a new definition, including Chalcedon's (Vol. VI, Ephesus).

    The Formula of Reunion (433)

    Under imperial pressure, Cyril and John were reconciled in 433. John accepted the deposition of Nestorius. Cyril accepted a confession of faith drafted by the Antiochenes, probably by Theodoret, which spoke of two natures:

    …of the same substance with his Father according to his Divinity, and of the same substance with us according to his humanity; for there became a union of two natures. Wherefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord. According to this understanding of this unmixed union, we confess the holy Virgin to be Mother of God…

    The Formula of Reunion (433), quoted in Cyril’s letter to John of Antioch (Laetentur caeli). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14. Q17 · checked

    Many of Cyril's own supporters thought he had conceded too much. His followers' reading of his work, and especially his formula "one incarnate nature of God the Word" (mia physis tou theou logou sesarkōmenē), which he believed came from Athanasius but actually derived from Apollinarius, would become the rallying point after Chalcedon (Vol. V ch. 2).4

    Notes

    1. Grillmeier 1975, vol. 1; McGuckin 1994. ↩
    2. Cyril's twelve anathemas: DH 252–263 (DH); Price & Graumann 2020. ↩
    3. The acts in Price & Graumann 2020; narrative in McGuckin 1994, ch. 1. Cyril's gifts to court officials are documented in a list preserved in the Collectio Casinensis. ↩
    4. McGuckin 1994; Frend 1972. ↩

    Volume IV · Chapter 12

    From Eutyches to Chalcedon (448–451)

    Eutyches

    Eutyches was an elderly archimandrite in Constantinople, a passionate Cyrillian with influence at court. In November 448 he was accused before the "home synod" of Bishop Flavian of Constantinople. When questioned, he confessed that Christ was "of two natures before the union, but after the union one nature". He was reluctant to say that Christ was consubstantial with us in his humanity. The synod deposed him. His exact views remain debated. He may have been more confused than heretical. But "Eutychianism", the belief that Christ's humanity was absorbed into or mixed with his divinity, became the name for a position that all later parties, including the opponents of Chalcedon, condemned.1

    Leo's Tome and Ephesus II (449)

    Eutyches appealed to Pope Leo I and to Dioscorus, Cyril's successor at Alexandria. Leo replied with a dogmatic letter to Flavian dated 13 June 449, the "Tome". It set out Western Christology in balanced antitheses:

    For each form does what is proper to it with the co-operation of the other; that is the Word performing what appertains to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what appertains to the flesh.

    Leo I, Letter 28 (the Tome) 4, dated 13 June 449. Trans. C. L. Feltoe, NPNF II/12 (1895). Q18 · checked

    Theodosius II called a council to Ephesus in August 449, presided over by Dioscorus. The Tome was not read. Eutyches was rehabilitated. Flavian and other leading "two-nature" bishops, including Domnus of Antioch, Ibas of Edessa and Theodoret, were deposed. Flavian died soon after. Later Chalcedonian accounts say he died from beatings at the council; the evidence is partisan and the details are disputed. Leo, whose legate Hilarus escaped, denounced the assembly. In a letter to the empress Pulcheria he called it a latrocinium, a "robber council", and the name has stuck.2

    Chalcedon (451)

    On 28 July 450 Theodosius II died after a fall from his horse. His sister Pulcheria married the officer Marcian, who became emperor and reversed his predecessor's church policy. A new council was summoned. It met at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from the capital, from 8 October to around 1 November 451. About 350–370 bishops took part, almost all from the East. Later tradition gives 630. Roman legates (Paschasinus, Lucentius and the priest Boniface) took a leading place, and imperial officials directed proceedings.3

    • Session 1. The council reviewed Ephesus II and condemned its proceedings.
    • Session 3. Dioscorus was deposed, formally for disciplinary reasons (refusing to appear when summoned), not for heresy.
    • Leo's Tome was read and acclaimed. Bishops from Illyricum and Palestine were concerned about some passages, and the commissioners had those passages checked against Cyril's writings before the Tome was accepted.

    This is the faith of the fathers, this is the faith of the Apostles. So we all believe, thus the orthodox believe. Anathema to him who does not thus believe. Peter has spoken thus through Leo. So taught the Apostles. Piously and truly did Leo teach, so taught Cyril.

    Acclamations after the reading of the Tome, Chalcedon, Session 2 (in Percival’s numbering; Session 3 in some editions). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Q19 · checked

    The acclamation "Peter has spoken through Leo" is cited by Catholic writers as evidence of recognised papal teaching authority. Orthodox and many other scholars point to its immediate qualification, "so taught Cyril", and to the council's own examination of the Tome as showing that the bishops judged Leo's letter by its agreement with tradition rather than accepting it on authority. Both readings appeal to the same text.

    The emperor insisted, against the wishes of many bishops, on a new definition of faith. It was agreed at Session 5 on 22 October and proclaimed in Marcian's presence on 25 October. Its central clause:

    Following the holy Fathers we teach with one voice that the Son [of God] and our Lord Jesus Christ is to be confessed as one and the same [Person], that he is perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, very God and very man, of a reasonable soul and [human] body consisting, consubstantial with the Father as touching his Godhead, and consubstantial with us as touching his manhood; made in all things like unto us, sin only excepted; begotten of his Father before the worlds according to his Godhead; but in these last days for us men and for our salvation born [into the world] of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God according to his manhood. This one and the same Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son [of God] must be confessed to be in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united], and that without the distinction of natures being taken away by such union, but rather the peculiar property of each nature being preserved and being united in one Person and subsistence, not separated or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son and only-begotten, God the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ…

    Chalcedon, Definition of Faith (22–25 October 451). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q20 · checked

    The phrase "in two natures" (en dyo physesin) is the reading of the Latin version and of the version known to later Greek writers. Some argued that the original draft had read "out of two natures" (ek dyo physeōn), a formula Dioscorus could have accepted, and that it was changed at the insistence of the Roman legates and the emperor. The four adverbs, often called the "Chalcedonian fences", exclude both confusion of the natures ("unconfusedly, immutably", against Eutyches) and division ("indivisibly, inseparably", against Nestorius).

    The Chalcedonians regarded this as a synthesis of Cyril and Leo. Its opponents saw it as a betrayal of Cyril and a return to Nestorius under a new formula. The consequences, including the separation of the Oriental Orthodox Churches, are the subject of Volume V ch. 2. The council's canons, especially the disputed canon 28 on Constantinople, are treated in Volume VI and Volume VII.

    Notes

    1. The minutes of the 448 synod survive because they were read into the acts of Ephesus II and then of Chalcedon (Session 1); see Price & Gaddis 2005, vol. 1. ↩
    2. Leo, Letter 95.2 (20 July 451): "in illo Ephesino non iudicio, sed latrocinio". The Latin phrase is cited from the standard edition. The NPNF translation of this letter renders the sense differently and was checked only for context. ↩
    3. Attendance figures from the subscriptions as analysed in Price & Gaddis 2005, vol. 1, introduction. ↩

    Volume IV · Terminology

    Key Greek terms

    Much of the history in Volumes IV–VI turns on a handful of Greek words whose meanings were still being fixed during the controversies themselves. The same word could mean different things to different writers, and translation into Latin and Syriac added further shifts. The table summarises how each word was eventually used. The notes after it explain the most important ambiguities.

    TermRoot meaningTrinitarian use (after c. 380)Christological use (after 451)Latin / Syriac
    ousia οὐσίαbeing, essence, substance; what something isThe one divine essence shared by Father, Son and SpiritRarely used; Christ is homoousios with the Father and with usessentia, substantia · Syr. ītūthā
    hypostasis ὑπόστασις"standing under": underlying reality, concrete existenceEach of the three: Father, Son, SpiritChalcedon: the one hypostasis (subject) of Christ, the Wordsubsistentia, often persona · Syr. qnōmā (but see note)
    physis φύσιςnature; what something is by its constitutionSometimes equivalent to ousiaChalcedon: two natures (divine, human). Cyril: often used to mean a concrete individual, hence "one nature"natura · Syr. kyānā
    prosopon πρόσωπονface, mask, role; the outward presentation of someoneUsed, but suspected of modalism ("three masks")Antiochenes: one prosopon of union. Chalcedon: equated with hypostasispersona · Syr. parṣōpā
    homoousios ὁμοούσιος"of the same being"The Son (and later the Spirit) is of the same essence as the Father (Nicaea 325)Christ is consubstantial with the Father in divinity and with us in humanity (Chalcedon)consubstantialis
    Theotokos Θεοτόκος"God-bearer", the one who gave birth to God—Affirmed at Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) as a Christological statement: the one born of Mary is God the WordDei Genitrix, popularly Mater Dei · Syr. yāldat alāhā

    Notes on the ambiguities

    • Ousia vs hypostasis. In 325 these were synonyms. Nicaea's anathema condemns those who say the Son is "of another hypostasis or ousia". The Cappadocians separated them in the 360s–370s (ch. 8).
    • Physis in Cyril. Cyril of Alexandria often used physis almost as a synonym for hypostasis, meaning a concrete, individual reality. His "one incarnate nature of God the Word" therefore meant "one concrete subject, the Word, now incarnate". It did not mean that the humanity had been absorbed. Chalcedon used physis in the more abstract sense of "nature as a set of properties". For this reason, modern dialogues have concluded that the Oriental Orthodox "one nature" and the Chalcedonian "two natures" can express the same faith (Vol. V ch. 2).
    • Qnōmā. The Church of the East confesses in Christ "two natures, two qnōmē, one parṣōpā". This sounds like "two hypostases", which Chalcedon rejected. Syriac scholars such as Sebastian Brock have argued that qnōmā here denotes the individuated nature (a particular instance of a nature), not an independent subject. If so, the formula does not mean "two persons".1
    • Theotokos is a statement about Christ before it is a statement about Mary. The controversy of 428–431 was about whether the one born of Mary is identical with the eternal Word.

    Notes

    1. Brock 1996; Baum & Winkler 2003, ch. 2. ↩

    Volume V · 5th–7th centuries, with modern sequels

    The First Major Divisions of Christianity

    The first lasting divisions in the Christian world did not run between East and West, but within the East. By the sixth century three communions existed that did not share the Eucharist:

    • the imperial Church that accepted Chalcedon;
    • the Churches that rejected Chalcedon, today called the Oriental Orthodox;
    • the Church of the East in the Persian Empire.

    All three still exist. This volume explains how they came about, why the standard labels for them ("Nestorian", "Monophysite") are misleading, and how twentieth-century dialogues re-examined the old condemnations.

    In this volume

    1. The Church of the East
    2. Chalcedon’s aftermath and the Oriental Orthodox Churches
    3. Miaphysite, Eutychian, Dyophysite: why the terminology matters
    4. How the families of Churches formed (diagram)
    5. Modern Christological dialogues

    Volume V · Chapter 1

    The Church of the East

    The Church of the East is the historic Church of Syriac-speaking Christians in Mesopotamia and Persia, outside the Roman Empire. It is often called "the Nestorian Church". That name was applied by its opponents and has been rejected by the Church itself, and it gives a misleading account of the Church's origins. The Church of the East did not begin as a breakaway from the Council of Ephesus. It already existed, and was already organised separately, before Nestorius was born.

    Origins in Mesopotamia

    Christianity reached northern Mesopotamia and Adiabene (around Erbil) by the second century. Tradition attributes the mission to the apostle Thomas and to Addai (Thaddaeus) and his disciple Mari. These traditions are attested in later sources such as the Doctrine of Addai (c. 400), and their details cannot be confirmed. The first secure evidence comes from the third century. Bishops are attested in the Persian Empire, which the Sasanian dynasty ruled from 224. Romans deported from Syria by Shapur I (in the 250s–260s) brought many Christians into Persia.1

    Christians in Persia were a minority under a Zoroastrian monarchy. After Constantine they could be suspected of sympathy with Rome. Under Shapur II (c. 340–379), Persian Christians suffered severe persecution, recorded in the Syriac Acts of the Persian Martyrs.

    Becoming a self-governing Church: 410, 424, 486

    The Church of the East's constitution was laid down in a series of synods whose acts survive in the Synodicon Orientale, edited by J.-B. Chabot (1902).2

    • 410, Seleucia-Ctesiphon (Synod of Isaac). Held with the permission of Shah Yazdegerd I and in the presence of the Roman envoy Marutha of Maypherqat. It adopted the Creed and canons of Nicaea and recognised the bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon as head ("Catholicos") of the Persian Church, with metropolitans under him.
    • 420, Synod of Yahballaha I. Accepted further Western canons.
    • 424, Markabta (Synod of Dadisho'). Declared that the Catholicos could not be judged by the "Western" (Roman-empire) bishops, and that any complaint against him must be settled within the Persian Church. This was a declaration of jurisdictional independence, not a doctrinal schism. It came before the Council of Ephesus.
    • 486, Synod of Acacius. Adopted a Christological statement affirming two natures in one Christ and rejecting "mixture". It also permitted clergy, including bishops, to marry. An earlier synod at Beth Lapat (484) under Barsauma of Nisibis had moved in the same direction, though its acts were later set aside.

    The theological orientation of the Church of the East was shaped less by Nestorius than by Theodore of Mopsuestia (d. 428), whose biblical commentaries were translated into Syriac at the "School of the Persians" in Edessa. When the emperor Zeno closed that school in 489, its teachers moved across the border to Nisibis. The School of Nisibis became the intellectual centre of the Church. Theodore was venerated there as "the Interpreter". Nestorius, too, is commemorated in the Church's liturgy as a Greek doctor. He was never its founder, and the Church did not take its theology from him.3

    The definitive Christological formulation came in the early seventh century from Babai the Great (d. 628): two natures (kyānē), two qnōmē, one parṣōpā (person) of Christ. On the meaning of qnōmā, see Key terms. The Church of the East did not accept the Council of Ephesus (431), which had condemned Nestorius. Nor did it accept Constantinople II (553), which condemned Theodore. It therefore stands outside the conciliar tradition of the Byzantine and Latin Churches from 431 onwards, while professing the faith of Nicaea.

    Expansion across Asia

    From the fifth to the fourteenth century the Church of the East was geographically the most extensive Church in the world.

    • India. The Saint Thomas Christians of the Malabar coast received bishops from Persia. Copper-plate grants from Kollam (Quilon), datable to around 849, and "Persian crosses" with Pahlavi inscriptions document an established community. Their own tradition of evangelisation by the apostle Thomas in AD 52 cannot be independently verified.
    • Central Asia. Metropolitan sees existed at Merv and Herat by the sixth century, and Christian communities among Sogdians, Turks and later the Uyghurs. Hundreds of Syriac-Turkic gravestones (13th–14th c.) survive from the Chüy valley in Kyrgyzstan.
    • China. The monk Aluoben (Alopen) reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635. The Chinese-Syriac stele erected in 781 (now in the Beilin Museum, Xi'an) records the mission's history and the "Luminous Teaching" (Jingjiao). The stele was rediscovered c. 1623–25. Its authenticity was once doubted by some European writers but is now accepted.4 The mission declined after the anti-foreign persecution of 845. It reappeared under the Mongol Yuan dynasty (1271–1368).
    • Under Islam. After the Arab conquests the Catholicos moved, under Timothy I (780–823), to Baghdad. Syriac Christian scholars were central to the translation of Greek philosophy and science into Arabic. Timothy's letters mention metropolitans for Turks and for China (Beth Sinaye).
    • Mongol period. Two Uyghur or Öngüt monks travelled from Khanbaliq (Beijing) westwards. One, Markos, became Catholicos Yahballaha III (1281–1317). The other, Rabban Sauma, travelled as an envoy to Constantinople, Rome, Paris and Bordeaux in 1287–88, met Pope Nicholas IV, and received communion from him. His Syriac travel account survives.5

    Decline and later divisions

    The conversion of the Ilkhanate to Islam (1295), the Black Death and the campaigns of Timur (late 14th century) devastated the Church outside its Mesopotamian and Kurdish mountain heartlands. In 1552, a dispute over hereditary patriarchal succession led a party to elect Yohannan Sulaqa, who went to Rome and entered communion with Pope Julius III (1553). From this and later unions descends the Chaldean Catholic Church, an Eastern Catholic Church whose patriarchate was consolidated in its present form in 1830. The historic hereditary line continued as the Assyrian Church of the East, which formally adopted that name in 1976. A dispute in the 1960s, partly over adopting the Gregorian calendar and hereditary succession, produced the Ancient Church of the East (1968), based in Baghdad. The Saint Thomas Christians of India also divided after Portuguese latinisation at the Synod of Diamper (1599). See ch. 2.6

    Key takeaways

    • The Church of the East's independence was jurisdictional (410–424) before it was doctrinal, and it was shaped by the Persian political context.
    • Its theology descends from Theodore of Mopsuestia and the School of Nisibis. "Nestorian" is a polemical misnomer.
    • In 1994 the Catholic Church and the Assyrian Church of the East declared that they share the same faith in Christ (ch. 5).

    Volume V · Chapter 2

    Chalcedon’s aftermath and the Oriental Orthodox Churches

    Chalcedon did not produce an immediate, clean split. It produced more than a century of contested reception. In Egypt and much of Syria, large parts of the Church regarded the council as having betrayed Cyril. Emperors alternately enforced Chalcedon, tried to set it aside, and sought compromise formulas. Separate hierarchies, and therefore separate Churches, emerged gradually, mainly between the 510s and the 570s.

    Resistance and compromise (451–518)

    • Egypt. After Dioscorus' deposition the Chalcedonian Proterius was installed at Alexandria. He was lynched in 457. The anti-Chalcedonian Timothy Aelurus was then consecrated, and Alexandria had rival bishops for long periods. Palestine saw a monastic revolt in 451–453.
    • The Henotikon (482). The emperor Zeno, with Acacius of Constantinople, issued an "instrument of union". It affirmed Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus and Cyril's Twelve Anathemas, condemned Nestorius and Eutyches, and passed over Chalcedon in silence, condemning anyone who held otherwise "whether at Chalcedon or at any synod whatever". It satisfied neither side fully.1
    • The Acacian schism (484–519). Pope Felix III excommunicated Acacius for this compromise, opening the first prolonged break in communion between Rome and Constantinople. It ended only in 519, when the emperor Justin I and Patriarch John II accepted the Formula of Hormisdas. That document affirmed Chalcedon and the Tome and struck Acacius and his successors from the diptychs. Its claims for the Roman see are discussed in Vol. VII ch. 4.
    • Severus of Antioch. Patriarch of Antioch from 512, Severus was the most important theologian of the anti-Chalcedonian movement. He was deposed under Justin I in 518. A systematic Cyrillian, he rejected Eutyches as firmly as Nestorius. He affirmed that Christ's humanity is complete and consubstantial with us, but insisted that after the union one should speak of "one incarnate nature" and "one composite hypostasis", and that "two natures" after the union implied division.2

    Separate hierarchies (518–c. 580)

    From 518 Justin I and Justinian (527–565) removed anti-Chalcedonian bishops in Syria. Justinian's wife Theodora (d. 548) protected exiled anti-Chalcedonian leaders in the palace. The critical step was the consecration of new bishops independent of the imperial Church. Around 542/543, at the request of the Ghassanid Arab ruler al-Harith and with Theodora's support, the monk Jacob Baradaeus was consecrated bishop of Edessa. Travelling in disguise, he is said to have ordained dozens of bishops and thousands of clergy before his death in 578.3 Opponents called his Church "Jacobite", a name the Syriac Orthodox Church does not use for itself.

    Justinian also tried theological reconciliation. He promoted "Neo-Chalcedonian" theology, which read Chalcedon through Cyril, and condemned the "Three Chapters" (writings of Theodore, Theodoret and Ibas). That condemnation was the business of Constantinople II (553). It failed to win back the anti-Chalcedonians, and it caused schism in the West (see Vol. VI). The seventh-century attempts at union through Monenergism and Monothelitism likewise failed (Constantinople III). The Arab conquests of the 630s–640s then removed Egypt and Syria from imperial control, and the separation became permanent.

    The Oriental Orthodox Churches

    The modern Oriental Orthodox communion consists of six Churches in full communion with one another. They accept the first three councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus) and reject Chalcedon and later councils.

    Coptic Orthodox Church

    The majority Church of Egypt, continuing the line of Alexandrian popes through Dioscorus and Timothy Aelurus. Its head is the Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the See of St Mark. Coptic (the latest stage of Egyptian) was its liturgical and literary language. Arabic became dominant in daily use from about the 10th–13th centuries.4

    Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch

    Descends from Severus and Jacob Baradaeus. Its patriarch, who uses the title of Antioch, has resided at various places, including Mor Hananyo monastery near Mardin, Homs and, since 1959, Damascus. Its liturgy is in Syriac.

    Armenian Apostolic Church

    Armenia's royal conversion under Tiridates and Gregory the Illuminator is traditionally dated 301. Many historians prefer c. 314. Armenia sent no bishops to Chalcedon: in 451 it was fighting Persia at the battle of Avarayr. Armenian synods at Dvin in 506 and c. 555 aligned the Church with the Henotikon and then rejected Chalcedon, partly in reaction to Persian-sponsored Church of the East influence. The exact content and dates of these synods are debated.5 Its head is the Catholicos of All Armenians at Etchmiadzin. There is also a Catholicosate of Cilicia, now at Antelias in Lebanon.

    Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church

    King Ezana of Aksum adopted Christianity in the mid-fourth century; his coinage shifts from pagan symbols to the cross. Frumentius was consecrated bishop by Athanasius. For sixteen centuries Ethiopia's metropolitan (the abuna) was an Egyptian monk sent from Alexandria. The Church gained autocephaly in stages: an Ethiopian archbishop in 1948–51 and a patriarch in 1959. Tewahedo means "made one", a reference to the union of natures in Christ.6

    Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church

    Separated from the Ethiopian Church after Eritrea's independence (1993). Its autocephaly was granted by the Coptic Orthodox Church in the 1990s, and its first patriarch was enthroned in 1998. The Ethiopian Church did not initially recognise the separation. In the 2000s the Eritrean government removed Patriarch Antonios, a removal the Coptic Church and others did not regard as canonical.

    Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church

    One branch of the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala. After Portuguese latinisation (Synod of Diamper, 1599), the Coonan Cross Oath (1653) rejected Jesuit authority. Bishop Gregorios Abdul Jaleel of Jerusalem arrived in 1665 and brought West Syriac (Syriac Orthodox) liturgy and allegiance. A Catholicate was established in India in 1912. Disputes over whether the Church is autocephalous or under the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch have divided the community. That side is now the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church, which is part of the Syriac Orthodox Church. The dispute has repeatedly gone to the Supreme Court of India.7

    The Saint Thomas Christians today are divided among several Churches: the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholic Churches, the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian Churches, the Mar Thoma Syrian Church (reformed in the 19th century under Anglican influence), and others. The Chaldean Syrian Church in Thrissur belongs to the Assyrian Church of the East.

    Not every Christian community in these regions is Oriental Orthodox. Egypt and Syria also have Greek Orthodox (Chalcedonian, historically "Melkite", from the Syriac for "imperial") patriarchates, and Eastern Catholic Churches. The Maronite Church of Lebanon emerged from the monastic community of St Maron in the Chalcedonian milieu of northern Syria. Its history in the seventh century, including the question of Monothelitism, is disputed. It will be treated fully in Volume XIII.

    Volume V · Chapter 3

    Miaphysite, Eutychian, Dyophysite: why the terminology matters

    For centuries Western and Byzantine writers called the anti-Chalcedonian Churches "Monophysite", meaning "those who hold one nature", and treated them as followers of Eutyches. Modern historical and ecumenical scholarship rejects both identifications.

    PositionFormulaHeld byCondemned by
    Eutychianism (also "real" or "Eutychian monophysitism")After the union the humanity is absorbed into, mixed with, or changed into the divinity, so that Christ is not consubstantial with usAttributed to Eutyches. No organised Church has held it.Chalcedon; and also the Oriental Orthodox, who anathematise Eutyches
    Miaphysitism"One incarnate nature of God the Word" (Cyril): one composite nature or hypostasis from two, divinity and humanity each remaining complete and unconfusedDioscorus (as he presented himself), Severus, the Oriental Orthodox ChurchesChalcedonians (historically), as an incorrect rejection of "two natures"
    Chalcedonian dyophysitismOne hypostasis (person) in two natures, unconfused and undividedCatholic, Eastern Orthodox, and most Protestant ChurchesOriental Orthodox (historically), as implying two subjects
    Church of the East dyophysitismTwo natures, two qnōmē, one parṣōpāChurch of the East (Babai the Great)Chalcedonians and Oriental Orthodox (historically), as "Nestorian"

    The prefix matters. Mia (μία) means "one" in the sense of a single united reality. Monos (μόνος) suggests "one alone". The Oriental Orthodox Churches use "miaphysite" and reject "monophysite". The distinction is not modern special pleading. Severus of Antioch wrote at length against the Eutychian Sergius the Grammarian and against the Julianists, who held that Christ's body was incorruptible before the resurrection. In doing so he defended the reality of Christ's human nature, activity and suffering.1

    Why did the division happen?

    Historians weigh several factors. Their relative importance remains debated.

    • Theology and terminology. The parties used physis in different senses (Key terms). Each heard the other's formula as heresy: "two natures" as Nestorian division, "one nature" as Eutychian confusion. Modern dialogues have concluded the disagreement was largely verbal, while acknowledging real differences in emphasis.
    • Loyalty to Cyril and Alexandria. In Egypt, Chalcedon's deposition of Dioscorus was felt as an attack on Cyril's see and legacy.
    • Imperial coercion. Forcible installation of Chalcedonian bishops, sometimes with troops, hardened resistance and associated Chalcedon with imperial power. Hence the name "Melkite" ("imperial") for the Chalcedonians of the East.
    • Language and regional identity. An older theory saw the schisms as expressions of Coptic and Syrian "nationalism" against Greek rule. A. H. M. Jones and W. H. C. Frend argued about this in the 1950s–70s, and most historians now consider it anachronistic. Anti-Chalcedonian leaders such as Severus and Timothy Aelurus wrote in Greek and thought of themselves as the true Church of the empire. Language and region did, however, shape how communities later remembered the councils.2
    • Jurisdiction. Chalcedon's canon 28 and its rearrangement of the Antiochene and Jerusalem jurisdictions gave ecclesiastical-political grievances a doctrinal expression.
    • The Arab conquests froze the division by ending imperial power to enforce or negotiate union.

    Notes

    1. Allen & Hayward 2004, introduction; Grillmeier 1975, vol. 2/2 (on Severus). ↩
    2. Frend 1972, introduction and conclusion; the nationalist thesis was criticised by A. H. M. Jones, "Were Ancient Heresies National or Social Movements in Disguise?", Journal of Theological Studies n.s. 10 (1959). ↩
