    Volume V · Diagram

    How the families of Churches formed

    Popular charts draw Christian history as a tree that splits cleanly at 431, 451 and 1054. The evidence supports a different picture. Each division has a zone of separation lasting decades or centuries, made up of contested councils, rival bishops, partial reconciliations and, eventually, distinct hierarchies. The diagram shows these zones as gradients rather than lines. Hover over or tap a band for details.

    Original diagram for this edition. The gradients indicate the approximate period over which separate hierarchies and broken communion became established. They are interpretive, not exact.

    • Church of the East: separate jurisdiction from 410/424; dyophysite formulation in 486; no reception of Ephesus.
    • Oriental Orthodox: rejection of Chalcedon from 451; separate hierarchy from c. 518–580.
    • Eastern Orthodox and Catholic: recurrent breaks (the Acacian schism 484–519, the Photian crisis 863–880); mutual excommunications in 1054 that targeted persons; a decisive popular estrangement after 1204; failed unions in 1274 and 1439; and a formal Orthodox rejection of Florence in 1484. See Volume IX.

    Volume V · Chapter 5

    Modern Christological dialogues

    From the 1960s, theologians of the separated Eastern Churches and of the Catholic Church re-examined the fifth-century disputes. They found substantial agreement in faith behind the opposed formulas. The dialogues did not restore communion, because questions of authority, the reception of councils and the status of persons anathematised by one side remain open. But they changed the official stance of several Churches towards the others.

    Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox

    • Aarhus (1964), Bristol (1967), Geneva (1970), Addis Ababa (1971). Unofficial consultations, held in connection with the World Council of Churches, concluded that the two families share the same Christological faith.
    • Official Joint Commission. Its First Agreed Statement (Anba Bishoy monastery, Egypt, 1989) and Second Agreed Statement (Chambésy, 1990) declared both families faithful to the same Orthodox Christology. They proposed that the anathemas pronounced against each other's councils and fathers be lifted. As of 2026 the Churches have not implemented that proposal by a common act of reception.1

    Catholic and Oriental Orthodox

    • 10 May 1973. Pope Paul VI and Coptic Pope Shenouda III signed a common declaration of faith in Christ.
    • 23 June 1984. Pope John Paul II and Syriac Orthodox Patriarch Ignatius Zakka I Iwas did the same. Their declaration also permitted limited pastoral sacramental sharing in cases of need.
    • 13 December 1996. John Paul II and Armenian Catholicos Karekin I.
    • Since 2003. An official Joint International Commission has met regularly. Its Executive Committee met in Rome on 12–13 May 2026 to assess twenty years of dialogue.2

    Catholic and Assyrian Church of the East

    On 11 November 1994 Pope John Paul II and Catholicos-Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV signed a Common Christological Declaration. It stated that the Catholic title "Mother of God" and the Assyrian "Mother of Christ our God and Saviour" express the same faith:

    We both recognize the legitimacy and rightness of these expressions of the same faith…

    Common Christological Declaration between the Catholic Church and the Assyrian Church of the East, 11 November 1994 (vatican.va). Short quotation from a copyrighted text. Q38 · checked

    The declaration attributes past divisions largely to misunderstanding. It does not establish full communion. In 2001 the Holy See recognised the validity of the ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari, a Eucharistic prayer that lacks an explicit institution narrative, in guidelines for Eucharistic sharing between the Chaldean Catholic and Assyrian Churches. A joint commission continues to meet; its seventeenth plenary was held in Rome on 27–28 October 2025.3

    What the dialogues did and did not do

    • Did: establish that the Christological formulas of 431 and 451 need not be read as contradictory confessions.
    • Did not: settle the status of the councils themselves, or of figures venerated by one side and anathematised by the other (Dioscorus and Severus; Leo; Nestorius and Theodore), or questions of church authority.

    Volume VI · 325–787 and later

    The Ecumenical Councils

    This volume studies, council by council, the seven councils that the Eastern Orthodox Church recognises as ecumenical, together with other councils and synods that shaped the period. Each of the seven is analysed under the same eleven headings so they can be compared.

    The narrative of the fourth- and fifth-century councils is given in Volume IV. To avoid repetition, the entries for Nicaea, Constantinople I, Ephesus and Chalcedon summarise that narrative and concentrate on the analytical headings.

    What made a council “ecumenical”?

    Oikoumenē meant "the inhabited world", in practice the Roman Empire. An "ecumenical" synod was in the first instance one summoned by the emperor for the whole empire. Being summoned as ecumenical did not guarantee recognition. The council of 449 was summoned as ecumenical and was rejected. Constantinople 381 was a regional Eastern council that was later accepted as ecumenical. What made a council's authority endure was its reception: acceptance by the Churches, and in particular by the five major sees and, in Western and later Catholic theology, by the bishop of Rome. How reception works, and whose acceptance is decisive, remains a point of difference between the traditions.

    The eleven headings used for each council

    A. Historical context · B. Participants · C. Political context · D. Theological issues · E. Competing arguments · F. Decisions · G. Reception · H. Consequences · I. Primary-source quotations · J. Historical controversies · K. Legacy

    See also the interactive Council table showing which traditions recognise which councils.

    Volume VI · First Ecumenical Council

    Nicaea I (325)

    A. Historical context
    The dispute between Arius and Bishop Alexander of Alexandria (from c. 318–321) had divided the Eastern episcopate. Constantine had just become sole emperor (324) and wanted religious unity. Other issues were outstanding too: the date of Easter, and the Melitian schism in Egypt. Narrative in Vol. IV ch. 5–6.
    B. Participants
    Between about 250 and 300 bishops, overwhelmingly from the Greek East; tradition later fixed the number at 318. Leading figures: Alexander of Alexandria with his deacon Athanasius; Eustathius of Antioch; Eusebius of Caesarea; Eusebius of Nicomedia; Marcellus of Ancyra; Ossius of Córdoba. Pope Silvester did not attend and was represented by the presbyters Vitus and Vincentius. Bishops also came from Persia (a "John the Persian" is listed in some subscription lists), Armenia and Gothia.1
    C. Political context
    Constantine convened the council, paid for travel, opened it in person and took part in debate. Eusebius credits him with proposing or endorsing homoousios. The council's sentences of exile were enforced by imperial authority.
    D. Theological issues
    Whether the Son is eternal and of the same divine being as the Father, or a creature brought into existence by the Father's will. Which terms could express the answer without falling into modalism (Sabellianism).
    E. Competing arguments
    Arius and his sympathisers: only the Father is unbegotten and without beginning; to say the Son is "from the Father's substance" implies division or emanation in God; Scripture calls the Son "firstborn of all creation" (Col. 1:15) and "created" (Prov. 8:22, LXX). Alexander and his allies: Scripture calls the Son God, Word, Wisdom and Image, eternal with the Father (John 1:1; Heb. 1:3); a creature cannot reveal or save; "Father" implies an eternal Son. Many bishops were uneasy with non-scriptural terminology but more uneasy with Arius' statements.
    F. Decisions
    The Creed with anathemas; twenty canons (including canon 6 on Alexandria, Rome and Antioch, canon 7 on Jerusalem, and canon 19 on followers of Paul of Samosata); a settlement of the Melitian schism; a decision for a common Easter. Arius was exiled with Theonas and Secundus.
    G. Reception
    Accepted by all historic Churches: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, the Church of the East (adopted at the Persian synod of 410), and the main Protestant confessions. In the decades after 325, however, its creed was contested and frequently bypassed. Its authority was secured only by the 360s–380s (Vol. IV ch. 7).
    H. Consequences
    Short term: renewed conflict, the rehabilitation of Arius (who died in 336, before he could be readmitted to communion), and the exile of Athanasius. Long term: the precedent of imperially summoned councils issuing binding creeds, and the use of non-scriptural technical language in dogma.
    I. Primary sources
    The Creed (quoted in full, Vol. IV ch. 6). Canon 6:

    Let the ancient customs in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis prevail, that the Bishop of Alexandria have jurisdiction in all these, since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also.

    Nicaea, canon 6. Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). The opening clause was checked; the remainder follows the same translation and was checked for sense. Q24 · partly checked
    J. Historical controversies
    The number of participants; how far Constantine shaped the creed; whether homoousios was proposed by Ossius or the Western delegation; the authenticity of the Arabic "canons of Nicaea", which are later compilations (Misconceptions). Canon 6 is read differently. Catholic commentators often see it as recognising a pre-existing Roman authority used as a model. Orthodox and many historians read it as recognising regional supra-metropolitan authority, with Rome cited as a parallel.2
    K. Legacy
    The defining moment of Trinitarian orthodoxy and the model of a general council. Its 1700th anniversary was marked jointly by Pope Leo XIV, Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew and other Christian leaders at İznik on 28 November 2025. Their joint declaration of 29 November called the council "a providential event of unity".3

    Notes

    1. The subscription lists are discussed by E. Honigmann and summarised in Hanson 1988, and Ayres 2004. ↩
    2. Nicaea, canon 6 (Tanner 1990, vol. 1); Dvornik 1966; Schatz 1996. ↩
    3. Joint Declaration of Pope Leo XIV and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, Istanbul, 29 November 2025 (vatican.va; ec-patr.org), consulted November 2026. ↩

    Volume VI · Second Ecumenical Council

    Constantinople I (381)

    A. Historical context
    The end of Homoian imperial policy after Valens' death (378). Theodosius' law Cunctos populos (380). A disputed succession at Antioch (Meletius vs Paulinus). The need to secure the Nicene faith in the capital, where Gregory of Nazianzus had led a small Nicene congregation. Narrative in Vol. IV ch. 9.
    B. Participants
    About 150 Eastern bishops (36 "Macedonians" attended but withdrew). No Western bishops and no Roman legates. Presidents: Meletius of Antioch (d. during the council), Gregory of Nazianzus (resigned), Nectarius. Egyptian bishops arrived late and objected to Gregory's appointment.1
    C. Political context
    Summoned by Theodosius. Its decisions were enforced by imperial law (CTh 16.1.3, 30 July 381, naming bishops in communion with whom orthodoxy was to be judged).
    D. Theological issues
    The divinity of the Holy Spirit; the remaining non-Nicene positions; Apollinarianism.
    E. Competing arguments
    The Pneumatomachians argued that Scripture does not call the Spirit "God" and that the Spirit is a ministering power. The Cappadocians argued from baptism in the threefold name, from the Spirit's work of sanctification and deification, and from worship. Only God can make us divine, and what is worshipped with the Father and Son must share their being.
    F. Decisions
    A doctrinal "tome" (lost). Canons 1–4 (Percival's numbering lists seven, but canons 5–7 are probably from a later synod of 382 or later): condemnation of heresies; limitation of bishops to their own civil "dioceses"; canon 3 on Constantinople's rank; invalidation of the ordination of Maximus the Cynic. The creed attributed to the council (see the debate in Vol. IV ch. 9).
    G. Reception
    Initially an Eastern synod. Its ecumenical standing was established when Chalcedon (451) read its creed alongside Nicaea's. Rome accepted its doctrine but not canon 3 until much later. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) recognised the Latin patriarch of Constantinople in second place; the Council of Florence (1439) listed the patriarchal order with Constantinople second. Accepted as ecumenical by Catholic, Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches, and recognised by the Church of the East.2
    H. Consequences
    Completion of the doctrine of the Trinity in conciliar form; elevation of Constantinople; the beginning of Alexandria–Constantinople rivalry, visible at Ephesus (431) and in 449–451.
    I. Primary sources
    The creed's article on the Spirit (Vol. IV ch. 9, Q11) and canon 3 (Q12).
    J. Historical controversies
    The origin of the creed; the authenticity and numbering of canons 5–7; whether the council intended canon 3 as a slight to Alexandria rather than Rome.3
    K. Legacy
    The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed is the most widely shared text in Christianity. Its original text, without the Filioque, became central to East–West controversy (Vol. VIII ch. 5).

    Notes

    1. Socrates, Church History 5.8 (NPNF II/2); Gregory of Nazianzus, De vita sua. See Hanson 1988 and Behr 2004. ↩
    2. On the creed, Kelly 1972; on its reception in the Church of the East, Baum & Winkler 2003. ↩
    3. Constantinople I, canon 3 (Tanner 1990, vol. 1); Dvornik 1966; Schatz 1996. ↩

    Volume VI · Third Ecumenical Council

    Ephesus (431)

    A. Historical context
    Nestorius' objections to the title Theotokos (428); Cyril's campaign; Celestine's Roman synod (430). Narrative in Vol. IV ch. 11.
    B. Participants
    About 150–200 bishops in Cyril's assembly, with Memnon of Ephesus and the Asian bishops. About 43 in John of Antioch's counter-council. The Roman legates were the bishops Arcadius and Projectus and the presbyter Philip. Nestorius was in the city but refused to attend.1
    C. Political context
    Theodosius II summoned the council. His commissioner Candidian opposed the opening of 22 June. Court factions, the empress Pulcheria (sympathetic to Cyril), and gifts to officials shaped the outcome.
    D. Theological issues
    Whether the eternal Word is the single subject of the incarnate life, so that Mary is truly Theotokos; how to speak of the union of divinity and humanity.
    E. Competing arguments
    Cyril: the Word himself was born, suffered "in the flesh" and died; to deny this divides Christ and empties salvation. Nestorius: the divine nature cannot be born or suffer; Scripture attributes these things to the man; Christ is one prosopon of union of two complete natures; Theotokos risks pagan "mother goddess" language and Apollinarianism.
    F. Decisions
    Deposition of Nestorius. Approval of Cyril's Second Letter to Nestorius as consonant with Nicaea; the status of the Third Letter and Twelve Anathemas is debated. Canon 7 against "a different faith". Condemnation of the Messalians and of Pelagian supporters.
    G. Reception
    Recognised as ecumenical by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches. Rejected by the Church of the East. Its reception depended on the reunion of 433, and Chalcedon later read Ephesus as including the Formula of Reunion.2
    H. Consequences
    Precedent for the term Theotokos and for single-subject Christology. Grievance in the Antiochene and Persian Churches. The question of "two natures" was left open and re-erupted in 448.
    I. Primary sources
    Q14 (Cyril's first anathema); Q15 (sentence against Nestorius); canon 7:

    …the holy Synod decreed that it is unlawful for any man to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith as a rival to that established by the holy Fathers assembled with the Holy Ghost in Nicæa.

    Ephesus, canon 7. Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). The opening was checked; the final clause follows the same translation. Q16 · partly checked
    J. Historical controversies
    Whether Cyril's assembly was a valid council or a partisan synod; whether Nestorius actually taught "two sons". His later Book of Heracleides, rediscovered in Syriac in 1889, shows him accepting much of Chalcedon's language.3 Whether the Twelve Anathemas were formally adopted.
    K. Legacy
    Theotokos became the defining Marian title of the Chalcedonian and Oriental Orthodox traditions (Key terms). The council remains the main point of separation from the Church of the East, a separation softened by the 1994 declaration.

    Notes

    1. Price & Graumann 2020; McGuckin 1994. ↩
    2. Price & Gaddis 2005; Grillmeier 1975. ↩
    3. Nestorius, The Bazaar of Heracleides, trans. G. R. Driver and Leonard Hodgson (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1925). See Grillmeier 1975, vol. 1, and Brock 1996. ↩

    Volume VI · Fourth Ecumenical Council

    Chalcedon (451)

    A. Historical context
    The condemnation of Eutyches (448), Leo's Tome (449), the "Robber Council" of Ephesus (449), the death of Theodosius II (450). Narrative in Vol. IV ch. 12.
    B. Participants
    About 350–370 bishops, almost all Eastern; tradition says 630. Roman legates Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, Lucentius of Asculum and the presbyter Boniface. About 19 high imperial officials directed proceedings. Dioscorus attended the first session as a defendant.1
    C. Political context
    Marcian and Pulcheria wanted to reverse 449 and restore unity, and pressed for a written definition. Marcian attended Session 6 in person. Imperial commissioners managed the agenda, the order of business and the drafting.
    D. Theological issues
    How to affirm both the single subject (Cyril) and the completeness and distinction of divinity and humanity (Leo, the Antiochenes). Whether "in two natures" was compatible with Cyril.
    E. Competing arguments
    Dioscorus and his supporters: Cyril's "one incarnate nature"; "from two natures" is acceptable, "in two natures" is Nestorian; Ephesus canon 7 forbids a new definition. Leo and the Easterners loyal to Flavian: the Tome's "each form does what is proper to it"; to deny two natures after the union is Eutychian. Many bishops, including some of Dioscorus' former supporters, wanted Cyril without Eutyches. Passages of the Tome were compared with Cyril's writings before it was approved.
    F. Decisions
    The Definition of Faith (Q20). Deposition of Dioscorus. Rehabilitation of Theodoret and Ibas, after they anathematised Nestorius. Jerusalem raised to a patriarchate. Twenty-seven canons plus canons 28–30. The definition reaffirmed the creeds of 325 and 381, Cyril's Second Letter and the Letter to John, and Leo's Tome.
    G. Reception
    Rejected by most of Egypt and much of Syria, and by Armenia (after 506/555). Accepted by Rome, which rejected canon 28, and by the Greek Church. Not part of the Church of the East's tradition. Accepted as ecumenical by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and most Protestant Churches.2
    H. Consequences
    The division between Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Churches (Vol. V ch. 2). Two further councils (553, 680–81) tried to reconcile the two. Canon 28 strained Rome–Constantinople relations (Vol. VII ch. 3).
    I. Primary sources
    Definition (Q20); acclamation "Peter has spoken thus through Leo" (Q19); canon 28:

    For the Fathers rightly granted privileges to the throne of old Rome, because it was the royal city. And the One Hundred and Fifty most religious Bishops, actuated by the same consideration, gave equal privileges (ἴσα πρεσβεῖα) to the most holy throne of New Rome, justly judging that the city which is honoured with the Sovereignty and the Senate, and enjoys equal privileges with the old imperial Rome, should in ecclesiastical matters also be magnified as she is, and rank next after her…

    Chalcedon, canon 28. Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q21 · checked
    Canon 9 (on appeals):

    And if a bishop or clergyman should have a difference with the metropolitan of the province, let him have recourse to the Exarch of the Diocese, or to the throne of the Imperial City of Constantinople, and there let it be tried.

    Chalcedon, canon 9 (final clause). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14. Checked. Q22 · checked
    J. Historical controversies
    "In" or "from" two natures in the original text. Whether canon 28 was validly passed (in the legates' absence) and what "equal privileges" meant. Whether Leo's confirmation (Letter 114, March 453) was required for the council's validity or was an act of reception. How far the outcome was imposed by the state. Whether the Tome was "received" on its own authority or after examination (Q19 discussion).3
    K. Legacy
    The Chalcedonian Definition remains the reference point for Christology in Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant theology. It is also the most important single cause of division among the ancient Churches, and the subject of the most productive modern dialogues (Vol. V ch. 5).

    Notes

    1. Attendance lists and the officials present at session 1: Price & Gaddis 2005, vol. 1. ↩
    2. Frend 1972; Menze 2008; Grillmeier 1975. ↩
    3. Leo's Tome and its reception: Price & Gaddis 2005, vol. 2, sessions 2–4; DH 290–295 (DH). ↩

    Volume VI · Fifth Ecumenical Council

    Constantinople II (553)

    A. Historical context
    Justinian sought to reconcile the anti-Chalcedonians without abandoning Chalcedon. Anti-Chalcedonians objected especially that Chalcedon had rehabilitated Theodoret and Ibas and failed to condemn Theodore of Mopsuestia. In 543/544 Justinian issued an edict condemning these "Three Chapters": the person and works of Theodore, certain writings of Theodoret against Cyril, and a letter of Ibas to Mari the Persian. He also condemned Origenist teachings, partly in response to disputes in Palestinian monasteries.
    B. Participants
    About 150–165 bishops, almost all Eastern, under Patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople. Pope Vigilius was in Constantinople, having been effectively detained there since 547, but refused to attend.1
    C. Political context
    The council's agenda was Justinian's. The treatment of Vigilius is the period's most striking case of imperial pressure on a pope. In 551 Vigilius took refuge in the church of St Euphemia at Chalcedon, and the council later struck his name from the diptychs. He issued a Constitutum (May 553) refusing to condemn the dead who had died in communion with the Church. After the council he reversed himself and accepted its decisions (December 553 and a second Constitutum, February 554). He died on his way back to Rome in 555.2
    D. Theological issues
    Whether one could condemn persons who had died in the Church's communion. Whether condemning the Three Chapters undermined Chalcedon. How to interpret Chalcedon in a Cyrillian sense: "Neo-Chalcedonianism", which used the formula "one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh" and allowed "one incarnate nature" if correctly understood.
    E. Competing arguments
    For condemnation: Theodore's Christology was the source of Nestorius' error, and removing it would show the anti-Chalcedonians that Chalcedon was not Nestorian. Against (most Western bishops, especially in Africa and northern Italy): Chalcedon had accepted Ibas and Theodoret; condemning them impugned Chalcedon; condemning the dead was unprecedented.
    F. Decisions
    Fourteen anathemas (the "Capitula") defining Chalcedon in Cyrillian terms and condemning the Three Chapters; condemnation of Origen, whose name appears in anathema 11. The fifteen anathemas against Origenism usually attached to this council were probably adopted by the bishops before the council formally opened.
    G. Reception
    Accepted by the Greek Church and, after Vigilius' acceptance, by Rome. The bishops of northern Italy (Aquileia, Milan) broke communion with Rome in the "Schism of the Three Chapters", which lasted in Aquileia until about 698–700. The council did not reconcile the anti-Chalcedonians. The Church of the East rejected it as a condemnation of its revered Interpreter.3
    H. Consequences
    Theological clarification of Chalcedon in a Cyrillian direction, which is standard in Byzantine theology. Further alienation of the Church of the East. Damage to papal prestige in the West.
    I. Primary sources

    If anyone defends the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia, who has said that the Word of God is one person, but that another person is Christ…

    Constantinople II, anathema 12 (opening). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q36 · checked
    J. Historical controversies
    Whether the anti-Origenist canons belong to the council. How far later Byzantine summaries reshape the acta (the Greek acta survive only in part; the Latin version may have been edited to favour Vigilius). Whether Vigilius' reversal was free.
    K. Legacy
    Defines the Byzantine reading of Chalcedon. A test case in debates about the relationship of pope and council.

    Notes

    1. Price 2009, vol. 1. ↩
    2. Price 2009, vol. 1, introduction; Meyendorff 1989, ch. 7. ↩
    3. Price 2009; Baum & Winkler 2003; on Aquileia, Chadwick 2003. ↩

    Volume VI · Sixth Ecumenical Council

    Constantinople III (680–681)

    A. Historical context
    To win back the anti-Chalcedonians in the provinces under threat from Persia and then from the Arabs, Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople and Emperor Heraclius promoted the formula of "one activity" (energeia) in Christ (Monenergism, 630s). After protests led by Sophronius of Jerusalem, this became the formula of "one will" (thelēma), set out in the Ekthesis (638) (Monothelitism). Pope Honorius (625–638), in correspondence with Sergius, had spoken of "one will" in Christ. Opposition was led by Maximus the Confessor and by Rome. The Lateran Synod of 649 under Pope Martin I condemned Monothelitism. Emperor Constans II had Martin arrested and exiled to Cherson, where he died (655). Maximus was mutilated and exiled, and died in 662.
    B. Participants
    About 150 bishops at the final session (fewer at first). Emperor Constantine IV presided at many sessions. Papal legates brought the letter of Pope Agatho and a Roman synod. Patriarch George of Constantinople came to accept dyothelitism. Macarius of Antioch defended Monothelitism and was deposed.1
    C. Political context
    By 680 Egypt and Syria had been lost to the Arab caliphate, so concessions to win over the anti-Chalcedonians no longer had a political purpose. Constantine IV sought reconciliation with Rome.
    D. Theological issues
    Whether will and activity belong to the person (so one in Christ) or to the nature (so two in Christ). Whether two wills imply conflict within Christ.
    E. Competing arguments
    Monothelites: one subject must have one will; two wills would mean two willing subjects in conflict (Gethsemane being read as the human will following the divine without resistance). Dyothelites (Maximus, Agatho): will is a property of nature; if Christ has a complete human nature he has a human will; "what is not assumed is not healed", and that applies to the human will. In Gethsemane ("not my will but yours") the human will freely submits to the divine.
    F. Decisions
    A definition affirming two natural wills and two natural activities. Condemnation of Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, Macarius of Antioch, and Pope Honorius.
    G. Reception
    Accepted in Rome by Pope Leo II (682), who confirmed the condemnation of Honorius, and by the Greek Church. Its reception among the Maronites is a contested historical question (Vol. XIII ch. 5). Not received by Oriental Orthodox or the Church of the East, who were not parties to it.2
    H. Consequences
    The end of imperial attempts to reach Christological compromise. Doctrinal unity between Rome and Constantinople restored for a time. The condemnation of a pope by an ecumenical council became a major point in nineteenth-century debates on papal infallibility.
    I. Primary sources

    …we likewise declare that in him are two natural wills and two natural operations indivisibly, inconvertibly, inseparably, inconfusedly, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers. And these two natural wills are not contrary the one to the other (God forbid!) as the impious heretics assert, but his human will follows and that not as resisting and reluctant, but rather as subject to his divine and omnipotent will.

    Constantinople III, Definition of Faith (Session 18, 16 September 681). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q33 · checked
    The Session 13 sentence rejects the letters of Sergius and "Honorius some time Pope of Old Rome" as "foreign to the apostolic dogmas" (Q34, checked).
    J. Historical controversies
    The "Honorius question". Was Honorius condemned as a heretic, or for negligence in failing to suppress heresy? Leo II's confirmation speaks of his having permitted the faith to be stained, and Catholic apologists of 1870 stressed this. Did his letters intend a moral unity of will rather than a single faculty? Critics of papal infallibility at Vatican I (notably Döllinger and Hefele) argued that the condemnation was incompatible with the doctrine.3
    K. Legacy
    Completed the classical Christological settlement. Maximus the Confessor became a central figure in both Orthodox and Catholic theology.

    Notes

    1. Definition: DH 553–559 (DH); Tanner 1990, vol. 1. See Meyendorff 1989. ↩
    2. Meyendorff 1989; on the Maronites, Moosa 1986 and Salibi 1988. ↩
    3. Constantinople III, definition: DH 553–559 (DH). See O’Malley 2018 for its use at Vatican I. ↩

    Volume VI · Seventh Ecumenical Council

    Nicaea II (787)

    A. Historical context
    Byzantine iconoclasm: imperial policy against religious images, conventionally dated from Leo III (from 726/730) and certainly pursued by Constantine V. Constantine V's council of Hieria (754) condemned images. After his death, Empress Irene, regent for her son Constantine VI, reversed this policy. A first attempt to hold a council in Constantinople (786) was broken up by iconoclast soldiers. Narrative in Vol. VIII ch. 3.
    B. Participants
    About 350 bishops, together with many monks. Presided over by Patriarch Tarasius, a former lay official. Legates of Pope Hadrian I attended, as did two monks claiming to represent the Eastern patriarchs under Islamic rule, whose credentials were questionable.
    C. Political context
    Irene's regency; the purge of iconoclast officers; Byzantine efforts to improve relations with Rome. Frankish exclusion from the process later fed Charlemagne's hostile response.
    D. Theological issues
    Whether images of Christ, Mary and the saints are idolatrous. Whether an image of Christ either divides his natures (by depicting only the humanity) or confuses them (by claiming to depict the divinity), as Hieria had argued. Whether images may be venerated.
    E. Competing arguments
    Iconoclasts: the prohibition of images in the Decalogue (Exod. 20:4); the only true image of Christ is the Eucharist; images cannot depict divinity. Iconophiles (John of Damascus, Patriarch Germanos, later Theodore the Studite and Nikephoros): the incarnation made the invisible God visible, so to refuse to depict Christ is to deny the incarnation. Images depict the person (hypostasis), not a nature. The veneration given to images passes to their prototype (Basil, Q10). Veneration (proskynēsis) is distinct from worship (latreia), which is due to God alone.
    F. Decisions
    A definition restoring images and their veneration. Twenty-two canons, including canon 7 requiring relics in the consecration of churches. Condemnation of Hieria.
    G. Reception
    Iconoclasm was renewed in Byzantium (815–843). The decisive restoration came on 11 March 843, still celebrated as the "Triumph of Orthodoxy" on the first Sunday of Lent. Rome accepted the council. The Franks, working from a defective Latin translation that seemed to require images to be adored like the Trinity, rejected it in the Opus Caroli regis (Libri Carolini) and at the Council of Frankfurt (794). The West came to count it as the seventh ecumenical council only gradually, by the late ninth century. Most Protestant traditions reject its decisions on images.
    H. Consequences
    It fixed the theology of the icon that is central to Orthodox identity. It exposed the difference in religious culture between Byzantium and the Frankish West. With the Filioque, it supplied an issue in Carolingian polemic against the "Greeks".
    I. Primary sources

    For the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented.

    Nicaea II, Decree (Definition) of the Council. Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q35 · checked
    J. Historical controversies
    When iconoclasm began, and how far Leo III was an active iconoclast. Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon argue that most narrative evidence for the 720s–730s comes from later iconophile writers and is unreliable.1 The representativeness of the "Eastern" delegates. The precise Frankish misunderstanding.2
    K. Legacy
    The last council recognised as ecumenical by both Catholic and Orthodox Churches. A pivotal moment in the history of Christian art.

    Notes

    1. Brubaker & Haldon 2011; Nicaea II, DH 600–603 (DH); Price 2018. ↩
    2. Brubaker & Haldon 2011, chs. 2–3; Noble 2009, chs. 4–5; Price 2018, introduction. ↩

    Volume VI · Other councils

    Other councils and synods of the period

    These councils are not counted as ecumenical by the Eastern Orthodox. Several of them are central to the history of authority and division.

    Antioch, “Dedication Council” (341)

    About 90–97 Eastern bishops met for the dedication of Constantine's Golden Church. They produced several creeds avoiding homoousios and rejected Marcellus. Its canons, possibly originating from an earlier Antiochene synod (c. 328), entered Eastern and Western canon law. They include canon 9, on the metropolitan system, and canons 4 and 12, on deposed bishops appealing to the emperor.1

    Serdica (c. 343)

    Summoned by Constans and Constantius to resolve the Athanasius affair. The Easterners refused to sit with Athanasius and Marcellus, met separately, and excommunicated Julius of Rome. The Westerners, under Ossius, issued canons, including canons 3–5 (Latin numbering varies) providing for a deposed bishop to appeal to the bishop of Rome, who might order a retrial by neighbouring bishops:

    …let us, if it seem good to your charity, honour the memory of Peter the Apostle, and let those who gave judgment write to Julius, the bishop of Rome, so that, if necessary, the case may be retried by the bishops of the neighbouring provinces and let him appoint arbiters…

    Serdica, canon 3 (Greek). Trans. Percival, NPNF II/14 (1900). Checked. Q25 · checked
    Rome later cited these canons as "Nicene", a mistake exposed by the African bishops in the Apiarius affair (419). The Eastern Church received Serdica's canons through the Trullan council (692).2

    Ephesus II (449)

    Summoned as ecumenical and presided over by Dioscorus. It reinstated Eutyches and deposed Flavian, Domnus, Ibas and Theodoret. Annulled at Chalcedon. Leo's term latrocinium stuck. The Oriental Orthodox do not count it among the ecumenical councils, but they reject the condemnation of Dioscorus that followed it. See Vol. IV ch. 12.

    Lateran Synod (649)

    A Roman synod under Martin I, with substantial input from Maximus and Greek monks in Rome. It condemned Monothelitism and the imperial Typos (648). Its acts were composed in Greek and Latin. Recent research (Riedinger) shows they were drafted in advance, largely by Greek monks.3

    Quinisext / Council in Trullo (691–692)

    Convened by Justinian II to issue the disciplinary canons that the fifth and sixth councils had not issued (hence "fifth-sixth"). Its 102 canons form the backbone of Orthodox canon law. Several criticised Roman practices: canon 13 defends married priests living with their wives; canon 55 condemns fasting on Saturdays in Lent as practised in Rome; canon 36 re-enacts Constantinople 3 and Chalcedon 28. Pope Sergius I refused to sign, and an imperial attempt to arrest him was thwarted by Italian troops. Anastasius the Librarian (9th century) reports that Rome later accepted the canons only insofar as they did not contradict earlier canons, papal decrees and good custom.

    Hieria (754)

    About 338 bishops under Constantine V condemned images. No patriarchs were present: the see of Constantinople was vacant, and the others were under Islamic rule. Its definition survives because it was quoted for refutation at Nicaea II. Its decisions were repudiated in 787.

    Frankfurt (794)

    A Frankish synod under Charlemagne, with papal legates present. It condemned Spanish Adoptionism and rejected the "Greek synod" on images, meaning Nicaea II as known through a faulty translation. See Vol. VIII ch. 3.

    Constantinople 861, 869–870 and 879–880 (the Photian councils)

    861: with papal legates present, confirmed the deposition of Ignatius and the election of Photius. Pope Nicholas I repudiated his legates' actions. 869–870: under Basil I and in the presence of Hadrian II's legates, condemned Photius and restored Ignatius. Counted by the Catholic Church as the Eighth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople IV), a count that became established in Western canon law from the late eleventh century. 879–880: with the legates of John VIII, restored Photius, annulled the council of 869–870, and reaffirmed the creed without additions. Some Orthodox theologians call it the "Eighth Ecumenical Council", though it has not been formally proclaimed as such. See Vol. VIII ch. 6.

    Constantinople 1341, 1347, 1351 (Hesychast councils)

    Endorsed Gregory Palamas' distinction between God's unknowable essence and his uncreated energies against Barlaam of Calabria and Gregory Akindynos. They are authoritative in Orthodoxy, and some Orthodox writers call them a "ninth ecumenical council". See Vol. IX ch. 6.

    Medieval Western councils relevant to East–West relations

    Lateran IV (1215: canon 4 on Greek practices, and canon 5 on patriarchal order), Lyon II (1274) and Ferrara-Florence (1438–1445). See Vol. IX ch. 4. The full treatment of medieval Western councils belongs to Volume X.

    Notes

    1. Antioch (341), canons 4 and 12, in NPNF II/14. ↩
    2. Trullo, canon 2, received the canons of Serdica (NPNF II/14). See Erickson 1991. ↩
    3. Rudolf Riedinger's critical edition of the Lateran Council of 649 (ACO, ser. 2, vol. 1, 1984) underlies this conclusion. English translation and analysis in Price, Booth & Cubitt 2014; Ekonomou 2007. ↩

    Volume VII · c. 96–1054, with modern dialogue

    The Rise of Rome and Constantinople

    No question has divided Catholic and Orthodox Christians more persistently than the authority of the bishop of Rome. Both sides appeal to the first millennium, often to the same texts. This volume sets out what those texts say, when they were written, and how each tradition reads them. It does not assume that the structures of either the modern Catholic or the modern Orthodox Church existed in the same form in the early centuries.

    In this volume

    1. The early Church of Rome (c. 50–260)
    2. Metropolitans, Nicaea and Serdica
    3. The rise of Constantinople
    4. Papal theory from Damasus to Gregory the Great
    5. The Pentarchy
    6. Primacy, supremacy and the modern dialogue

    Volume VII · Chapter 1

    The early Church of Rome (c. 50–260)

    Peter and Paul in Rome

    Paul's letter to the Romans (c. 57) shows a Christian community already established in the capital, which he had not founded. Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome. No New Testament text explicitly says that Peter went to Rome. 1 Peter 5:13 sends greetings from "Babylon", widely read as a code name for Rome. Early non-biblical evidence includes:

    • 1 Clement 5 (c. 96): presents Peter and Paul as recent "pillars" who suffered martyrdom, without stating where.
    • Ignatius, Romans 4.3 (c. 110): tells the Romans, "I do not command you as Peter and Paul did".
    • Dionysius of Corinth (c. 170): Peter and Paul taught in Italy and were martyred at the same time.
    • The Roman presbyter Gaius (c. 200): could show the "trophies" (tropaia) of the apostles on the Vatican hill and the Ostian Way. Both Dionysius and Gaius are quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25.

    Excavations under St Peter's (1940s–1950s) found a modest shrine of about 160, matching Gaius' "trophy". Whether bones found nearby are Peter's is not established.

    Assessment. Most historians, including many Protestant and secular scholars, accept that Peter was in Rome and died there under Nero (c. 64–67). The claim that Peter was Rome's first bishop and governed it for twenty-five years is a later tradition. It is dogmatically significant for Catholic teaching () but is not documented in first-century sources.1

    When did Rome have a single bishop?

    1 Clement is sent in the name of "the Church of God which sojourns at Rome", not of a named bishop. Clement's name comes from later tradition. The letter speaks of "bishops and deacons" or "presbyters" in the plural. The Shepherd of Hermas (2nd c.) also refers to "the presbyters who preside over the Church". Many historians (for example Peter Lampe and Allen Brent) conclude that Rome was led by a group of presbyter-bishops until the mid-second century. On this view a single ruling bishop (monepiscopacy) is clearly attested from about the time of Anicetus (c. 155–166). Others argue for an earlier presiding figure within the college. The succession lists given by Irenaeus (c. 180) and Hegesippus show that by the late second century Rome's Church traced its continuity through a single line of names.2

    Owing, dear brethren, to the sudden and successive calamitous events which have happened to ourselves, we feel that we have been somewhat tardy in turning our attention to the points respecting which you consulted us…

    1 Clement 1.1 (Rome to Corinth, c. 96). Trans. Roberts and Donaldson, ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q26 · checked

    The letter intervenes in a dispute at Corinth, where presbyters had been deposed. Catholic writers have seen in it an early exercise of Roman responsibility for other Churches. Others note that it presents itself as fraternal counsel, not a judicial ruling, and that Corinth had apparently "consulted" Rome.

    Ignatius and Irenaeus

    Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the Church which has obtained mercy … which also presides in the place of the region of the Romans … and which presides over love…

    Ignatius of Antioch, To the Romans, salutation (c. 110). Trans. Roberts and Donaldson, ANF 1 (1885). Checked. Q27 · checked

    Ignatius addresses Rome with uniquely elaborate praise and, unusually, names no bishop there. "Presiding in love" (prokathēmenē tēs agapēs) has been read as primacy in charity or as presiding over the "love-feast" (the community of the Churches).

    …by indicating that tradition derived from the apostles, of the very great, the very ancient, and universally known Church founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul … For it is a matter of necessity that every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its pre-eminent authority…

    Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.2 (c. 180). Trans. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF 1 (1885). The original Greek is lost; the Latin reads ad hanc enim ecclesiam propter potentiorem principalitatem necesse est omnem convenire ecclesiam. Some editions read potiorem, as printed in the ANF bracket. English text checked; Latin given from the standard editions. Q28 · checked

    This is the most debated sentence in early ecclesiology. Convenire can mean "agree with" or "resort to". Potentior principalitas may mean "more powerful origin" (apostolic foundation) or "superior authority". Irenaeus' argument is that the true apostolic tradition can be found in any apostolic Church through its succession of bishops. Rome is his example because "it would be very tedious, in such a volume as this, to reckon up the successions of all the Churches".

    Victor and Stephen

    • Victor (c. 189–199) tried to excommunicate the Churches of Asia, which kept Easter on 14 Nisan (the Quartodecimans). Irenaeus and others rebuked him, and the Asian bishops did not comply. Victor's attempt shows a Roman claim to wide authority. The resistance shows that the claim was not accepted as binding.3
    • Stephen (254–257) clashed with Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea over rebaptising those baptised by heretics. Firmilian's letter mocks Stephen for boasting of his succession from Peter.4 Cyprian rejected Rome's position:

      Nor ought custom, which had crept in among some, to prevent the truth from prevailing and conquering; for custom without truth is the antiquity of error.

      Cyprian, Ep. 73.9 (ANF numbering; Ep. 74 in modern editions), to Pompey, against Stephen’s letter (256). Trans. Ernest Wallis, ANF 5 (1886). Checked. Q30 · checked
    Scholarly debate: Cyprian’s “primacy text”

    Cyprian's treatise On the Unity of the Church, chapter 4, survives in two versions. One of them, the "Primacy Text", adds that "primacy is given to Peter" and refers to the "chair of Peter". The nineteenth-century ANF editor (A. C. Coxe) declared the additions "beyond all question spurious".5 The Jesuit scholar Maurice Bévenot argued in the 1930s–60s, and most scholars now accept, that both versions are Cyprian's. On this view he wrote the Primacy Text first and revised it during his quarrel with Stephen. Even in the Primacy Text, Cyprian's "chair of Peter" is a symbol of unity that every bishop shares, not a jurisdiction belonging to Rome alone.

    Notes

    1. For the evidence, see Schatz 1996, ch. 1, and Lampe 2003, parts 1 and 5. ↩
    2. Lampe 2003, part 5, ch. 41; Schatz 1996, ch. 1. ↩
    3. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.23–25. ↩
    4. Cyprian, Ep. 74 (ANF numbering; Firmilian's letter = Ep. 75 in modern editions), §17. ↩
    5. ANF 5, notes to De unitate 4. Checked: the note reads that the passage "is beyond all question spurious". ↩

    Volume VII · Chapter 2

    Metropolitans, Nicaea and Serdica

    By the fourth century, bishops were organised in provinces matching Roman civil provinces. Each was headed by the bishop of the provincial capital, the . Nicaea's canons 4–5 confirm this system. Canon 6 recognises that some sees exercised authority beyond a single province:

    • Alexandria over Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis "since the like is customary for the bishop of Rome also" (Q24);
    • Antioch and "other provinces" retaining their privileges;
    • Jerusalem (canon 7) honoured, without prejudice to its metropolitan, Caesarea.1

    The canon grounds these powers in "ancient custom", not in apostolic foundation or in civil rank.

    The canons of Serdica (c. 343) gave the bishop of Rome a defined appellate role: to order a retrial by neighbouring bishops (Q25). These canons are the earliest conciliar legislation conferring a specific jurisdiction on Rome beyond its own region. They were Western canons from a council the Easterners had boycotted. When Rome cited them as Nicene in the Apiarius affair (418–424), the African bishops checked copies from the East and found no such canon. They wrote to Pope Celestine (c. 424/5) asking him not to receive appeals from Africa.2

    In the same period the bishops of Rome began issuing decretals, letters answering questions in the style of imperial rescripts. The first surviving example is Siricius' letter to Himerius of Tarragona (385). Damasus (366–384) and his successors increasingly presented Rome as the "Apostolic See" (sedes apostolica) whose authority derived from Peter.3

    Notes

    1. Nicaea, canons 4–7 (Tanner 1990, vol. 1; NPNF II/14). ↩
    2. The African correspondence (the letter Optaremus) is in the Codex Canonum Ecclesiae Africanae; NPNF II/14. ↩
    3. Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona (385), the earliest surviving decretal: DH 181–185 (DH). See Schatz 1996. ↩

    Volume VII · Chapter 3

    The rise of Constantinople

    Byzantium was a modest suffragan see of Heraclea in Thrace when Constantine refounded it as his capital (324–330). Within a century its bishop was the most powerful in the East. The steps can be traced:

    1. 381. Constantinople I, canon 3: "prerogative of honour next after the bishop of Rome, because Constantinople is new Rome" (Q12). The justification is political.
    2. c. 381–451. Constantinople's bishops in practice adjudicated disputes and consecrated bishops in Thrace, Asia and Pontus. John Chrysostom, for example, deposed bishops in Asia in 401–402. The "home synod" (synodos endēmousa) of bishops visiting the capital became a standing tribunal.
    3. 451. Chalcedon, canons 9 and 17, allowed appeals to "the throne of Constantinople" (Q22). Canon 28 confirmed "equal privileges" with Rome and gave Constantinople the right to ordain the metropolitans of the Pontic, Asian and Thracian dioceses (Q21).

    Leo's rejection of canon 28

    The Roman legates protested canon 28 at Session 16. Leo refused to confirm it. He wrote to Marcian, to Pulcheria and to Anatolius of Constantinople (Letters 104–106, May 452) that it violated the Nicene canons and the rights of Alexandria and Antioch:

    Let it be enough for Anatolius that by the aid of your piety and by my favour and approval he has obtained the bishopric of so great a city. Let him not disdain a city which is royal, though he cannot make it an Apostolic See…

    Leo I, Letter 104.3, to the emperor Marcian (22 May 452). Trans. Feltoe, NPNF II/12 (1895). Checked. Q23 · checked

    The exchange captures two principles of ecclesiastical rank. Rome grounded rank in apostolic foundation, above all Peter's. Constantinople and much Eastern practice grounded it in a city's place in the empire, while acknowledging Rome's precedence. The East continued to apply canon 28, and the Quinisext council re-enacted it in 692 (canon 36).1 On the meaning of "equal privileges", see ch. 6.

    “Ecumenical Patriarch”

    From the late fifth or early sixth century the bishop of Constantinople was styled "ecumenical patriarch" in imperial documents and synodal acts. The title probably meant "patriarch of the imperial capital" rather than "universal bishop". When John IV "the Faster" used it in synodal acts (587/588 and 595), Pope Gregory I protested vigorously (ch. 4).2

    Justinian's legislation gave the order of sees legal form. His Novel 131 (545) declared that the pope of Old Rome is "first of all priests" and the archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, holds second place, following the canons of the councils.3

    Notes

    1. Chalcedon, canon 28 (Price & Gaddis 2005, vol. 3); Trullo, canon 36 (NPNF II/14). ↩
    2. Gregory I, letters of 595 to John IV of Constantinople, the emperor Maurice and the empress Constantina (Registrum, book 5; English in NPNF II/12–13). ↩
    3. Justinian, Novel 131.2 (545). Paraphrased. On Justinian's ecclesiastical legislation, see Dagron 2003, ch. 9, and Meyendorff 1989, ch. 6. ↩

    Volume VII · Chapter 4

    Papal theory from Damasus to Gregory the Great

    Leo I (440–461)

    Leo the Great gave the most developed early statement of Roman primacy. In his sermons on the anniversary of his consecration, Peter speaks and acts in his successor. The bishop of Rome is Peter's "unworthy heir" (indignus heres) and exercises the care of all the Churches. In a letter to his vicar at Thessalonica he described a graded structure culminating in Rome:

    …that certain whose appointment is in the greater cities should undertake a fuller responsibility, through whom the care of the universal Church should converge towards Peter's one seat, and nothing anywhere should be separated from its Head.

    Leo I, Letter 14.11, to Anastasius of Thessalonica (c. 446). Trans. Feltoe, NPNF II/12 (1895). Checked. Q31 · checked

    Leo's claims were real and far-reaching. They were also exercised mainly in the West and in Illyricum. In the East his authority was recognised chiefly when it supported Eastern orthodoxy, as with the Tome, and resisted when it did not, as with canon 28.

    Gelasius and the “two powers” (494)

    During the Acacian schism, Pope Gelasius I wrote to the emperor Anastasius I. His letter became the foundational Western text on church and state:

    Duo quippe sunt, imperator auguste, quibus principaliter mundus hic regitur: auctoritas sacrata pontificum et regalis potestas.

    “There are two, august emperor, by which this world is chiefly ruled: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power.”

    Gelasius I, Letter 12 (Famuli vestrae pietatis), to Anastasius I (494). Latin as in the standard edition (Thiel, Epistolae Romanorum Pontificum, 1868). Translation by this edition. The Latin was not checked against the edition during preparation; see register. Q40 · not re-checked

    Gelasius distinguished auctoritas (moral authority) from potestas (executive power). He insisted that in sacred matters the emperor must submit to the bishops, "and above all to the bishop of that see which the Most High wished to be pre-eminent". Byzantine political theology, by contrast, developed the ideal of symphōnia (harmony) between priesthood and empire, set out in the preface to Justinian's Novel 6 (535).1

    The Formula of Hormisdas (519)

    To end the Acacian schism, Constantinople's patriarch John II (28 March 519), followed by most Eastern bishops, signed a formula drafted by Pope Hormisdas.2 It asserted that in the Apostolic See "the catholic religion has always been kept undefiled", alluding to Matthew 16:18. Catholic theologians, including at Vatican I, cited it as early Eastern acknowledgement of Roman doctrinal authority. Orthodox historians note that it was signed under imperial pressure, that Patriarch John added a statement of the unity of the sees of Old and New Rome, and that it did not prevent later Eastern resistance.

    Gregory the Great (590–604)

    Gregory, a former prefect of Rome and papal envoy to Constantinople, administered a Rome devastated by war and plague. He sent the mission to the English (597). His Pastoral Rule and Dialogues shaped medieval Christianity. He styled himself servus servorum Dei, "servant of the servants of God". He protested strongly against the title "ecumenical patriarch". When Eulogius of Alexandria applied a similar title to Gregory himself, he refused it:

    Away with words that inflate vanity and wound charity. … For my honour is the honour of the universal Church. My honour is the solid vigour of my brethren.

    Gregory I, Register 8.29 (NPNF 8.30), to Eulogius of Alexandria (598). Trans. James Barmby, NPNF II/12 (1895). Checked; the ellipsis omits intervening sentences. Q32 · checked

    Orthodox writers cite Gregory's protest as evidence that the early Roman see rejected universal jurisdiction. Catholic writers note that Gregory also exercised appellate authority over Eastern bishops in several cases, wrote that he knew of no bishop not subject to the Apostolic See if a fault were found, and objected to the title because it seemed to deny other bishops their dignity, not because Rome lacked primacy.3

    Notes

    1. Justinian, Novel 6, preface. See Dagron 2003. ↩
    2. Text in Collectio Avellana; DH 363–365 (DH). Later sources give larger numbers of signatories, which cannot be checked. ↩
    3. Gregory I, letter of 598 to Eulogius of Alexandria (Registrum, book 8), in which he refuses the title 'universal pope' (NPNF II/13). ↩

    Volume VII · Chapter 5

    The Pentarchy

    From the mid-sixth century, Byzantine law and theology described the Church's government as resting on five patriarchates: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, in that order. Modern historians call the idea the "Pentarchy".

    • Origins. The order combines Nicaea canon 6 (Rome, Alexandria, Antioch), Constantinople's elevation (381, 451) and Jerusalem's elevation (451). It is set out in Justinian's legislation (Novels 109, 123, 131).1
    • Theology. Theodore the Studite (d. 826) and the council of 869–870 (canon 21) treated the five as jointly responsible for the Church. Theodore, while appealing to the pope against the emperor, described the Church as a "five-headed" body. Patriarch Peter III of Antioch, writing in 1054, compared the five patriarchs to the five senses of one body.2
    • Limits. The Pentarchy described the imperial Church. It ignored the Church of the East and the Catholicos of Armenia. After the Arab conquests, three of the five patriarchs lived under Islamic rule. Alexandria and Antioch each had rival anti-Chalcedonian patriarchs who commanded the larger communities.

    Interpretations. Orthodox ecclesiology sees in the Pentarchy a model of collegial or conciliar government with a primacy of honour, which passed to Constantinople when Rome broke communion. Catholic historians stress that the Pentarchy always placed Rome first and that Byzantine writers often recognised Rome's role as a court of appeal. Most historians see the Pentarchy as an idealised, imperial theory rather than a working constitution.

    Notes

    1. Justinian, Novels 109, 123 and 131. See Dagron 2003 and Dvornik 1966. ↩
    2. Constantinople IV (869–870), canon 21 (Tanner 1990, vol. 1); the letters of Peter III of Antioch are edited in Will 1861. ↩

    Volume VII · Chapter 6

    Primacy, supremacy and the modern dialogue

    Distinguishing the terms

    ConceptMeaningFirst-millennium evidence
    Primacy of honour (presbeia timēs)First place in order and precedence: presiding, being commemorated first, speaking firstUniversally acknowledged for Rome (Constantinople c. 3; Chalcedon c. 28; Justinian)
    Appellate authorityThe right to receive appeals and order a rehearingSerdica cc. 3–5 (Rome). Chalcedon cc. 9 and 17 (Constantinople). Exercised by Rome in specific Eastern cases (Athanasius, Chrysostom, Flavian, Photius) with mixed reception
    JurisdictionOrdinary governing power: consecrating, deposing and legislating within a territoryExercised by Rome in the suburbicarian dioceses and increasingly in the West. Not exercised in the East's internal administration
    Doctrinal authorityA distinctive role in judging the faithThe Tome (451), Agatho's letter (680) and the Hormisdas formula (519) were received in the East, but after examination. Honorius was condemned (681)
    SupremacyUniversal, immediate, ordinary jurisdiction over all Churches and all faithfulDefined as Catholic dogma at Vatican I (Pastor aeternus, 1870) and reaffirmed at Vatican II (Lumen gentium 22). Rejected by the Orthodox

    Two readings of the same evidence

    Catholic reading

    Christ gave Peter a unique role (Matt. 16:18–19; Luke 22:32; John 21:15–17) that continues in the bishops of Rome. The first millennium shows this primacy in germ: Rome's interventions, appeals to it, the reception of its doctrinal letters, and Eastern appeals to it against heretical emperors. Development, as in the theology of Newman, explains how its later forms unfold what was implicit. Vatican I's definitions express what was always believed, even if not always exercised in the same way.1

    Orthodox reading

    Peter's confession (the faith) is the rock. Every bishop sits in the "chair of Peter" (Cyprian). Rome held the first place by the canons, because of its apostolic foundation and imperial dignity, and as a primacy within communion, not above it. The first millennium shows Rome's teaching accepted when orthodox and rejected when not, with ecumenical councils, not Rome alone, as the final authority. Later papal claims, from Gregory VII to Vatican I, are innovations.2

    Both sides now accept that some forms of later doctrine cannot simply be read back into early texts. Both also accept that Rome held an acknowledged first place in the first millennium. The dispute concerns what that place entailed.3

    The modern dialogue

    • 1995. John Paul II's encyclical Ut unum sint (§95) invited other Churches to help find a way of exercising the primacy that would be open to a new situation without renouncing what is essential to its mission.
    • 2007, Ravenna. The Joint International Commission for Theological Dialogue agreed that primacy and conciliarity are interdependent at the local, regional and universal levels, and that Rome occupied the first place (taxis) among the patriarchates in the first millennium. It noted that the two Churches disagree on how to interpret the historical evidence. The Moscow Patriarchate was absent, having withdrawn over the presence of the Estonian Apostolic Orthodox Church.
    • 2016, Chieti. Synodality and Primacy during the First Millennium: a common historical reading of the first millennium, with Georgian reservations recorded.
    • 2023, Alexandria. Synodality and Primacy in the Second Millennium and Today.
    • 2025–2026. The Coordinating Committee worked on draft texts on the Filioque and on infallibility. In June 2026 at Pannonhalma it decided that the infallibility text required further revision before a plenary.4

    Notes

    1. Vatican I, Pastor aeternus (1870): DH 3053–3064 (DH). ↩
    2. Meyendorff 1989; Ware 1993; Siecienski 2017. ↩
    3. Ravenna Document 2007; Chieti Document 2016. ↩
    4. Communiqués of the Coordinating Committee, Rethymno (8–12 September 2025) and Pannonhalma (15–19 June 2026), Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity and Ecumenical Patriarchate, consulted November 2026. ↩

    Volume VIII · c. 400–1050

    East and West before the Great Schism

    The break between Rome and Constantinople was not caused by one quarrel. It was the outcome of a long process in which Latin and Greek Christians came to share less: less language, less political framework, less common experience, and therefore less ability to read each other charitably. This volume traces the separate strands of that process, and then how they came together.

    In this volume

    1. Two worlds: language and politics (c. 400–750)

    Volume VIII · Chapter 1

    Two worlds: language and politics (c. 400–750)

    Language

    The Roman Church used Greek until the third century. By the late fourth century, Latin was its liturgical and theological language. Educated Westerners increasingly lacked Greek: Augustine read it only with difficulty, and Leo the Great could not read Eutyches' dossier without translators. From the late sixth century, knowledge of Latin also declined in Constantinople. Each side came to know the other's theology through translations, sometimes faulty ones, as the Frankish reception of Nicaea II shows. Terms that seemed equivalent were not: hypostasis and persona; ekporeusis and processio.1

    Political separation

    • 476. The last Western emperor at Ravenna, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer. Constantinople's emperor remained, in law, the emperor of the West too. Western Christians increasingly lived under Germanic kings, many of them Homoian ("Arian") Christians until the sixth century.
    • 535–554. Justinian's wars reconquered Italy at catastrophic cost. Rome remained part of the empire. Popes needed imperial confirmation of their election, and several were coerced: Vigilius (553) and Martin I (653–655).
    • 568. The Lombards invaded Italy. Imperial control shrank to Ravenna, Rome, Naples, Sicily and the south.
    • The "Byzantine papacy" (537–752). Many popes of the late seventh and early eighth centuries were Greek- or Syriac-speaking, often refugees from the Arab conquests. Eastern feasts and practices entered Roman use, among them Marian feasts and the Agnus Dei under the Syrian pope Sergius I.2 The period shows that Rome was still culturally part of the Byzantine world well into the eighth century.
    • The Arab conquests (630s–710s). The conquest of Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Spain removed the Mediterranean's southern half from Christian rule. It reduced Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem to minority Churches under Islamic rule and left Rome and Constantinople as the two great sees of Christendom.

    The historian Henri Pirenne argued that Islam's expansion, more than the Germanic invasions, broke the Mediterranean unity of the ancient world and turned the West towards the north. His thesis in its strong form is contested, but most historians accept the general shift it describes.3

    Notes

    Volume VIII · Chapter 2

    The Franks, the papacy, and the coronation of 800

    In the mid-eighth century the papacy turned from Constantinople to the Franks. The reasons were mainly practical:

    • Iconoclast emperors were unable or unwilling to defend Rome against the Lombards.
    • Leo III's government (c. 732–733) had transferred papal estates in Sicily and Calabria, and jurisdiction over Illyricum, southern Italy and Sicily, from Rome to Constantinople. The date and circumstances are debated.
    • The Lombards took Ravenna in 751, ending the Byzantine exarchate.

    Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps in 753–754 and anointed the Frankish king Pippin at Saint-Denis. Pippin campaigned against the Lombards and gave the conquered territories to "St Peter" (the "Donation of Pippin", 756). This was the foundation of the Papal States, which lasted until 1870.1 The forged Donation of Constantine, which claimed that Constantine had granted the pope authority over the West, was probably composed in this period (mid- to late eighth century). Lorenzo Valla exposed it as a forgery in 1440.2

    Christmas Day, 800

    On 25 December 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in St Peter's, and the Roman people acclaimed him emperor. In Constantinople the throne was held by Irene. She ruled in her own name from 797, the first woman to do so. Westerners could argue that the imperial office was vacant; Byzantines regarded the coronation as usurpation. After years of conflict, Michael I recognised Charlemagne as basileus in 812, but not as "emperor of the Romans", a title Byzantium reserved for itself.3

    From now on there were two Christian empires. Each claimed to be Roman, and each had a Church closely tied to its ruler. The Carolingian Church was confident, reforming and theologically assertive. As the next chapters show, it became the main source of Western positions that Byzantium found objectionable, notably on images and on the Filioque. The papacy was caught between the two.4

    Volume VIII · Chapter 3

    Iconoclasm and the Western reaction

    Byzantine iconoclasm, the official hostility to religious images, lasted with an interval from the 720s or 730s to 843. Its causes have been sought in several places :

    • Old Testament prohibitions, perhaps sharpened by contact with Islam and Judaism. Caliph Yazid II issued an edict against images in 721.
    • Military defeat, interpreted as divine punishment for idolatry.
    • Imperial suspicion of the power of monasteries and holy objects.
    • Theological concerns about depicting the divine.

    Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon have argued that the iconophile sources exaggerate both the scale of persecution and the role of Leo III, and that coherent iconoclast policy began with Constantine V (741–775).1

    The decisive theological defence came from John of Damascus (d. c. 750). He was a monk at Mar Saba near Jerusalem, writing in the caliphate, beyond the emperor's reach. His three Treatises on the Divine Images argued that the incarnation makes the invisible God depictable, that matter can mediate grace, and that veneration differs from worship. The council of Nicaea II (787) adopted these arguments. After a second iconoclasm (815–843), Empress Theodora restored the icons on 11 March 843.

    The Western response

    Rome consistently opposed iconoclasm. Gregory II, Gregory III (Roman synod of 731) and Hadrian I all did so. The Frankish court reacted differently. It received Nicaea II's acts in a Latin translation that appeared to require that images be given the same adoration (adoratio) as the Trinity. Theodulf of Orléans, in the name of Charlemagne, composed the Opus Caroli regis contra synodum (the "Libri Carolini", c. 790–793). It rejected both the iconoclast council of 754 and the "adoration" of images it attributed to 787. Images were permitted for decoration and instruction, but not to be venerated. The Council of Frankfurt (794) adopted this position. Pope Hadrian I defended Nicaea II in a reply.

    The episode matters for three reasons:

    • It shows the Frankish Church asserting its own theological judgement against a council received in Rome and Constantinople.
    • The Opus Caroli also criticises the Greek profession that the Spirit proceeds "through the Son" and defends the Filioque, an early sign of the controversy to come.
    • It shows how far mistranslation was already shaping East–West perceptions.2

    Notes

    Volume VIII · Chapter 4

    Customs, discipline and liturgy

    Much of the medieval polemic between Greeks and Latins concerned practice rather than doctrine. Lists of Latin "errors" circulated in Byzantium from the ninth century, and Latin counter-lists answered them.1 Some differences were long established and had been tolerated. Others became controversial only when other tensions made them signs of a different "faith".

The Armenians' use of unleavened bread was associated with heresy in Byzantine eyes.2
    Clerical marriageFrom the late 4th century Roman decretals required continence of bishops, priests and deacons. Celibacy for higher clergy was increasingly enforced, and decisively so in the Gregorian reform (11th c.)Married men may be ordained deacon and priest and continue married life. Bishops are celibate (Trullo cc. 12, 13, 48)Trullo canon 13 (692) criticised Roman practice explicitly. Humbert and Niketas Stethatos exchanged polemics on the subject in 1054

    Historians stress that these differences divided because of what they came to symbolise. Each side read the other's customs as evidence of a deeper deviation: Judaising in the use of azymes; contempt for marriage in the demand for celibacy.

    Volume VIII · Chapter 5

    The Filioque

    The Creed of 381 says the Holy Spirit "proceeds from the Father" (John 15:26). The Latin Church came to add Filioque, "and [from] the Son". This one word became the most persistent doctrinal issue between East and West. Two questions have always been intertwined:

    • Is the doctrine true?
    • Did the Western Church have the right to add it to the common creed?

    Origins of the doctrine and of the addition

    • Latin theology. Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose and above all Augustine taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Augustine added that the Spirit proceeds "principally" (principaliter) from the Father, who gives the Son the ability to breathe forth the Spirit.1
    • Greek theology. Greek fathers, including Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Alexandria and John of Damascus, could speak of the Spirit as coming "through the Son" or as "proper to the Son", while insisting that the Father is the sole cause (aitia) within the Trinity.
    • Maximus the Confessor. In his Letter to Marinus (c. 655), Maximus defended the Roman usage of his day. He explained that the Latins did not make the Son a cause of the Spirit, but meant the Spirit's coming forth through the Son. He suggested that difficulties arose from the limits of Latin vocabulary. This text is central to modern dialogue.
    • Spain. The phrase appears in creeds associated with the Third Council of Toledo (589), where the Visigothic king Reccared renounced Homoian Christianity. Its presence in the original text of that council has been questioned, but most scholars accept early Spanish use.
    • Frankish adoption. The Franks adopted the Spanish creed with the Filioque in their liturgy (late 8th century). The Council of Friuli (796/797) defended it. Frankish monks in Jerusalem were accused by Greek monks of heresy for singing it (808). Charlemagne's Council of Aachen (809) then asked Pope Leo III to approve the addition.
    • Rome's refusal and adoption. Leo III accepted the doctrine but refused to add it to the creed. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he had the creed engraved without the Filioque, in Greek and Latin, on two silver shields placed in St Peter's. Rome adopted the sung creed with the Filioque only in 1014, at the request of Emperor Henry II, for his coronation by Benedict VIII. The source is Berno of Reichenau.

    The arguments

    Eastern objections (from Photius onwards)

    • Canonical. Ephesus canon 7 forbids "a different faith" (Q16). A common creed may not be altered by one Church without an ecumenical council.
    • Theological. The Father is the sole source (the "monarchy" of the Father). Procession from two sources introduces two principles. Making procession a property shared by Father and Son confuses the persons, or leaves the Spirit subordinate.
    • Scriptural. John 15:26 says "from the Father". Texts on the Son "sending" the Spirit refer to his mission in time, not his eternal origin.

    Western defence (from the Carolingians to Florence)

    • Scriptural. The Spirit is "the Spirit of the Son" (Gal. 4:6) and "receives from what is mine" (John 16:14). The Son's sending of the Spirit reflects his eternal relation.
    • Theological. The persons are distinguished only by opposed relations, so if the Spirit did not proceed from the Son, Son and Spirit would not be distinguished. Father and Son spirate "as one principle" (Lyon II, 1274; Florence, 1439), with the Father as source of the whole Godhead.
    • Canonical. The addition clarifies the creed and does not change its faith. Ephesus canon 7 forbids a contrary creed, not an explanatory word.

    Modern clarifications

    • 1995. The Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity's document The Greek and Latin Traditions regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit distinguished the Greek ekporeusis, the origin of the Spirit from the Father as sole source, from the Latin processio, a broader term. It affirmed the Father's monarchy and the normative value of the Greek creed of 381.
    • 2003. The North American Orthodox–Catholic Theological Consultation, in The Filioque: A Church-Dividing Issue?, recommended that the Catholic Church use the original creed in catechetical and liturgical texts. It also proposed that the Filioque need not be church-dividing.
    • Liturgical practice. Popes have on several occasions recited the creed without the Filioque with Orthodox patriarchs, and Eastern Catholic Churches commonly omit it.
    • Since 2024. The question is on the agenda of the Joint International Commission (Vol. VII ch. 6).2

    Original diagram: three ways of expressing the Spirit's origin. Simplified; each tradition contains further nuances.

    Volume VIII · Chapter 6

    Photius, Bulgaria and the ninth-century crisis

    The "Photian schism" was the first East–West crisis in which papal claims, the Filioque and missionary rivalry all came together. Its story was later retold by both sides in polemical forms. Francis Dvornik's research (1948) overturned much of the traditional Western account.1

    The events

    1. 858. Patriarch Ignatius was forced out amid court politics. Photius, a lay scholar and senior civil servant, was ordained through all the clerical ranks in six days and made patriarch. Ignatius' supporters appealed to Rome.
    2. 861. A council in Constantinople, with papal legates, confirmed Ignatius' deposition. Pope Nicholas I (858–867) disowned his legates and, at a Roman synod of 863, declared Photius deposed. Nicholas held a strong theory of papal authority over the whole Church.
    3. 864–866. Khan Boris of Bulgaria was baptised under Byzantine sponsorship, but then turned to Rome for an independent Church. Nicholas sent bishops and a long letter of guidance, the Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum (866). Latin missionaries in Bulgaria taught the Filioque and repeated chrismations administered by Greek priests.
    4. 867. Photius' Encyclical to the Eastern Patriarchs denounced the Latin practices in Bulgaria and, for the first time officially, the Filioque as heresy. A council in Constantinople declared Nicholas deposed. Weeks later the new emperor Basil I deposed Photius and restored Ignatius.
    5. 869–870. A council in Constantinople with Hadrian II's legates condemned Photius. (The Catholic Church counts it as the "Eighth Ecumenical Council".) In a separate session immediately afterwards, the emperor and the Eastern representatives assigned Bulgaria to Constantinople's jurisdiction, over the legates' protests.
    6. 877–880. On Ignatius' death (877), Photius returned. The council of 879–880, with John VIII's legates, recognised him, annulled 869–870 and reaffirmed the creed without additions.
    7. 886. Leo VI deposed Photius. Dvornik showed that the alleged "second Photian schism", a second papal excommunication of Photius, is a later legend. Photius died in communion with Rome.2

    Photius' Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit (c. 885/6) gave the classic Eastern case against the Filioque. In it he describes the popes Leo III and John VIII as defenders of the unaltered creed.3

    Cyril and Methodius

    Meanwhile, the brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius of Thessalonica were sent by Photius' government to Great Moravia (863). They created the Glagolitic alphabet and a Slavonic liturgy. Popes Hadrian II and John VIII approved the Slavonic liturgy against Frankish opposition. The Frankish clergy expelled Methodius' disciples after his death (885). They took the Slavonic tradition to Bulgaria, where it flourished, and from there it reached Serbia and Rus'. This mission, sponsored from Constantinople and approved by Rome, is now honoured by both Churches.
