    Volume VIII · Chapter 7

    How the factors accumulated

    By the mid-eleventh century every factor discussed in this volume was in place. None was new. What changed was that they reinforced one another and that the conditions that had previously contained them weakened.

    • Distinct theological cultures. Latin Augustinian and Greek Cappadocian-Byzantine traditions developed with little contact. Each became fluent in its own terms and suspicious of the other's.
    • Distinct political frameworks. There were two empires, and the papacy had become a territorial power allied to the Western one. That made every ecclesiastical quarrel a political one.
    • Competing ecclesiologies. The papacy's sense of its universal authority was growing, and would grow sharply with the eleventh-century reform. Byzantium's model was pentarchic and synodal.1
    • Competing jurisdictions. These ran along a long frontier: Illyricum, Bulgaria, southern Italy and Sicily.
    • Customs as identity markers (ch. 4), and a doctrinal issue, the Filioque, that could be presented as heresy.
    • Precedents of rupture. The Acacian schism (484–519), the Monothelite crisis and the Photian conflict had already accustomed both sides to breaks in communion, and to their eventual repair.2

    Until the eleventh century, breaks were followed by reconciliation. Whether the break of 1054 was different, and if so why, is the subject of Volume IX.

    Volume IX · 1009–1484, with modern dialogue

    The East–West Schism

    The year 1054 is the date textbooks give for the division between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches. The events of that summer were real and bitter, but they were not understood at the time as the permanent separation of two Churches. This volume follows the multi-century process of separation: the excommunications of 1054, their limited scope, the Crusades and the sack of Constantinople, the failed unions of Lyon and Florence, and the modern efforts at reconciliation. It ends with a side-by-side comparison of the doctrinal issues as they stand today.

    In this volume

    1. Before 1054: Normans, reformers and a patriarch
    2. The events of July 1054
    3. After 1054: Crusades and the sack of Constantinople
    4. Lyon (1274), Florence (1439) and the fall of Constantinople
    5. Toward reconciliation (1964–2026)
    6. Catholic and Orthodox doctrine compared
    7. When did the schism happen? Historians' views

    Volume IX · Chapter 1

    Before 1054: Normans, reformers and a patriarch

    A silent break?

    A church showed it was in communion with another by commemorating that church's bishop in the , the lists of names read at the Eucharist. Byzantine sources report that the name of the pope was not commemorated in Constantinople from about 1009, under Pope Sergius IV. One explanation offered is that his letter of enthronement contained the Filioque. The evidence is late and thin, and whether this was a deliberate break or neglect is unclear.1 In the 1020s, Patriarch Eustathius and Pope John XIX discussed a formula recognising Constantinople's autonomy within its sphere. The negotiations collapsed in the face of reformist protest in the West.

    The reform papacy

    From 1046 a series of German-sponsored popes undertook a programme of reform. Its targets were simony (the buying of church offices) and clerical marriage. Its aim was the "freedom of the Church" from lay control. The movement is named after its greatest representative, Gregory VII (1073–1085). Leo IX (1049–1054) was its first great figure. He travelled widely and held synods. His closest adviser was Humbert of Silva Candida, a learned and combative cardinal from Lorraine. The reformers held an exalted view of Roman authority, informed in part by forgeries such as the Donation of Constantine and the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals. They tended to see Eastern differences, such as married priests, as abuses requiring correction.2

    Southern Italy

    Byzantium still ruled Apulia and Calabria, where Greek and Latin rite communities lived side by side. Norman adventurers were carving out lordships at the expense of both Byzantium and local Lombard princes. Leo IX allied with the Byzantine governor Argyros against them. On 18 June 1053, at Civitate, the Normans destroyed the papal army and captured the pope. Leo was held at Benevento until March 1054 and died in Rome on 19 April 1054. Meanwhile, the reform papacy was introducing Latin practices, including azymes and celibacy, to the Greek communities of southern Italy.

    Michael Cerularius and Leo of Ohrid

    Michael Cerularius, patriarch 1043–1058, was a forceful aristocrat. He is reported to have closed the Latin-rite churches in Constantinople, probably in 1052–53, in reaction to latinisation in southern Italy. In 1053 Leo, archbishop of Ohrid, wrote a letter, probably at Cerularius' prompting, to John, bishop of Trani in Apulia, addressed to "all the bishops of the Franks and the most reverend pope". It attacked the Latin use of unleavened bread and Saturday fasting as Jewish practices. Humbert translated it into Latin and composed sharp replies. Cerularius and Emperor Constantine IX, who needed papal support against the Normans, then sent conciliatory letters to Rome. Leo IX responded by sending a legation.3

    Volume IX · Chapter 2

    The events of July 1054

    The legates were Cardinal Humbert, Frederick of Lorraine (chancellor of the Roman Church, later Pope Stephen IX), and Archbishop Peter of Amalfi. They reached Constantinople in April 1054. Their letters, drafted by Humbert, demanded that the patriarch submit to Rome and denied him the title "ecumenical". The emperor received them honourably. Cerularius refused to deal with them, questioning their credentials. He suspected collusion between them and Argyros, his enemy. Humbert debated publicly with the monk Niketas Stethatos, who retracted his treatise against the Latins under imperial pressure.

    16 July 1054

    On Saturday 16 July 1054, as the afternoon liturgy was about to begin, the legates entered Hagia Sophia and laid a bull of excommunication on the altar. They then left, shaking the dust from their feet. The bull, written by Humbert, excommunicated Michael Cerularius, Leo of Ohrid, the patriarchal official Constantine, and their followers. It praised the emperor and the citizens of Constantinople as orthodox. Among its charges, it compared the Greeks to a series of ancient heretics. It also accused them of having removed the Filioque from the creed, inverting the actual history.1

    Leo IX had died three months earlier. Canonists have argued that the legates' mandate lapsed on his death, so that the excommunication was of doubtful validity. In 1054 no successor had yet been elected (Victor II took office in 1055).

    The patriarch's response

    After an attempt to recall the legates for a meeting failed, rioting broke out. The emperor allowed Cerularius to act. A synod in Constantinople (with a document dated 20/24 July) anathematised the authors of the bull and those who had helped them, and ordered the bull burned. It did not anathematise the pope or the Latin Church.2

    What was, and was not, excommunicated

    • Both sentences were directed at persons, not at Churches.
    • Neither side declared the other Church heretical as a whole. Neither required other patriarchs to break communion.
    • Patriarch Peter III of Antioch, consulted by Cerularius, urged restraint. He wrote that the Latins were brothers, that most of their customs were tolerable, and that only the Filioque was serious.
    • Contemporaries in the West paid little attention to the episode. Many Byzantine chroniclers do not mention it.

    The 1965 joint declaration (ch. 5) acknowledged this. It described the sentences as directed against persons and not intended to break ecclesiastical communion between the sees.

    Key takeaways

    • 1054 was an exchange of personal excommunications between a papal legate and a patriarch. The pope who sent the legate was already dead, and the patriarch did not anathematise the Latin Church.
    • It became symbolically decisive only later, when it was remembered as the start of a schism that subsequent events made real.

    Volume IX · Chapter 3

    After 1054: Crusades and the sack of Constantinople

    Continuing contact

    Relations continued after 1054. Gregory VII contemplated sending aid to Byzantium after Manzikert (1071). In 1089 Emperor Alexios I convened a synod at Pope Urban II's request. According to the account reconstructed by Walther Holtzmann, it found no written record of a canonical break with Rome and expressed willingness to restore the pope's name to the diptychs once he sent a profession of faith.1 Urban preached the First Crusade at Clermont in November 1095, partly in response to Alexios' request for military help.

    The Crusades and local schism

    The Crusades brought large numbers of Latins and Greeks into contact, and often into conflict. The decisive ecclesiastical change came in the conquered territories:

    • At Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (1099) the crusaders installed Latin patriarchs, and the Greek patriarchs went into exile in Constantinople. For the first time there were rival patriarchs of the same see, one Latin and one Greek. Steven Runciman argued that this, rather than 1054, is when the schism became real for ordinary Christians in the East.
    • At the Council of Bari (1098), Anselm of Canterbury defended the Filioque before Greek bishops of southern Italy.
    • In the 1100s, exchanges of theological debate (Anselm of Havelberg's debates at Constantinople in 1136) coexisted with growing popular hostility.
    • In 1182 the Latin (largely Italian) population of Constantinople was massacred during a political coup.

    1204

    The Fourth Crusade set out to attack Egypt. Unable to pay Venice for its fleet, it was diverted first to the Christian city of Zara (1202). It then went to Constantinople to restore a deposed Byzantine prince, Alexios IV, who promised money and church union. When Alexios was overthrown and his promises unpaid, the crusaders stormed the city on 12–13 April 1204. Three days of plunder followed, including the desecration of Hagia Sophia. The Venetian Thomas Morosini was installed as Latin patriarch. A Latin Empire ruled Constantinople until 1261, when Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered it. Byzantine Greek government continued in exile at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond.2

    Innocent III had forbidden attacks on Christians and condemned the sack in strong terms when he learned of it. He nonetheless accepted the new Latin hierarchy as a means of bringing the Greek Church under Rome. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), canon 4, rebuked Greeks who rebaptised Latins or washed altars after Latin masses. Canon 5 ranked the patriarchates with Constantinople second, meaning in practice its Latin patriarch.

    Most historians regard 1204 as the event that made the schism irreversible in Greek popular feeling. Union with Rome came to mean submission to those who had sacked the city.

    Volume IX · Chapter 4

    Lyon (1274), Florence (1439) and the fall of Constantinople

    The Second Council of Lyon (1274)

    Michael VIII was threatened by Charles of Anjou's plans to restore the Latin Empire. He sought papal protection through church union. At the fourth session of the Second Council of Lyon (6 July 1274), his envoys, led by George Akropolites, presented a profession of faith in his name. It accepted the Filioque, purgatory, seven sacraments and Roman primacy, and the Greek clergy sang the creed with the Filioque. The council's constitution on the Holy Spirit defined procession "from the Father and the Son … not as from two principles but as from one principle".1

    The union was imposed in Constantinople against fierce resistance. The unionist patriarch John Bekkos was installed in 1275. Michael VIII was excommunicated by Pope Martin IV in 1281, for political reasons, and died in 1282. His son Andronikos II repudiated the union immediately. A council at Blachernae (1285) condemned Bekkos and adopted the Tomus of Patriarch Gregory II of Cyprus. It acknowledged an eternal "manifestation" of the Spirit through the Son while rejecting the Filioque as cause.

    Interlude: the Hesychast controversy (1337–1351)

    Barlaam of Calabria, a Greek from southern Italy, attacked the claims of hesychast monks on Athos to see the uncreated light of Christ's Transfiguration. Gregory Palamas defended them by distinguishing God's unknowable essence (ousia) from his uncreated energies (energeiai), in which God is truly participated. Councils in Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 endorsed Palamas. Barlaam and Akindynos, who cited Thomas Aquinas and Western scholasticism, were condemned. Palamism became a defining element of Orthodox theology and a later point of East–West theological difference (ch. 6).

    Ferrara-Florence (1438–1439)

    In the fifteenth century the Ottomans had reduced Byzantium to Constantinople and a few territories. Emperor John VIII Palaiologos, Patriarch Joseph II and a delegation of some 700, including bishops representing the other patriarchs and the Russian Church (led by Metropolitan Isidore of Kiev), came to Italy. The council opened at Ferrara in April 1438 and moved to Florence in January 1439. It was also contending with the rival Council of Basel. Unlike Lyon, it involved more than a year of genuine theological debate on purgatory, the Filioque (both its doctrine and its addition), azymes and primacy. The leading figures were Bessarion of Nicaea, the unionist Isidore, and Mark Eugenikos of Ephesus, the leader of the opposition. Patriarch Joseph II died in Florence on 10 June 1439.2

    The decree of union, Laetentur caeli, was signed and promulgated on 6 July 1439. In summary :

    • Filioque. The Latin doctrine was declared legitimate, explained as equivalent to the Greek "through the Son", with the Father as the source. The addition to the creed was declared licit. The Greeks were not required to use it.
    • Bread. Both leavened and unleavened bread are valid.
    • Purgatory. Souls who die in God's love before completing satisfaction are purified after death and helped by the prayers of the living. The decree avoided the image of fire, to which the Greeks objected.
    • Primacy. The Roman pontiff holds primacy over the whole world as successor of Peter, with full power to govern the universal Church, "as is contained also in the acts of the ecumenical councils and in the sacred canons". The rights and privileges of the Eastern patriarchs were reserved.

    Mark of Ephesus alone among the Greek bishops refused to sign. He is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church. The union was rejected by most clergy and people in Constantinople and by Moscow, where Isidore was arrested on his return in 1441. It was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia only on 12 December 1452. On 29 May 1453 Constantinople fell to Mehmed II. In 1454 the Sultan installed Gennadios Scholarios, a former unionist turned opponent of the union, as patriarch. A synod of Constantinople in 1484 formally repudiated Florence.3

    Scholarly debate: why did Florence fail?

    Explanations include:

    • Popular memory of 1204.
    • The perception that the Greeks had signed under political duress and in hope of military aid that came too late (the Crusade of Varna, 1444, ended in disaster).
    • The monastic and lower-clergy resistance led by Mark's followers.
    • The decree's ambiguity: Latins read it as Eastern acceptance of Latin doctrine; Greek unionists read it as Latin recognition of Eastern tradition.
    • Its failure to reckon with how Eastern Churches receive a council: through acceptance by the whole Church, not just the signatures of delegates.4

    Later unions

    Florence became the model for later partial unions, in which Eastern communities entered communion with Rome while keeping their liturgy and discipline. Examples are the Union of Brest (1595–96) with Ruthenian bishops in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the Union of Uzhhorod (1646), and the Melkite division of 1724. These unions produced today's Eastern Catholic Churches. Orthodox critics call such unions "uniatism". The Joint Commission's Balamand document (1993) rejected uniatism as a method for the future while recognising the right of existing Eastern Catholic Churches to exist. In 1755 the patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria and Jerusalem required Latin converts to be rebaptised. This was a sign of how far estrangement had gone. These developments are treated in Volume XIII.

    Volume IX · Chapter 5

    Toward reconciliation (1964–2026)

    • 5–6 January 1964. Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I met in Jerusalem, the first meeting of a pope and an ecumenical patriarch since 1439.
    • 7 December 1965. A Joint Catholic–Orthodox Declaration was read simultaneously in Rome, at the last public session of Vatican II, and at the Phanar in Istanbul. Both sides regretted the offensive words and acts of 1054 and resolved to "remove both from memory and from the midst of the Church" the sentences of excommunication. The declaration explicitly stated that this act of justice and mutual pardon was not sufficient to end the differences between the Churches.1
    • 1979–1980. The Joint International Commission for Theological Dialogue between the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church was established. Its first plenary was held on Patmos and Rhodes in 1980. It produced agreed statements on the Church and Eucharist (Munich, 1982), faith and sacraments (Bari, 1987) and priesthood (Valamo, 1988).
    • 1993. The Balamand statement on uniatism.
    • 2000. The Baltimore plenary failed over uniatism. Dialogue was suspended until 2006 (Belgrade).
    • 2007, 2016, 2023. The Ravenna, Chieti and Alexandria documents on primacy and synodality (Vol. VII ch. 6).
    • 2018–2019. In the dispute over Ukrainian autocephaly, the Moscow Patriarchate broke communion with the Ecumenical Patriarchate (October 2018). It has since stayed out of dialogue bodies chaired by Constantinople, including this Commission.
    • 28–29 November 2025. Pope Leo XIV and Patriarch Bartholomew commemorated the 1700th anniversary of Nicaea at İznik and signed a joint declaration in Istanbul. It marked the sixtieth anniversary of the 1965 declaration and expressed hope for a common date of Easter.
    • 2025–2026. Draft texts on the Filioque and infallibility were under discussion in the Commission's Coordinating Committee (Vol. VII ch. 6).

    Formal full communion has not been restored. Both Churches officially describe each other as "sister Churches", a term whose precise implications are themselves debated.2

    Volume IX · Chapter 6

    Catholic and Orthodox doctrine compared

    This chapter sets the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox positions side by side on ten issues. Each entry states the position as found in authoritative documents of the tradition, outlines how it developed, and notes internal diversity. Use the filter to show one topic at a time.

    A note on sources: for the Catholic Church, the teaching of councils, papal definitions and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992/1997) is binding in a way that has no exact Orthodox equivalent. Orthodox positions are drawn from councils, from patristic consensus, and from widely received texts such as the Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848). Orthodox theologians themselves debate the authority of some of these, such as the seventeenth-century "confessions".

    Show:

    1. Papal primacy

    Catholic

    The bishop of Rome, as successor of Peter, has primacy not only of honour but of jurisdiction, by divine institution (Vatican I, Pastor aeternus, 1870, chs. 1–3). This is exercised collegially with the bishops (Vatican II, Lumen gentium 22).1

    Orthodox

    Rome held the first place (presbeia) in the communion of Churches by the canons. After the schism, that place among the Orthodox belongs to Constantinople. Primacy exists at every level, but as presidency within a synod, not authority over it.

    Development and diversity: see Vol. VII ch. 6. Some Orthodox theologians (e.g. Afanasiev) and the Ravenna document (2007) accept a universal primacy in principle. The disputed questions are its nature and its relation to the bishop of Rome.

    2. Universal jurisdiction

    Catholic

    The pope has "full, supreme and universal power over the whole Church, a power which he can always exercise unhindered" (Lumen gentium 22, paraphrasing Vatican I). This power is ordinary and immediate over all Churches and faithful.2

    Orthodox

    No bishop holds jurisdiction in another's Church. Each local Church is fully the Church. Autocephalous Churches govern themselves through their own synods.

    Development: Catholic theology of universal jurisdiction developed through the Gregorian reform and canon law (11th–13th c.) and was defined in 1870. Eastern Catholic Churches retain their own synods and patriarchs within Catholic communion.

    3. Infallibility

    Catholic

    When the pope defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra, he possesses the infallibility with which Christ endowed the Church (Pastor aeternus ch. 4). The college of bishops with the pope, and ecumenical councils, also teach infallibly (Lumen gentium 25).

    Orthodox

    The Church as a whole is preserved in truth by the Holy Spirit. No individual bishop is infallible. Councils are authoritative through their reception by the whole Church. The 1848 Encyclical states that the guardian of piety is the whole body of the Church, the people itself.3

    Development: The term and the debate are medieval. In Brian Tierney's influential (and contested) account, the doctrine was first articulated by the Franciscan Peter Olivi (13th c.). The 1870 definition was contested within Catholicism; the Old Catholic Churches separated over it. The condemnation of Honorius was a central historical argument. Infallibility is now under study in the Joint Commission (Vol. VII ch. 6).

    4. Filioque

    Catholic

    The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle (Lyon II, 1274; Florence, 1439). The Father is the source of the whole Trinity. The Greek formula "through the Son" is recognised as expressing the same faith (Florence; PCPCU clarification, 1995).

    Orthodox

    The Spirit proceeds (ekporeuetai) from the Father alone as sole cause. The Son's role may be expressed as an eternal manifestation or shining forth (Blachernae, 1285). The unilateral addition to the creed is uncanonical.

    Diversity: Some Orthodox theologians (e.g. Bolotov, 19th c.) treated the Filioque as a permissible theological opinion (theologoumenon). Others (e.g. Lossky) saw it as the root of all Western divergence. See Vol. VIII ch. 5.

    5. Original / ancestral sin

    Catholic

    Through Adam's sin, all humans are born deprived of original holiness and justice. This is "original sin", a state "contracted" and not committed, which baptism removes (Council of Trent, Session 5; Catechism 404–405). The concept is shaped by Augustine.4

    Orthodox

    Humans inherit the consequences of the ancestral sin (mortality, corruption, a tendency to sin), but not personal guilt for Adam's act. Many Orthodox writers prefer the term "ancestral sin" (propatorikē hamartia).

    Diversity: The sharpness of this contrast is partly a twentieth-century construction (e.g. John Romanides, 1957). Earlier Orthodox confessional texts use language close to Latin usage. The Catechism itself states that original sin is called "sin" only in an analogical sense.

    6. Purgatory and purification after death

    Catholic

    Those who die in God's grace but imperfectly purified undergo purification after death. The living help them through prayer and the Eucharist (Lyon II; Florence; Trent, Session 25; Catechism 1030–1032). The image of fire is traditional but not defined.5

    Orthodox

    Prayer for the dead is ancient and constant, and the departed are helped by the Church's prayers. The Orthodox reject a distinct place or state of satisfaction-paying, punitive purification, and the associated system of indulgences. Mark of Ephesus argued this at Ferrara (1438).

    Development: The term purgatorium appears as a noun in the 12th century (J. Le Goff). The issue was first a point of East–West dispute in the 13th century. Many modern theologians on both sides consider the difference reconcilable.

    7. Immaculate Conception

    Catholic

    Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception, by a singular grace in view of Christ's merits (Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus, 8 December 1854).6

    Orthodox

    Mary is Panagia, "all-holy", and the Orthodox celebrate her conception (9 December). The dogma is rejected, as unnecessary given the Orthodox understanding of ancestral sin and as implying that Mary was removed from the common human condition.

    Development and diversity: The doctrine was debated in the West for centuries. Bernard and Aquinas opposed it; Duns Scotus defended it. Some late Byzantine homilists used language of Mary's purity from conception, and Orthodox opposition hardened after 1854.

    8. Grace and deification

    Catholic

    Grace is a participation in the divine life (Catechism 1996–1997, citing 2 Pet. 1:4). Western theology also developed a distinction between "created grace" (a habit in the soul) and uncreated grace (God himself). Deification language is ancient in the West too (Augustine; Aquinas, ST III q.1 a.2).

    Orthodox

    Salvation is theosis: real participation in God through his uncreated energies, by the Spirit, in the Church's sacramental and ascetic life. The Latin concept of created grace is often criticised.

    Diversity: Recent scholarship (e.g. Norman Russell, A. N. Williams) has emphasised a shared patristic heritage of deification and found less contrast than older polemics claimed.7

    9. Essence and energies

    Catholic

    God is simple. Distinctions in God are conceptual, not real (Lateran IV's teaching on the incomprehensibility of God; the Thomist tradition). The saints in heaven see the divine essence (Benedict XII, Benedictus Deus, 1336). There is no dogmatic condemnation of Palamism.8

    Orthodox

    God's essence is utterly unknowable, even to the blessed. God is truly known and participated in his uncreated energies, which are God himself and not created effects (councils of 1341–1351).

    Diversity: Some Catholic theologians accept Palamite theology as compatible with Catholic faith, and Eastern Catholics honour Palamas. Some Orthodox theologians question how sharply the distinction should be opposed to Western simplicity.

    10. Liturgy and discipline

    Catholic

    Latin rite: unleavened bread; celibate clergy as a rule (with exceptions); confirmation normally by a bishop and, in many places, deferred to later childhood or adolescence; Communion under one kind is common; Gregorian calendar. Eastern Catholic Churches follow Eastern practice.

    Orthodox

    Leavened bread; married priests and deacons (bishops celibate); chrismation and communion given to infants at baptism; Communion in both kinds; many Churches keep the Julian calendar for some or all feasts.

    Status: Both Churches now officially recognise the other's liturgical practices as legitimate, though popular polemic persists. The Easter date question is under active discussion (ch. 5).

    Notes

    Volume IX · Chapter 7

    When did the schism happen? Historians' views

    Historians do not agree on a single date. Their answers depend on what they take "schism" to mean.

    Proposed dateArgumentAssociated scholars
    9th century (863–867)The first doctrinal condemnation (the Filioque) and mutual depositionsOlder Western and Orthodox polemical histories
    1054The symbolic rupture; later remembered as decisiveTraditional textbooks
    1098–1100Rival Latin and Greek patriarchs in the crusader statesSteven Runciman (The Eastern Schism, 1955)
    1182 / 1204Popular estrangement; the sack and the Latin EmpireMost modern historians as the decisive turn in feeling
    1484 or laterFormal Orthodox rejection of Florence. Some even point to the 1724 Melkite split or the 1755 rebaptism decree as the moment of definitive mutual non-recognitionVarious; e.g. Henry Chadwick on the long process

    The most accurate answer is that the schism was a process rather than an event. Communion between Rome and Constantinople broke several times before 1054. After 1054 it did not break completely or everywhere at once: in some places, Latins and Greeks still shared sacraments into the eighteenth century. By the late fifteenth century, both Churches nevertheless regarded themselves as separated.1

    Notes

    1. Chadwick 2003, conclusion; Runciman 1955; Papadakis 1994. ↩

    Volume X · c. 1000–1500

    Medieval Christianity

    Between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries the Latin Church became the most powerful institution in western Europe. It reformed itself, claimed authority over kings, founded universities, codified its law, launched crusades and repressed dissent. It also divided over who should lead it, and by 1500 faced demands for reform that it could not contain. Eastern Christianity lived through the same centuries under growing Turkish pressure. This volume follows both.

    In this volume

    1. The reform papacy and the investiture conflict
    2. Monks, canons and friars
    3. Scholasticism and the universities
    4. Crusades, military orders, Muslims and Jews
    5. Canon law, heresy and the inquisitions
    6. Papal monarchy, Avignon, the Western Schism and conciliarism
    7. The Black Death, Wycliffe, Hus and late medieval piety
    8. Cathedrals, art and the Byzantine Church under pressure

    The East–West schism of this period is treated in Volume IX; the Slavic and Russian Churches in Volume XIII.

    Volume X · Chapter 1

    The reform papacy and the investiture conflict

    From 1046 the German emperor Henry III installed reforming popes. The reform party they brought to Rome (Leo IX, Humbert, Hildebrand) attacked simony (the sale of church offices) and clerical marriage ("Nicolaitism").1 They also pursued a larger aim, the "freedom of the Church" (libertas ecclesiae) from lay control. The Lateran synod of 1059 reserved papal elections to the cardinals.2

    Hildebrand became Pope Gregory VII (1073–1085). A set of propositions entered in his register in 1075, the Dictatus papae, claimed among other things that the Roman Church had never erred, that the pope alone could depose bishops, and that he could depose emperors. Historians debate whether it was a programme, an index of canon-law texts, or a private memorandum.3

    Investiture

    The conflict came to a head over who should invest bishops with ring and staff, the symbols of their spiritual office. In much of Europe bishops were also great lords and royal officials. When Henry IV insisted on investing them, Gregory excommunicated and deposed him (1076). Henry did penance at Canossa in January 1077 and was absolved, but war followed. Gregory died in exile in Salerno (1085). A compromise was reached in the Concordat of Worms (1122): the emperor renounced investiture with ring and staff, while keeping a role in elections and investiture with temporal rights.4

    The "Gregorian reform" made clerical celibacy a general rule in the Latin Church. The First and Second Lateran Councils (1123, 1139) declared marriages of priests invalid. It also built up papal government through legates, appeals and canon law, and sharpened the distinction between clergy and laity. Historians differ on whether it was a "revolution" (Harold Berman, Gerd Tellenbach) or the acceleration of longer trends.5 It also widened the gap with the Greek Church, where married clergy and imperial involvement were accepted (IX.1).

    Notes

    Volume X · Chapter 2

    Monks, canons and friars

    MovementOriginCharacter
    Cluny909/910, BurgundyBenedictine monastery exempt from local lords and bishops, placed under the papacy. It became the head of hundreds of dependent houses, with a splendid liturgy and great influence on reform.1
    CisterciansCîteaux, 1098A return to a strict reading of the Rule of Benedict: manual labour, simplicity and lay brothers. Spread rapidly under Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), preacher of the Second Crusade and mystical writer.
    Carthusians1084, Bruno of CologneHermits living in community.
    Canons regular11th–12th c.Clergy living in common under the Rule of Augustine (Augustinians, Premonstratensians).
    FranciscansFrancis of Assisi (c. 1181–1226); rule approved orally 1209/10, confirmed 1223Absolute poverty and itinerant preaching. Disputes over poverty divided the order (Spirituals vs Conventuals). John XXII condemned the doctrine of Christ's absolute poverty in 1323. Clare of Assisi founded the Poor Clares.
    DominicansDominic de Guzmán; approved 1216Order of Preachers, founded to combat Catharism by preaching and learning. Prominent in the universities and later in the inquisitions.
    Beguines12th–13th c., Low CountriesLay women living religious lives without permanent vows. Their mysticism (e.g. Mechthild of Magdeburg) was valued, but the women were sometimes suspected. Marguerite Porete was burned in 1310.

    The friars, or mendicants, transformed the medieval Church. They preached in the growing cities, staffed universities, and took missions as far as the Mongol court.2 The Franciscans John of Plano Carpini (1245–47) and William of Rubruck (1253–55) travelled to the Mongols; John of Montecorvino became the first Latin archbishop of Khanbaliq (1307). There he met members of the Church of the East (V.1).3

    Major women writers of the period include Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), Julian of Norwich (c. 1343–after 1416) and Catherine of Siena (1347–1380).

    Volume X · Chapter 3

    Scholasticism and the universities

    "Scholasticism" is the method of the medieval schools. Authorities were collected and contradictions identified. Questions were posed, arguments for and against set out, and the questions resolved by reasoning.1

    • Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) described his theology as "faith seeking understanding" (fides quaerens intellectum, the original title of the Proslogion, 1077–78). In the Proslogion he gave the "ontological argument" for God's existence. In Cur Deus homo (1098) he gave the satisfaction theory of the atonement. At the Council of Bari (1098) he defended the Filioque (IX.3).
    • Peter Abelard (1079–1142) wrote Sic et non, a collection of apparently contradictory authorities. Bernard of Clairvaux had him condemned at Sens (1141).
    • Peter Lombard's Sentences (c. 1150s) became the standard theology textbook until the sixteenth century.
    • The recovery of Aristotle, through Latin translations from Arabic and Greek in the 12th–13th centuries, often with the commentaries of Averroes (Ibn Rushd), transformed philosophy and caused conflict. In 1277 the bishop of Paris condemned 219 propositions.
    • Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a Dominican, synthesised Aristotle and Christian theology in the Summa theologiae (unfinished at his death).

      Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity.

      Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I, q. 1, a. 8, ad 2. Trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1911–25). Checked. Q63 · checked
      His "five ways" argue from the world to God:

      Therefore it is necessary to arrive at a first mover, put in motion by no other; and this everyone understands to be God.

      Aquinas, ST I, q. 2, a. 3. Same translation. Checked. Q64 · checked
    • Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Franciscan, wrote the Journey of the Mind into God and offered a more Augustinian alternative. John Duns Scotus (d. 1308) argued for the univocity of being and defended the Immaculate Conception. William of Ockham (d. c. 1347) was associated with nominalism and criticised papal power.

    Some propositions of Aquinas were caught up in the 1277 condemnation. He was canonised in 1323, and Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris (1879) made him the model for Catholic theology (XIV.7).2 Universities grew from cathedral schools and guilds of masters and students: Bologna (law, traditionally 1088), Paris (theology, c. 1200), Oxford (c. 1167), and many more by 1500. The often repeated claim that the medieval Church opposed natural inquiry is examined in Misconceptions and XIV.1.

    Notes

    Volume X · Chapter 4

    Crusades, military orders, Muslims and Jews

    Urban II's appeal at Clermont (1095) launched the First Crusade. Crusaders took Jerusalem in July 1099 with a massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants that the Latin sources themselves describe.1 The crusader states lasted until the fall of Acre in 1291. Crusading ideas were extended against Muslims in Spain (the Reconquista, completed with the fall of Granada in 1492), against pagans in the Baltic, against heretics (the Albigensian Crusade, 1209–1229), and against the popes' political enemies. Historians disagree about crusaders' motives. Religious devotion, the penitential indulgence, land and family strategy all played a part, with different weight for different people.2 The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople is in IX.3.

    Military orders. The Templars (c. 1119), the Hospitallers and the Teutonic Knights combined monastic vows with warfare. The Templars were arrested in France in 1307 on charges extracted by torture and suppressed by Clement V in 1312, at the Council of Vienne, under pressure from Philip IV. Most historians consider the charges of heresy unfounded.3

    Jews in medieval Christendom

    The First Crusade began with massacres of Jewish communities in the Rhineland (1096), which some bishops tried to stop.4 Other measures followed:

    • Lateran IV (1215), canon 68, required Jews and Muslims to wear distinctive dress.
    • Ritual-murder and host-desecration libels spread, often repudiated by popes and bishops but also exploited.
    • Jews were expelled from England (1290), France (1306 and later) and Spain (1492).

    Augustine's teaching that the Jews should be preserved as "witnesses" underlay a papal policy of protection (Sicut Iudaeis, from c. 1120) that coexisted with degradation. See also Part IV study H.

    Christians and Muslims

    Muslim–Christian relations included war, trade, translation and debate. Peter the Venerable of Cluny commissioned the first Latin Qur'an (1143). Francis of Assisi met Sultan al-Kamil at Damietta (1219). Ramon Llull (d. c. 1316) promoted the study of Arabic for mission. In the East, Christians living under Muslim rule were a majority in some regions until roughly the ninth to fourteenth centuries. The timing of their conversion to Islam is debated (Part IV, study G).

    Notes

    2. Riley-Smith 2014. ↩

    Volume X · Chapter 5

    Canon law, heresy and the inquisitions

    Canon law. Gratian's Decretum (c. 1140) organised a millennium of conciliar and papal texts. Papal decretals were added (the Liber Extra, 1234), forming the Corpus iuris canonici, which remained in force until the Code of 1917. Canon lawyers developed ideas of corporations, representation and natural rights that influenced Western legal thought.

    Lateran IV (1215). The largest medieval council. Its decisions included:

    • the first conciliar use of the language of transubstantiation: in its creed (canon 1), the bread and wine are transsubstantiatis, “changed in substance”;
    • annual confession and Easter communion for all the faithful (canon 21);
    • a ban on new religious orders;
    • regulation of Jews (canons 67–70);
    • a call for crusade.

    1

    Dissent

    Popular religious movements multiplied from the twelfth century. The Waldensians (from c. 1170) were lay preachers of poverty, excommunicated in 1184. They survived and later joined the Reformed movement. The Cathars of southern France and Italy were described by their opponents as dualists with their own "perfect" clergy. Some historians (e.g. R. I. Moore, Mark Pegg) have argued that the image of an organised Cathar church owes much to inquisitors' constructions. Others defend its substantial reality.2

    The inquisitions

    "The Inquisition" was not a single institution.

    FormDateCharacter
    Episcopal inquisitionfrom 1184 (Ad abolendam)Bishops required to seek out heretics.
    Papal (medieval) inquisitorsfrom 1230sMostly Dominican and Franciscan friars commissioned by popes, chiefly in southern France and Italy. Innocent IV's Ad extirpanda (1252) permitted torture. Penalties ranged from penances and pilgrimages to imprisonment; obstinate or relapsed heretics were handed to secular authorities for burning.
    Spanish Inquisition1478 (bull), active from 1480 until 1834Under royal control. Aimed first at conversos (converted Jews) suspected of secret Judaism, later at Moriscos, Protestants and others.
    Portuguese Inquisition1536–1821Also in Goa (1560).
    Roman Inquisition (Holy Office)1542See XII.3.

    Death tolls have been exaggerated in popular accounts and minimised in apologetic ones. Archival research on the Spanish Inquisition (e.g. Gustav Henningsen and Jaime Contreras) suggests that a few thousand people were executed in total across its history, most of them before 1530, out of tens of thousands tried.3 The procedures still involved secret accusers, torture and the death penalty for beliefs. The Catholic Church has since expressed repentance for such methods, notably in John Paul II's "Day of Pardon" in 2000. Protestant authorities also executed people for heresy, for example Servetus at Geneva (1553) and Anabaptists in several territories (XI.4).4

    Notes

    Volume X · Chapter 6

    Papal monarchy, Avignon, the Western Schism and conciliarism

    Innocent III (1198–1216) took papal power to its height. He intervened in imperial elections, made England a papal fief (1213) and convened Lateran IV. Boniface VIII came into conflict with Philip IV of France over the taxation and trial of clergy, and issued the bull Unam sanctam (18 November 1302):

    Porro subesse Romano Pontifici omni humanae creaturae declaramus, dicimus, diffinimus et pronunciamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis.

    “…it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff.”

    Boniface VIII, Unam sanctam (1302), final sentence. English phrase checked against the translation at papalencyclicals.net; Latin from the standard text (not re-checked). Q65 · partly checked

    Philip's agents seized Boniface at Anagni (1303), and he died weeks later. How far Unam sanctam's claims are doctrinally binding has long been debated among Catholic theologians. Its final sentence is usually read in light of the Church's later teaching on salvation outside its visible bounds.1

    Avignon and the Great Western Schism

    From 1309 to 1377 the popes resided at Avignon. The papacy there was efficient and heavily taxing. Critics such as Petrarch called it the "Babylonian captivity". Catherine of Siena and Bridget of Sweden urged a return to Rome. Gregory XI returned in 1377. After his death, the disputed election of Urban VI (1378) led a group of cardinals to elect a rival, Clement VII, who went back to Avignon. From 1409, after the Council of Pisa, there were three claimants. Western Christendom divided its allegiance largely along political lines.

    Constance and conciliarism

    The Council of Constance (1414–1418) ended the schism. It deposed John XXIII (the Pisan line) and Benedict XIII (Avignon), accepted the resignation of Gregory XII (Rome), and elected Martin V (1417).2 Its decree Haec sancta (1415) declared that a general council holds its power immediately from Christ and that everyone, including the pope, must obey it in matters of faith, the ending of schism and reform. Frequens (1417) required regular councils.3 Whether Haec sancta was a dogmatic definition or an emergency measure is a classic dispute. Catholic doctrine since Vatican I rejects the superiority of council over pope. Conciliarist historians (Brian Tierney, Francis Oakley) stress its roots in canon law and its long afterlife.4 The Council of Basel (1431–1449) clashed with Eugenius IV, who moved the council to Ferrara-Florence (IX.4). Pius II's bull Execrabilis (1460) forbade appeals from pope to council.

    Notes

    Volume X · Chapter 7

    The Black Death, Wycliffe, Hus and late medieval piety

    The Black Death of 1347–1351 killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population. Estimates vary by region.1 Religious responses included penitential flagellant processions, condemned by Clement VI in 1349, and massacres of Jews accused of poisoning wells, which Clement VI also condemned. The plague brought new cults of plague saints and intensified attention to death, purgatory and intercession.

    John Wycliffe and the Lollards

    The Oxford theologian John Wycliffe (d. 1384) argued for the supreme authority of Scripture and attacked the wealth of the clergy and the doctrine of transubstantiation. His followers produced English translations of the Bible (the "Wycliffite Bible", 1380s–90s). His followers, the "Lollards", were persecuted after 1401. The Council of Constance condemned him posthumously.2

    Jan Hus

    Jan Hus, a Prague preacher influenced by Wycliffe, criticised indulgences and clerical abuses. He came to Constance under a safe-conduct from Emperor Sigismund, was condemned, and was burned on 6 July 1415.3 The Hussite movement that followed demanded communion in both kinds (the chalice for the laity, hence "Utraquists"). It fought off crusades (1420–1431) and secured the Compacts of Basel (1436). The Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum, 1457) descends from it and is an ancestor of the later Moravian Church. Luther later declared, "We are all Hussites."4

    Late medieval piety

    Older historiography (Protestant and Catholic alike) portrayed the late medieval Church as decadent. Recent research (Eamon Duffy, The Stripping of the Altars, 1992) stresses the vitality of lay religion on the eve of the Reformation, at least in England.5 Its features included:

    • parish guilds, pilgrimages and devotion to the saints and the Eucharist (the feast of Corpus Christi, 1264);
    • chantries for the dead;
    • books of hours;
    • the Devotio moderna of the Brethren of the Common Life (Geert Groote, d. 1384), and Thomas à Kempis' Imitation of Christ (c. 1418–27).

    Calls for reform "in head and members" were constant, and were echoed by humanists such as Erasmus (XI.1).

    Notes

    Volume X · Chapter 8

    Cathedrals, art and the Byzantine Church under pressure

    Architecture and art in the West

    Romanesque churches with thick walls and round arches (11th–12th c.) gave way to Gothic. Abbot Suger's rebuilt choir at Saint-Denis (dedicated 1144) is usually taken as the beginning. Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses allowed tall, light-filled cathedrals such as Chartres, Amiens and Cologne. Their stained glass and sculpture presented biblical history to their viewers. Giotto (d. 1337) and later Renaissance artists transformed religious painting. Church patronage was central to the Renaissance itself.

    Byzantium, 1081–1453

    Under the Komnenian emperors (1081–1185) Byzantium recovered, and the Church condemned the philosopher John Italos (1082) for an excessive use of Plato. After 1204 and the restoration of 1261, the empire shrank before the Ottomans. The Church nonetheless flourished in key respects :

    • Mount Athos (the Great Lavra was founded in 963) became the centre of Orthodox monasticism.1
    • The hesychast movement and Gregory Palamas (IX.4) shaped Orthodox spirituality, including the Jesus Prayer, later collected in the Philokalia (1782).2
    • Late Byzantine art, such as the mosaics and frescoes of the Chora monastery (c. 1315–21), shows the "Palaiologan renaissance".
    • Byzantine scholars, including Bessarion and Gemistos Plethon, carried Greek learning to Italy around the Council of Florence. Bessarion's library founded the Marciana in Venice.3

    The fall of Constantinople (1453) placed the Ecumenical Patriarchate under Ottoman rule (XIII.3).

    Notes

    2. Meyendorff 1964. The Philokalia was compiled by Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain and Makarios of Corinth (Venice, 1782). ↩
    3. Gill 1959. Bessarion's deed of gift to Venice dates from 1468. ↩

    Volume XI · c. 1500–1650

    The Protestant Reformation

    In 1517 an Augustinian friar's protest against indulgences began a chain of events that permanently divided Western Christianity. The "Reformation" was several movements: Lutheran, Reformed, Radical and English. Each had its own theology, politics and geography. This volume presents them separately, with the main theological disputes set out at the end in their own terms.

    In this volume

    1. Background: indulgences, humanism, printing and politics
    2. Martin Luther and the Lutheran Reformation
    3. Zwingli, Calvin and the Reformed tradition
    4. The Radical Reformation
    5. The English Reformation
    6. The theological disputes

    Volume XI · Chapter 1

    Background: indulgences, humanism, printing and politics

    • Indulgences. In Catholic theology an indulgence is a remission of the temporal punishment due to sins already forgiven. It draws on the "treasury of merits" of Christ and the saints, and can be applied to souls in purgatory "by way of suffrage" (Sixtus IV, 1476). In practice, indulgences were sold to fund projects. The St Peter's indulgence of 1515 was preached in Germany by the Dominican Johann Tetzel. Part of its proceeds repaid Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz's debts to the Fugger bank for papal dispensations.1
    • Humanism. The humanist call to return "to the sources" (ad fontes) produced critical editions of classical and Christian texts. Lorenzo Valla exposed the Donation of Constantine (1440). Erasmus published the first printed Greek New Testament (1516), with a new Latin translation and notes. His satire of clerical abuse and his "philosophy of Christ" prepared many readers for reform, though he did not join the Reformation himself and broke with Luther over free will (1524–25).2
    • Printing. Gutenberg's movable type (c. 1450s) made rapid, cheap circulation of pamphlets possible. Luther became the most published author of his age, and historians speak of the Reformation as a "media event" (Andrew Pettegree).3
    • Politics. The Holy Roman Empire was a patchwork of princes and free cities. The emperor Charles V (from 1519) also ruled Spain, the Netherlands and much of Italy, and was preoccupied with France and the Ottomans, who besieged Vienna in 1529. Princes and city councils could therefore protect reformers and control church property.4

    Notes

    Volume XI · Chapter 2

    Martin Luther and the Lutheran Reformation

    Martin Luther (1483–1546), an Augustinian friar and professor of Bible at Wittenberg, came to understand the "righteousness of God" (Romans 1:17) as a gift received by faith, not a standard to be achieved. He later described this as a sudden discovery. Historians debate whether it occurred c. 1513–15 or c. 1518–19.1

    The Ninety-Five Theses (1517)

    On 31 October 1517 Luther sent his Disputation on the Power of Indulgences to Archbishop Albrecht. The famous posting on the door of the Castle Church is first reported after his death, by Melanchthon. Its historicity was challenged by Erwin Iserloh (1961) and is still debated.2

    Dominus et magister noster Iesus Christus dicendo ‘Penitentiam agite &c.’ omnem vitam fidelium penitentiam esse voluit.

    “Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, in saying ‘Repent’, willed the whole life of the faithful to be one of repentance.”

    Luther, Ninety-Five Theses (1517), thesis 1. Latin from the standard text; translation by this edition, compared in sense with the English at luther.de. Q66 · not re-checked

    Hominem predicant, qui statim ut iactus nummus in cistam tinnierit evolare dicunt animam.

    “They preach human doctrine who say that as soon as the coin clinks in the chest, the soul flies out [of purgatory].”

    Thesis 27. Latin from the standard text; translation by this edition. Q67 · not re-checked

    The break (1518–1521)

    • 1519, Leipzig. In debate with Johann Eck, Luther said that popes and councils could err, and defended some teachings of Hus.
    • 1520. Three programmatic treatises: To the Christian Nobility (the priesthood of all believers), The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (reducing the sacraments to baptism, the Lord's Supper and, provisionally, penance), and The Freedom of a Christian. Pope Leo X's bull Exsurge Domine (15 June 1520) condemned 41 propositions; Luther burned it.
    • 3 January 1521. Excommunication (Decet Romanum Pontificem).
    • April 1521, Diet of Worms. Luther refused to recant unless convinced "by Scripture or by clear reason". The words "Here I stand, I can do no other" appear in early printed versions, but their authenticity is uncertain. The Edict of Worms outlawed him. Frederick the Wise had him hidden at the Wartburg, where he translated the New Testament into German (September 1522; the complete Bible appeared in 1534).

    Building a church

    Luther opposed both radical reformers and the Peasants' War (1524–25). His harsh tract against the rebels damaged his reputation among the poor.3 Lutheran reform was carried out by princes and cities through church orders, visitations and Luther's catechisms (1529). Philip Melanchthon drafted the Augsburg Confession, presented to Charles V on 25 June 1530. It remains the defining Lutheran confession. The "Protestants" took their name from the Protestation at Speyer (1529). After war (the Schmalkaldic War, 1546–47), the Peace of Augsburg (1555) recognised Lutheranism in the Empire on the principle later summarised as cuius regio, eius religio: the ruler decides the territory's religion. Reformed and Anabaptist Christians were excluded. Inner-Lutheran disputes were settled in the Formula of Concord (1577), and the Book of Concord (1580) collected the confessions. Lutheranism became the established religion of Scandinavia.4

    Luther's late writings against the Jews (1543), with their call to burn synagogues, are a grave stain on his legacy. Lutheran Churches have formally repudiated them, for example the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America in 1994. They are discussed in Part IV study H.5

    Notes

    2. Erwin Iserloh, Luthers Thesenanschlag: Tatsache oder Legende? (Wiesbaden: Steiner, 1962; lecture of 1961). See Roper 2016 and Leppin, SEP “Luther”. ↩

    Volume XI · Chapter 3

    Zwingli, Calvin and the Reformed tradition

    Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531) began preaching through Matthew's Gospel at Zurich in 1519. After public disputations in 1523, the city council abolished the Mass (1525), removed images and dissolved monasteries. Zwingli held that the Lord's Supper is a memorial in which Christ is spiritually present to faith, and that "is" in "This is my body" means "signifies". At the Marburg Colloquy (October 1529), Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles but not on the Supper. Zwingli was killed at the battle of Kappel (1531). Heinrich Bullinger continued his work.1

    John Calvin (1509–1564), a French humanist lawyer, published the Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536 and expanded it until the final Latin edition of 1559.

    Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.

    Calvin, Institutes 1.1.1 (1559). Trans. Henry Beveridge (1845). The second half was checked against the CCEL text; the opening follows the same translation. Q70 · partly checked

    Calvin was minister at Geneva in 1536–38 and again from 1541 to his death. There he established a consistory of ministers and elders to oversee morals, and an academy (1559) that trained pastors for France and beyond. Geneva also executed the anti-Trinitarian Michael Servetus (1553), with Calvin's support for the prosecution.2 Calvin's eucharistic theology taught that believers truly feed on Christ's body by the Spirit's power. It sought a middle path and led to agreement with Zurich (Consensus Tigurinus, 1549).3

    Spread and confessions

    The Reformed tradition was international, and was shaped by confessions rather than by one founder.

    • France: the Gallican Confession (1559). Huguenots faced the Wars of Religion and the St Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572). The Edict of Nantes (1598) granted them toleration until its revocation in 1685.
    • Scotland: John Knox's reformation produced the Scots Confession (1560) and a presbyterian church.
    • The Netherlands: the Belgic Confession (1561).
    • The Palatinate: the Heidelberg Catechism (1563).
    • Switzerland: the Second Helvetic Confession (1566).
    • Hungary, Poland and Transylvania also had substantial Reformed churches.

    The international Synod of Dort (1618–19) rejected the Remonstrants (followers of Arminius) and defined five points on predestination and grace, later summarised (in English, from the 20th century) by the acronym "TULIP". The Westminster Confession (1646) became the standard of English-speaking Presbyterianism.4

    Notes

    Volume XI · Chapter 4

    The Radical Reformation

    George H. Williams' term "Radical Reformation" (1962) groups very different movements that rejected both Catholic and magisterial Protestant church–state arrangements.1

    • Swiss Brethren. On 21 January 1525, in Zurich, Conrad Grebel baptised George Blaurock, and others followed: adult believers baptising each other in defiance of Zwingli and the council. Felix Manz was drowned by Zurich authorities in January 1527, the first Anabaptist executed by Protestants. The Schleitheim Confession (February 1527), drafted by Michael Sattler (burned in May 1527 by Catholic authorities), set out believers' baptism, church discipline (the ban), separation from the world, refusal of the sword and of oaths, and a congregationally chosen pastor.2
    • Apocalyptic radicals. Thomas Müntzer, executed after the Peasants' War in 1525. The Anabaptist kingdom at Münster (1534–35), which introduced polygamy and was crushed. Münster was used for centuries to discredit all Anabaptists.3
    • Menno Simons (1496–1561), a former priest, gathered the peaceable Dutch and North German Anabaptists, later called Mennonites. The Hutterites practised community of goods in Moravia. The Amish separated from the Swiss Brethren in 1693.
    • Spiritualists and anti-Trinitarians. Sebastian Franck and Caspar Schwenckfeld; Michael Servetus; Faustus Socinus and the Polish Brethren (the Racovian Catechism, 1605); the Unitarian church of Transylvania, under the Edict of Torda (1568).

    Thousands of Anabaptists were executed by Catholic and Protestant authorities in the sixteenth century. The Martyrs Mirror (1660) preserved their memory.4 In 2010 the Lutheran World Federation formally asked Mennonites for forgiveness for Lutheran persecution of Anabaptists.5 The Anabaptist emphasis on voluntary church membership and religious liberty became influential in later Baptist, Quaker and free-church traditions.

    Volume XI · Chapter 5

    The English Reformation

    The English Reformation began as an act of state. Henry VIII sought the annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and Clement VII, under pressure from Catherine's nephew Charles V, would not grant it. Henry broke with Rome.1

    • Henry VIII. The Act of Supremacy (1534) made the king Supreme Head of the Church of England. Thomas More and John Fisher were executed (1535). The monasteries were dissolved (1536–1540). The English Bible was authorised (the Great Bible, 1539), drawing heavily on William Tyndale, who had been executed in 1536 near Brussels. Henry's own doctrine remained largely Catholic (the Six Articles, 1539).
    • Edward VI (1547–53). Archbishop Thomas Cranmer introduced the Book of Common Prayer (1549; a more Protestant revision in 1552) and the Forty-Two Articles (1553).
    • Mary I (1553–58) restored Catholicism. About 280–290 Protestants were burned, including Cranmer (1556), commemorated in John Foxe's Acts and Monuments (1563).
    • Elizabeth I. The Elizabethan Settlement (1559) restored royal supremacy (as "Supreme Governor") and a revised Prayer Book. The Thirty-Nine Articles (1563; confirmed by Parliament in 1571) defined doctrine. Catholic priests were executed as traitors after the papal excommunication of Elizabeth (1570): about 180 Catholics in her reign, by common estimates.2

    We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ by Faith, and not for our own works or deservings…

    Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XI (1571). Text checked against the Church of England website. Q71 · checked

    Article VI holds that "Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation". Article XXI says that general councils "may err, and sometimes have erred".3

    Later developments:

    • Puritans sought further reform. Some separated, among them the first English Baptists: John Smyth in Amsterdam (1609) and Thomas Helwys in London (1612).
    • Civil war and Restoration. The civil wars brought presbyterian and independent church orders (1640s–50s). The Restoration (1660) and the 1662 Prayer Book re-established episcopacy and ejected about 2,000 nonconforming ministers.
    • Anglican identity. Its distinctive identity, called "via media" by later writers such as Newman, was articulated by Richard Hooker (Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, 1590s). It became a worldwide Communion through colonial and missionary expansion (Part III).

    Revisionist historians (Christopher Haigh, Eamon Duffy) argue that the English Reformation was imposed from above on a largely Catholic population. Others (A. G. Dickens) emphasised popular Protestant enthusiasm.4

    Volume XI · Chapter 6

    The theological disputes

    The Reformation disputes are often summarised in the later formula of the "solas": sola scriptura, sola fide, sola gratia (and in 20th-century usage, solus Christus and soli Deo gloria). The list as such is not a sixteenth-century formula.1

    Justification

    Lutheran (Augsburg Confession, 1530)

    Also they teach that men can not be justified [obtain forgiveness of sins and righteousness] before God by their own powers, merits, or works; but are justified freely [of grace] for Christ's sake through faith, when they believe that they are received into favor, and their sins forgiven for Christ's sake, who by his death hath satisfied for our sins. This faith doth God impute for righteousness before him.

    Augsburg Confession, Art. IV. English in Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom, vol. 3 (1877). Checked against CCEL. Q68 · checked

    Catholic (Council of Trent, 1547)

    If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to co-operate in order to the obtaining the grace of Justification, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be anathema.

    Trent, Session 6 (13 January 1547), canon 9. Trans. J. Waterworth (1848), as at papalencyclicals.net. Checked. Q69 · checked

    Note what Trent condemns. It does not reject justification by grace, which its decree affirms is unmerited (ch. 8). It rejects "faith alone" understood as excluding human cooperation and inner renewal. Lutherans spoke of righteousness imputed to the believer. Trent spoke of righteousness infused, with justification including sanctification. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (signed by the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church at Augsburg, 31 October 1999; later affirmed by Methodists in 2006, by the World Communion of Reformed Churches in 2017 and by the Anglican Communion) states a "consensus on basic truths". It declares that the sixteenth-century condemnations do not apply to the teaching it presents, while acknowledging remaining differences.2

    The Lord's Supper

    PositionHeld bySummary
    TransubstantiationCatholic (Lateran IV, 1215; Trent, Session 13, 1551)The substance of bread and wine is changed into Christ's body and blood; the appearances (accidents) remain. The Mass is a true propitiatory sacrifice, one with Calvary.
    Sacramental unionLutheranChrist's true body and blood are present "in, with and under" the bread and wine and received by all communicants. Rejects transubstantiation and the Mass as sacrifice. ("Consubstantiation" is a label used by critics, not by Lutheran confessions.)
    Spiritual real presenceCalvin; Reformed confessions; much Anglican teachingBelievers truly receive Christ's body by faith through the Spirit, lifted up to heaven where Christ is.
    MemorialZwingli (often simplified); many Baptists and free churchesThe Supper commemorates and proclaims Christ's death; Christ is present to faith, not in the elements.
    Mystery / change (metabolē)Eastern Orthodox (for comparison)Real change affirmed; the manner left a mystery. Some Orthodox confessions of the 17th century used the term metousiōsis (transubstantiation).

    Other issues

    • Scripture and tradition. The Reformers held Scripture to be the sole infallible rule. Trent (Session 4, 1546) received Scripture and unwritten apostolic traditions "with equal affection of piety", and defined the canon including the deuterocanonical books (II.9).
    • Sacraments. Catholics hold seven. Lutherans and Reformed hold two (baptism and the Supper), with penance or absolution valued by Lutherans. Anabaptists speak of "ordinances".
    • Baptism. Infant baptism was retained by Catholics, Lutherans, Reformed and Anglicans, and rejected by Anabaptists and later Baptists.
    • Predestination. All parties drew on Augustine. Reformed orthodoxy (Dort) taught unconditional election. Lutherans affirmed election to salvation but resisted double predestination. Arminians and later Methodists stressed resistible grace. Within Catholicism, Dominicans and Jesuits disputed grace and free will (the de auxiliis controversy, 1597–1607), as did the Jansenists later.
    • Ministry and authority. The priesthood of all believers; ordained ministry as office rather than sacrament (except for Anglicans and some Lutherans); rejection of papal authority; varied views of episcopacy.
    • Saints, Mary and purgatory. The Reformers rejected the invocation of saints and purgatory, while generally keeping Mary's title Theotokos and, in Luther's case, her perpetual virginity.

    For a tradition-by-tradition comparison of all these topics, see the Part III comparison matrix.

    Volume XII · c. 1500–1700

    The Catholic Reformation and Counter-Reformation

    Historians once spoke only of a "Counter-Reformation", a reaction against Protestantism. Hubert Jedin proposed the pairing "Catholic Reform and Counter-Reformation" to capture both the reform movements that predated Luther and the deliberate response to him. More recently John O'Malley suggested "Early Modern Catholicism". This volume covers the Council of Trent, the new orders and the saints, global missions, the instruments of control, and the religious wars, and compares Trent's decrees with the Protestant confessions.

    In this volume

    1. The Council of Trent (1545–1563)
    2. Jesuits, mystics and the new orders
    3. Inquisition, Index, wars and Westphalia
    4. Global Catholic missions
    5. Trent and the Protestant confessions compared

    Volume XII · Chapter 1

    The Council of Trent (1545–1563)

    The Council of Trent met in three periods (1545–47, 1551–52, 1562–63) under Paul III, Julius III and Pius IV. It met at Trent, an imperial city south of the Alps, as a compromise between the emperor's wish for a German venue and the pope's for an Italian one. Attendance was small at first: about 30 bishops opened it; at the close in December 1563, 255 fathers signed the decrees, about 200 of them bishops.1 Most participants were Italian, with significant Spanish contingents. Protestant envoys attended briefly in 1551–52 but did not participate as equals.2

    The council worked in tandem on doctrine and reform.3

    Session (date)DoctrineReform
    4 (April 1546)Scripture and unwritten traditions; the canon including deuterocanonical books; the Vulgate declared "authentic" for public useRegulation of printing and preaching
    5 (June 1546)Original sinLectureships in Scripture
    6 (January 1547)Justification (16 chapters, 33 canons) — see XI.6Residence of bishops
    7, 13, 14 (1547–1551)The sacraments in general; baptism and confirmation; the Eucharist (transubstantiation); penance and extreme unction—
    21–22 (1562)Communion under one kind; the sacrifice of the Mass—
    23 (July 1563)Holy ordersSeminaries in every diocese
    24 (Nov. 1563)MatrimonyTametsi: marriages require a priest and witnesses
    25 (Dec. 1563)Purgatory, saints, relics and images; indulgences (abuses condemned, the practice upheld)Religious orders

    The council's work was implemented through:

    • the Profession of Faith (1564);
    • the Roman Catechism (1566);
    • the Breviary (1568) and Missal (1570) of Pius V, which standardised the Roman Rite for four centuries;
    • the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592).

    Model reforming bishops such as Charles Borromeo in Milan (1564–84) showed what the decrees could achieve. Implementation was slow and uneven, and depended on rulers. France never formally received the reform decrees.4

    Volume XII · Chapter 2

    Jesuits, mystics and the new orders

    Reform movements predated Luther:

    • the Oratory of Divine Love (Genoa, 1497; Rome, c. 1514–17);
    • Cardinal Ximénez de Cisneros' reforms in Spain, including the Complutensian Polyglot Bible (printed 1514–17);
    • the Theatines (1524);
    • the Capuchins (1528), a reformed Franciscan branch.

    1

    The Society of Jesus

    Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), a Basque soldier converted while convalescing (1521), wrote the Spiritual Exercises and gathered companions in Paris. Paul III approved the Society in 1540. The Jesuits took a special vow of obedience to the pope concerning missions. They became famous for education: hundreds of colleges by 1600, under a common plan, the Ratio studiorum (1599). They were also active as missionaries and confessors to rulers, and as polemicists (Robert Bellarmine).2 Their success brought enemies. The order was expelled from Portugal (1759), France (1764) and Spain (1767), suppressed by Clement XIV (1773), and restored in 1814.3

    Mystics and saints

    • Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582) reformed the Carmelites (the Discalced, from 1562) and wrote The Interior Castle. She was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1970.
    • John of the Cross (1542–1591), her collaborator, wrote The Dark Night and The Spiritual Canticle. He was imprisoned by his own order in 1577–78.
    • Francis de Sales (1567–1622) wrote the Introduction to the Devout Life, addressed to lay people. Vincent de Paul (d. 1660) and Louise de Marillac founded the Daughters of Charity, an unenclosed women's community serving the poor. Mary Ward's attempts to found an active women's order modelled on the Jesuits were suppressed in 1631.

    Baroque art and architecture expressed the period's spirituality and its affirmation of the senses, of images and of sacraments: Bernini at St Peter's, Caravaggio, Rubens, and the churches of Spanish America. The church of the Gesù in Rome (consecrated 1584) became a model.4

    Volume XII · Chapter 3

    Inquisition, Index, wars and Westphalia

    • The Roman Inquisition. Paul III's bull Licet ab initio (1542) set up the Congregation of the Holy Office (Roman Inquisition), aimed mainly at Protestantism in Italy. Its records survive in the archives of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, opened to scholars in 1998. Notable cases include Giordano Bruno, burned in 1600 for theological heresies including denial of the Trinity, and Galileo (1633; see XIV.1).1
    • The Index of Prohibited Books. First issued in 1559 (Paul IV), revised after Trent (1564), and abolished in 1966. It shaped Catholic intellectual life and book production, though historians debate how effective it was.2
    • Wars of religion:
      • the French Wars of Religion (1562–1598);
      • the Dutch Revolt against Spain (from 1568);
      • the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which began with the Bohemian revolt and the Defenestration of Prague, and drew in Sweden and Catholic France on the Protestant side;
      • Ireland and the British civil wars.
      Historians debate how "religious" these wars were. Confessional loyalty was intertwined with dynastic and state interests.3 The Thirty Years' War (1618–48) killed perhaps a fifth of the Empire's population, around five million people, with far heavier losses in the worst-affected regions.4
    • The Peace of Westphalia (1648). Recognised Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism in the Empire, fixed confessional boundaries at their 1624 state, and gave some protection to private worship by minorities. Pope Innocent X protested against its religious clauses (Zelo domus Dei), to no effect. Westphalia is often taken as the start of an order of sovereign states in which religion was largely a matter of state policy. That reading is itself debated.5

    Notes

    Volume XII · Chapter 4

    Global Catholic missions

    Iberian expansion carried Catholicism worldwide under the padroado (Portuguese) and patronato (Spanish) systems of royal patronage over the Church.1 The missions spanned several regions:

    • The Americas. Conquest and evangelisation were bound together, with devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples. Most deaths came from epidemic disease, but violence, enslavement and forced labour (the encomienda) also took their toll. Dominicans such as Antonio de Montesinos (1511) and Bartolomé de las Casas denounced abuses. Paul III's Sublimis Deus (1537) affirmed the Indians' rationality and right to liberty and property. At the Valladolid debate (1550–51), Las Casas argued against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda's justification of conquest. Devotions such as Our Lady of Guadalupe (the apparition tradition is dated to 1531; documentation of it before the mid-17th century is debated) became central to Mexican Catholicism.2
    • Asia. Francis Xavier worked in India, Southeast Asia and Japan (d. 1552). In Japan there were perhaps 300,000 Christians by about 1600. Persecution and martyrdom followed under the Tokugawa (from 1614), leaving the "hidden Christians" (kakure kirishitan). Matteo Ricci reached Beijing (1601) and adapted Christianity to Confucian culture. The Chinese Rites controversy, over whether converts could honour ancestors and Confucius, ended with papal prohibitions (1715; 1742) that crippled the mission. They were relaxed in 1939. In India, Roberto de Nobili adopted Brahmin customs in Madurai. Portuguese latinisation of the Saint Thomas Christians culminated in the Synod of Diamper (1599) (XIII.7).
    • Africa. The Kingdom of Kongo, whose king Afonso I reigned c. 1509–1542, adopted Catholicism through its own elite and corresponded with Rome. Its Church was entangled with the Portuguese slave trade.3

    In 1622 the papacy created the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide) to direct missions independently of the Iberian crowns. Its 1659 instructions warned missionaries not to impose European customs.4 Christianity and slavery are treated in XIV.4.

    Volume XIII · 7th century to the present

    Eastern Christianity beyond Constantinople

    Histories written in the West often follow Eastern Christianity only as far as 1453. This volume follows its many Churches past that date. It covers the Slavs and Russia; the Churches under Islamic and Ottoman rule; Georgia, Armenia, Egypt and Ethiopia; the Maronite and other Antiochian Churches; the Eastern Catholic Churches; and the Saint Thomas Christians of India. Earlier periods for these Churches are in Volume V.

    In this volume

    1. Byzantine missions among the Slavs
    2. Rus', Moscow and the Russian Church
    3. Under Islamic and Ottoman rule
    4. Georgia, Armenia, Egypt and Ethiopia
    5. The Churches of Antioch and the Maronite tradition
    6. Eastern Catholic Churches and their relations
    7. The Saint Thomas Christians of India

    Volume XIII · Chapter 1

    Byzantine missions among the Slavs

    The mission of Cyril and Methodius to Moravia (863) and its Slavonic liturgy are described in VIII.6. Expelled from Moravia, their disciples Clement and Naum took the tradition to Bulgaria. There the Preslav and Ohrid schools developed Old Church Slavonic literature and the Cyrillic script, named in Cyril's honour but probably created in Bulgaria c. 890s–900s. Bulgaria's Church gained a patriarchate, recognised by Constantinople in 927. Serbia received an autocephalous archbishopric under St Sava (1219). The Serbian patriarchate was established in 1346, abolished by the Ottomans in 1766, and restored in 1920. Croats, Slovenes, Czechs and Poles entered the Latin Church. The line between Latin and Slavonic-Byzantine Christianity ran through central Europe and remains a cultural fault line.1

    Notes

    1. Ware 1993; Francis Dvornik, Byzantine Missions among the Slavs (New Brunswick: Rutgers University Press, 1970). ↩
