    Volume XIII · Chapter 2

    Rus', Moscow and the Russian Church

    • The baptism of Rus'. Princess Olga of Kiev was baptised in the 950s. Her grandson Vladimir adopted Byzantine Christianity c. 988, the date given by the Primary Chronicle, and married the emperor's sister Anna. The Chronicle's story of envoys comparing religions is literary. The political alliance is well attested.1 The metropolitan of Kiev was appointed from Constantinople, usually a Greek.
    • Mongol rule (from 1237–40) and the move of the metropolitan's residence to Vladimir (1299) and then Moscow (1325). The Church gained privileges under the khans. Sergius of Radonezh (d. 1392) renewed monasticism.
    • Autocephaly. Moscow rejected the Union of Florence and its metropolitan, Isidore (IX.4). In 1448 a Russian synod elected Jonah metropolitan without Constantinople's approval, a de facto autocephaly. The Moscow Patriarchate was created in 1589 with the consent of Patriarch Jeremias II, and confirmed by Eastern synods in 1590 and 1593.2
    • "Moscow, the Third Rome." The monk Philotheus of Pskov, in letters usually dated to the 1520s, wrote that two Romes had fallen, the third stood, "and a fourth there shall not be". Historians debate how much this eschatological idea shaped state ideology. Some see it as later nationalist retrojection.3
    • The Old Believers. Patriarch Nikon (1652–58, deposed 1666) aligned Russian rites with contemporary Greek practice. The changes included three fingers for the sign of the cross instead of two, and revised service books. Opponents led by Archpriest Avvakum refused. The councils of 1666–67 anathematised the old rites, and Avvakum was burned (1682). Old Believers, divided into priested and priestless groups, endured centuries of persecution. The Russian Orthodox Church lifted the anathemas in 1971.4
    • The Synodal period. Peter the Great abolished the patriarchate and created the Holy Synod (1721), supervised by a lay official. This lasted until the patriarchate was restored in 1917. The period also saw missions across Siberia to Alaska and Japan, the spiritual revival around the startsy (elders) of Optina and Seraphim of Sarov, and Russian religious philosophy. The twentieth century is in XV.2.

    Volume XIII · Chapter 3

    Under Islamic and Ottoman rule

    After the Arab conquests (630s–710s), Christians and Jews became dhimmī, protected but subordinate communities. They paid a poll tax (jizya) and were subject to restrictions associated with the "Pact of ʿUmar", a text whose attribution to the seventh century is doubted. Enforcement varied greatly by period and ruler.1 Christians remained a majority in many regions for centuries, and conversion to Islam was gradual. They also contributed to Arabic culture. Theodore Abu Qurrah wrote Christian theology in Arabic, and the translators Hunayn ibn Ishaq (Church of the East) and Yahya ibn ʿAdi (Syriac Orthodox) worked at Baghdad.2 See also Part IV, study G.

    The Ottoman millet

    After 1453 Mehmed II installed Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch (1454). The Ecumenical Patriarch became the civil as well as religious head of the Orthodox subjects of the Sultan (the Rum millet). This increased his authority over the other Orthodox patriarchates and over Slavs and Romanians, but exposed the office to purchase and deposition. There were very frequent changes of patriarch in the 17th–18th centuries. The "millet system" as a formal, uniform institution has been questioned as a later idealisation.3 Neomartyrs, Christians executed for apostasy from Islam or for refusing conversion, were venerated. The Greek Church's leadership was dominated by Phanariot families (named after the Phanar district of Istanbul).

    Patriarch Cyril Loukaris (d. 1638) published a Calvinist-leaning Confession (1629) and was strangled amid court intrigue. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672, under Dositheos) answered with a confession using Latin-influenced terms such as metousiōsis. This shows the complex relation of post-Byzantine Orthodoxy to Western confessional debates.4

    National Churches

    As the Ottoman Empire contracted in the nineteenth century, national Orthodox Churches claimed autocephaly:

    • Greece declared it in 1833, and Constantinople recognised it in 1850;
    • Serbia (1879);
    • Romania (1885);
    • the Bulgarian Exarchate (1870), which Constantinople declared schismatic in 1872 for "ethnophyletism" (organising the Church by ethnicity), a schism healed in 1945.

    The tension between universal Orthodoxy and national Churches, and between Constantinople and Moscow, continues today (XV.6).

    Volume XIII · Chapter 4

    Georgia, Armenia, Egypt and Ethiopia

    Georgia

    Royal conversion in Kartli in the 330s (St Nino). The Church followed the Armenians in hesitating over Chalcedon, then definitively accepted it c. 600–608, separating from the Armenian Church. Georgia is thus Eastern Orthodox. Its autocephaly is traditionally dated to the 5th century; the details and dates are debated. It was abolished by Russia (1811), restored in 1917, and recognised by Constantinople in 1990.

    Armenia

    The Armenian Church developed its own alphabet (Mesrop Mashtots, c. 405) and literature. Medieval centres included the Cilician kingdom (1198–1375), which had close contacts with the crusaders and Rome. The Catholicosate returned to Etchmiadzin in 1441, while a Cilician line continued at Sis. The genocide of 1915–1923 destroyed most of the Armenian population of Anatolia. Historians widely recognise it as genocide, a characterisation the Turkish state disputes.1

    Egypt

    Copts remained the majority in Egypt perhaps until the 10th–14th centuries; estimates of the timing differ.2 Arabic replaced Coptic in daily use and increasingly in church. The 13th-century "Coptic renaissance" produced the Awlad al-ʿAssal theologians. Since the 20th century the Church has seen a monastic and Sunday School revival (Matta al-Miskin; Pope Shenouda III, 1971–2012), alongside periodic sectarian violence, such as the 2015 killing of 21 Coptic Christians in Libya. Pope Francis enrolled them in the Roman Martyrology in 2023.

    Ethiopia

    Distinctive practices include circumcision, Sabbath observance alongside Sunday, and the tabot (altar tablet). The Zagwe dynasty (Lalibela rock churches, c. 12th–13th c.) and the "Solomonic" restoration (1270) were followed by a literary flowering (the Kebra Nagast, 14th c.). Survival through the Adal invasion (1529–43) and Portuguese Jesuit attempts at union (the conversion of Emperor Susenyos in 1622, reversed in 1632) shaped a fiercely independent Church. Patriarchate from 1959 (V.2).3

    Volume XIII · Chapter 5

    The Churches of Antioch and the Maronite tradition

    The apostolic see of Antioch (VII.3) today has five patriarchs who each claim its succession:

    • the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch (Damascus; Oriental Orthodox);
    • the Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (Damascus; Eastern Orthodox; largely Arabic-speaking, historically the "Melkites");
    • the Maronite Patriarch (Bkerke, Lebanon; Catholic);
    • the Melkite Greek Catholic Patriarch (Damascus; Catholic, Byzantine rite);
    • the Syriac Catholic Patriarch (Beirut; Catholic, West Syriac rite).

    This multiplicity is the product of the divisions after Chalcedon (V.2), the Arab conquests, crusader-era contacts, and the Catholic unions of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

    Maronite origins

    The Maronite Church takes its name from Maron, a Syrian hermit who died before c. 423. Theodoret describes him (Religious History 16). A monastery bearing his name, Beth Maron, existed in the province of Syria Secunda near Apamea in the 5th–6th centuries. Its monks were prominent defenders of Chalcedon. A letter of Syrian archimandrites to Pope Hormisdas (517), complaining that anti-Chalcedonians had killed 350 monks, is preserved in the acts of a council of 536 and is cited in Maronite tradition.1 Between the seventh and tenth centuries the community, under pressure from war and from other Christian groups, became concentrated in the mountains of Lebanon. It emerged under its own patriarch, separate from the Byzantine-rite Melkite patriarchate.

    John Maron (d. c. 707) is venerated as the first Maronite patriarch. Little reliable contemporary evidence about him survives, and his historicity and dates are debated by historians.2

    The question of Monothelitism and "perpetual communion"

    Two narratives meet here, and this edition sets them side by side.

    Maronite tradition

    The Maronites have always been orthodox and in communion with Rome. This position was developed systematically by Patriarch Stephen Douaihy (1670–1704) and earlier Maronite scholars in Rome. Charges of heresy are said to come from hostile sources, or from confusion with other groups. The Maronite Church officially teaches this "perpetual communion".

    Other historical sources

    William of Tyre (d. 1186), History 22.8, reports that the Maronites had followed the "error of Maron" (the doctrine of one will) for some 500 years, until about 1182, when they abjured it before the Latin patriarch of Antioch. Some Byzantine, Melkite and Syriac sources also associate them with Monothelitism. Medieval texts such as the 13th-century letter of Innocent III to the Maronites (1215) mention correcting their practices.

    Modern scholarship offers several explanations. One is that the Maronites accepted the Ekthesis-era compromise, the formula of "one will" (VI.6), which had imperial and papal support in the 630s (including from Honorius), and simply did not receive the 681 condemnation, cut off as they were by the Arab conquest. If so, they were "Monothelite" in the sense of preserving a formerly official position. Others, including Maronite scholars, argue that the medieval accusations rest on polemical sources and on confusion between different Syrian communities. Most historians accept that a formal reception of Roman doctrine and Latin contacts took place in the crusader period, whatever the earlier situation.3

    Medieval and modern history

    • 1215. Patriarch Jeremias al-Amshiti attended the Fourth Lateran Council.4
    • 1584. The Maronite College in Rome was founded. It produced scholars such as the Assemani family, who catalogued Syriac manuscripts for the Vatican.
    • 1736. The Synod of Mount Lebanon organised the Church on Tridentine lines. It introduced some latinisation, such as the use of unleavened bread, while preserving the Syriac-Antiochene liturgy.5
    • Monasticism and places. The Qadisha Valley, the Holy Valley (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998), was the refuge of patriarchs and hermits. The patriarchal seat moved to Bkerke, used from the 18th century and the principal see since the 19th.
    • Politics. The Maronites were central to the emergence of Mount Lebanon and, after the 1860 conflict with the Druze and the French Mandate, of the Lebanese state. Under the unwritten National Pact (1943), the president of Lebanon is a Maronite. Large diasporas exist in the Americas, Australia and Africa.
    • Saints. Charbel Makhlouf (d. 1898, canonised 1977), Rafqa (canonised 2001) and Nimatullah Kassab al-Hardini (canonised 2004).

    The other Antiochian Churches

    • Greek Orthodox (Rum) Patriarchate of Antioch. Chalcedonian, Byzantine-rite since about the 12th–13th centuries (earlier using the Syriac-Antiochene rite). Arab patriarchs since 1899. Seat in Damascus since the 14th century.
    • Melkite Greek Catholic Church. Formed after the contested election of 1724, when the pro-Catholic Cyril VI Tanas was elected and a rival, Sylvester, was appointed from Constantinople. Notable at Vatican II (Patriarch Maximos IV) for defending Eastern traditions.
    • Syriac Catholic Church. A Catholic patriarch first in 1662. Continuous since 1782 (Michael Jarweh).
    • Syriac Orthodox Church. See V.2. Its heartland in Tur Abdin, south-east Turkey, suffered the Sayfo ("sword") massacres of 1914–1924, alongside Assyrians and Armenians.

    Notes

    Volume XIII · Chapter 6

    Eastern Catholic Churches and their relations

    The Catholic Church today includes 23 Eastern Catholic Churches sui iuris. They are governed by the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), and several are led by patriarchs or major archbishops.1 They arose in different ways:

    • Some never had a separate non-Catholic counterpart: the Maronites, on their own account (ch. 5), and the Italo-Albanians.
    • Most arose from unions with parts of Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox or Church of the East communities:
      • the Union of Brest (1595–96)2, the Ruthenians, today the Ukrainian and Belarusian Greek Catholics;
      • Uzhhorod (1646);
      • Alba Iulia (1698–1700), Romanians;
      • the Melkites (1724);
      • Armenian Catholics (1742);
      • Chaldeans (1553/1830);
      • Syriac Catholics;
      • Coptic Catholics (1824/1895);
      • the Ethiopian and Eritrean Catholic Churches;
      • the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Churches (1930).

    Their history includes heavy latinisation, resisted by figures such as Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky in Ukraine. Vatican II's decree Orientalium Ecclesiarum (1964) affirmed their right to their own traditions. Under communism, the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church was forcibly absorbed into the Russian Orthodox Church at the Lviv pseudo-synod (1946) and survived underground until legalised (1989). The Romanian Greek Catholic Church was suppressed in 1948. Orthodox Churches have long regarded such unions ("uniatism") as an obstacle to dialogue. The 1993 Balamand document rejected uniatism as a method of seeking unity while recognising the existing Eastern Catholic Churches' right to exist and to pastoral care of their faithful (IX.4).3

    Volume XIII · Chapter 7

    The Saint Thomas Christians of India

    The Christians of Kerala trace their origin to the apostle Thomas, traditionally said to have arrived in AD 52. This tradition is ancient, but it cannot be confirmed from contemporary sources.1 They are attested from the sixth century at the latest (Cosmas Indicopleustes), were linked with the Church of the East, which supplied their bishops, and held privileges recorded in copper plates (c. 849). They used the East Syriac liturgy, while living as a high-status community with local customs.

    Their history after the arrival of the Portuguese fragmented the community:

    1. Latinisation. After the Portuguese arrived (1498), Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa held the Synod of Diamper (Udayamperur, 1599). It imposed Latin practices, condemned "Nestorian" books (many were burned) and placed the community under Jesuit bishops.2
    2. The Coonan Cross Oath (1653). Many swore at Mattancherry never to submit to the Jesuits. Rome sent Carmelites, and a large part of the community returned to Catholic communion; it became the Syro-Malabar Church. Others accepted the West Syriac (Syriac Orthodox) bishop Gregorios (1665), forming the Malankara tradition (V.2).3
    3. Later divisions:
      • the Mar Thoma Syrian Church, reformed in the 19th century under the influence of Anglican missionaries;
      • the Malabar Independent Syrian Church (Thozhiyur, 1772);
      • the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite division (1912 onwards);
      • the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church (1930, Mar Ivanios);
      • the Chaldean Syrian Church (Assyrian Church of the East, in Thrissur).

    The Syro-Malabar Church is today one of the largest Eastern Catholic Churches. A long dispute over the direction of celebrating the Eucharist (the "liturgy dispute") has troubled the archdiocese of Ernakulam-Angamaly since the 2020s.

    Volume XIV · 1600–1900

    Christianity and the Modern World (1600–1900)

    Between 1600 and 1900 Christianity met four great changes: modern science, the Enlightenment's critique of revealed religion, political revolution and the secular state, and industrialisation. At the same time it expanded across the globe, both with colonial empires and against them. Its centre of gravity began to shift south and east.

    In this volume

    1. Science and the Galileo affair
    2. Enlightenment, toleration and revolution
    3. Pietism, Methodism and the Awakenings
    4. Missions, colonialism, slavery and abolition
    5. New movements of the nineteenth century
    6. Biblical criticism, liberal and conservative theology
    7. The First Vatican Council and the end of the Papal States

    Volume XIV · Chapter 1

    Science and the Galileo affair

    The "conflict thesis", the idea that science and religion have always been at war, was popularised by J. W. Draper (1874) and A. D. White (1896). Historians of science now generally reject it as a generalisation.1 Medieval and early modern natural philosophy was largely practised by clerics. Many founders of modern science were devout: Kepler, Boyle and Newton, though Newton held anti-Trinitarian views. The Jesuits ran observatories and taught astronomy. Real conflicts did occur, and they need to be described precisely.

    Galileo

    • 1543. Copernicus' De revolutionibus proposed a heliocentric system. It attracted little official opposition for decades.
    • 1610. Galileo's telescopic discoveries (the moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus) supported Copernicanism, though they did not prove it.
    • 1616. Theologians of the Holy Office judged heliocentrism "formally heretical" (a consultants' opinion, not a papal definition). The Congregation of the Index suspended Copernicus' book "until corrected". Cardinal Bellarmine instructed Galileo not to hold or defend the doctrine.
    • 1632–33. Galileo published the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, which appeared to ridicule Urban VIII's position. He was tried by the Holy Office, found "vehemently suspect of heresy", made to abjure (22 June 1633), and kept under house arrest until his death (1642). He was not tortured, according to the trial records.
    • Later. Heliocentric books were removed from the Index in 1822 and 1835. In 1992 John Paul II, receiving a commission's report, acknowledged that theologians had erred in the case.

    Historians debate the causes. Proposed factors include Counter-Reformation anxieties about biblical interpretation, the state of the scientific evidence (Tycho Brahe's system was a serious alternative), Galileo's personality and his patron's politics, and papal pride.2 Darwin's Origin of Species (1859) produced a range of responses, from accommodation (Asa Gray; Anglican and Catholic writers) to rejection. Organised "creationism" as an anti-evolution movement is largely a twentieth-century, mainly American, development (XV.8).

    Notes

    1. Brooke 1991; Numbers 2009. ↩
    2. Documents in Finocchiaro 1989. ↩

    Volume XIV · Chapter 2

    Enlightenment, toleration and revolution

    • Toleration. After the wars of religion, arguments for toleration came from several directions:
      • the Dutch Republic's practice, and Spinoza;
      • Roger Williams in Rhode Island (1636);
      • Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration (1689), which excluded Catholics and atheists;
      • the English Toleration Act (1689), for Protestant dissenters;
      • Pierre Bayle.
      Many of these arguments were themselves religious.1
    • The Enlightenment was not uniformly anti-Christian. Deists such as Toland and Tindal, and Voltaire ("écrasez l'infâme", directed against intolerant ecclesiastical power), criticised revealed religion. A "religious Enlightenment" (David Sorkin) of rational Christians also existed. Kant confined religion "within the bounds of reason alone" (1793), and Hume's critiques of miracles and design were influential.2
    • The American founding separated church and state at the federal level (First Amendment, 1791). State establishments lasted until 1833, in Massachusetts.
    • The French Revolution nationalised church property (1789). The Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790) required clergy to take an oath. Pius VI condemned it, splitting the clergy into jurors and non-jurors. Dechristianisation followed in 1793–94, with closed churches, the Cult of Reason and the Supreme Being, and executions of priests, including the Carmelite nuns of Compiègne (1794). Napoleon's Concordat (1801) restored Catholic worship under state control. The 1905 law separated church and state in France (laïcité).3
    • Catholic responses. Gregory XVI's Mirari vos (1832) condemned "indifferentism" and freedom of conscience. Pius IX's Syllabus of Errors (1864) rejected the proposition that the pope should reconcile himself with "progress, liberalism and modern civilisation". Vatican II's Dignitatis humanae (1965) later affirmed religious freedom (XV.5). How these teachings fit together is debated among Catholic theologians (continuity or development).4

    Notes

    Volume XIV · Chapter 3

    Pietism, Methodism and the Awakenings

    Pietism in Lutheran Germany emphasised heartfelt faith, Bible study groups and practical charity. Its key figures were Philipp Jakob Spener (Pia desideria, 1675) and August Hermann Francke at Halle. Count Zinzendorf renewed the Moravian Church at Herrnhut (1727), which sent pioneering missionaries to the Caribbean (1732) and beyond.1

    Methodism began among John and Charles Wesley and George Whitefield, Anglican clergy at Oxford. John Wesley's account of a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738:

    I felt my heart strangely warmed.

    John Wesley, Journal, 24 May 1738. Standard text (public domain); not re-checked against an edition in this session. Q73 · not re-checked

    Wesley preached in the open air across Britain and organised converts into societies, classes and a "connexion" of lay preachers. He taught Arminian theology, assurance and "Christian perfection". Charles Wesley wrote about 6,000 hymns. Wesley remained an Anglican priest, but his ordinations for America (1784) led to the Methodist Episcopal Church, organised at the Christmas Conference in Baltimore in December 1784. British Methodism separated from the Church of England after his death (1791).2

    The Awakenings. In America the "Great Awakening" (1730s–40s) of Jonathan Edwards and Whitefield was followed by the Second Great Awakening (c. 1790s–1840s), with camp meetings and Charles Finney's "new measures". Baptists and Methodists grew rapidly, especially among the poor, on the frontier and among African Americans. Historians debate whether "Great Awakening" names a coherent event or a later construct (Jon Butler, 1982).3 Evangelicalism, characterised by conversion, the Bible, the cross and activism (David Bebbington's quadrilateral), became the dominant Protestant culture of the English-speaking world.4

    Volume XIV · Chapter 4

    Missions, colonialism, slavery and abolition

    Christianity and slavery

    Christian societies built and sustained the Atlantic slave trade, which forcibly transported about 12.5 million Africans between the 16th and 19th centuries (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database estimates).1 Christian complicity took many forms:

    • Theologians justified slavery from the Bible (the "curse of Ham"; Pauline instructions to slaves). Nicholas V's bull Dum diversas (1452) authorised the Portuguese to reduce "Saracens and pagans" to perpetual servitude.
    • Churches and religious orders owned slaves. Jesuits in Maryland sold 272 enslaved people in 1838, an act Georgetown University has since acknowledged.
    • Southern US denominations split over slavery: the Southern Baptist Convention was formed in 1845, and Methodists divided in 1844.

    Christians were also prominent in abolition:

    • Quakers (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, 1758–76);
    • evangelical Anglicans such as William Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect, and former slaves such as Olaudah Equiano. Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833;
    • American abolitionists, many motivated by revivalism.

    Gregory XVI condemned the slave trade in In supremo apostolatus (1839), though Catholic opinion on slavery itself remained divided. Enslaved and free Black Christians built their own churches and theologies of liberation from bondage. Richard Allen founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, and the "invisible institution" of slave religion produced the spirituals.

    The Protestant missionary movement

    William Carey's Enquiry (1792) and the Baptist Missionary Society were followed by the London (1795), Church (1799) and American (1810) missionary societies. Missionaries translated the Bible into hundreds of languages. They founded schools and hospitals, and also sometimes served colonial interests. Historians now stress that African, Asian and Pacific evangelists and translators did most of the work. Examples include Samuel Ajayi Crowther (1809–1891), a freed slave who became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864, and the Liberian prophet William Wadé Harris (c. 1860–1929), whose preaching in Côte d'Ivoire produced tens of thousands of converts. The relationship between mission and empire is debated: collaboration, critique, or both (Brian Stanley; Lamin Sanneh's argument that vernacular translation empowered local cultures).2 The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) marked the high point of Western mission confidence and the start of the ecumenical movement (XV.4).

    The shift of Christianity's centre of gravity

    In 1900 roughly two-thirds or more of Christians lived in Europe and North America. By 2020, according to the Pew Research Center, sub-Saharan Africa was home to the largest share of the world's Christians (31%), ahead of Europe (22%) (XV.8). The nineteenth century laid foundations for this shift through mission, migration and African and Asian initiative.

    Notes

    Volume XIV · Chapter 5

    New movements of the nineteenth century

    • Restorationism. The Stone–Campbell movement (Disciples of Christ, Churches of Christ) sought to restore New Testament Christianity beyond denominations.
    • Adventism. William Miller predicted Christ's return in 1843–44. After the "Great Disappointment" of 22 October 1844, one group, led by Ellen G. White, Joseph Bates and James White, adopted the Saturday Sabbath and the doctrine of a heavenly "investigative judgement" beginning in 1844. They organised as the Seventh-day Adventist Church in 1863. It emphasises health reform and education, and holds Ellen White's writings as a continuing (subordinate) prophetic authority.1
    • The Holiness movement and precursors of Pentecostalism. Methodist teaching on entire sanctification as a "second blessing" (Phoebe Palmer), the Keswick Convention (1875), and healing ministries prepared the ground for Pentecostalism (XV.3).
    • The Oxford Movement (from 1833) recovered Catholic doctrine and practice within Anglicanism. Its leaders were Keble, Pusey and Newman. Newman became a Catholic in 1845 and wrote the Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine (1845).
    • Movements outside historic Christian orthodoxy. These include the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (1830), the Bible Student movement that became the Jehovah's Witnesses (from the 1870s), and Christian Science (1879). They identify as Christian but reject the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity or add new scriptures, and most historic Churches do not regard them as within Nicene Christianity. This edition records the classification without adjudicating it.2
    • Social Christianity. Christian socialism (F. D. Maurice), the Salvation Army (1865/1878), the Social Gospel in America (Walter Rauschenbusch), and Catholic social teaching beginning with Leo XIII's Rerum novarum (1891), on labour and capital.

    Notes

    Volume XIV · Chapter 6

    Biblical criticism, liberal and conservative theology

    Historical-critical study of the Bible developed from Spinoza, Richard Simon (a French Catholic priest, 1678) and Enlightenment scholars, and flourished in nineteenth-century German universities. Major landmarks:

    • the documentary hypothesis of the Pentateuch (Julius Wellhausen, 1878);
    • David Friedrich Strauss' Life of Jesus (1835), which treated the Gospel miracles as myth;
    • the "quest of the historical Jesus", surveyed and ended by Albert Schweitzer (1906).1

    Responses spanned a spectrum.

    • Liberal Protestantism. Friedrich Schleiermacher (On Religion, 1799; The Christian Faith, 1821–22) grounded religion in the feeling of absolute dependence. Albrecht Ritschl and Adolf von Harnack (What Is Christianity?, 1900) stressed the ethical kingdom of God.2
    • Confessional and conservative responses. Revived Lutheran confessionalism; the Princeton theology of Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, with its doctrine of the inerrancy of Scripture; and the later American Fundamentals (1910–15), from which "fundamentalism" takes its name.
    • Catholic responses. Leo XIII's Providentissimus Deus (1893) cautiously addressed biblical study. The "Modernist crisis" followed. Pius X's Pascendi (1907) condemned Modernism, and the Anti-Modernist Oath (1910) was imposed on clergy. Pius XII's Divino afflante Spiritu (1943) later opened Catholic scholarship to historical methods.3
    • Orthodox theology engaged these questions mainly through Russian religious philosophy (Khomiakov, Soloviev) and later the "neo-patristic" movement (XV.6).

    Notes

    Volume XIV · Chapter 7

    The First Vatican Council and the end of the Papal States

    Pius IX's pontificate (1846–1878) was the longest verifiable in papal history. In it he defined the Immaculate Conception (Ineffabilis Deus, 1854) after consulting the bishops, issued the Syllabus (1864), and lost the Papal States to Italian unification.1 The trend of the period, called "ultramontanism" ("beyond the mountains", i.e. looking to Rome), strengthened papal authority against national churches (Gallicanism) and state control.

    The First Vatican Council opened on 8 December 1869. About 700 bishops attended. Its decrees were:

    • Dei Filius (April 1870), on faith and reason;
    • Pastor aeternus (18 July 1870), which defined the pope's universal jurisdiction ("full and supreme power of jurisdiction over the whole Church") and the infallibility of his ex cathedra definitions on faith and morals, "of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church" (short phrases from the standard English translation).

    The final vote was 533 to 2, after about 60 members of the minority, who considered a definition "inopportune", left Rome rather than vote against it.2 The minority included leading historians such as Hefele, who later accepted the decree. The Munich church historian Ignaz von Döllinger refused and was excommunicated (1871). The Old Catholic Churches (Union of Utrecht, 1889) emerged from those who rejected the decrees. They joined the Dutch Church of Utrecht, separated from Rome since 1724.3

    The Franco-Prussian War forced the council's suspension. Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870, and Pius IX considered himself "prisoner of the Vatican". The Roman Question was settled by the Lateran Treaty (1929), which created Vatican City.4 In Germany, Bismarck's Kulturkampf (1871–78) restricted the Catholic Church. Leo XIII (1878–1903) inaugurated a more engaged papacy. He revived Thomism (Aeterni Patris, 1879), wrote on labour (Rerum novarum, 1891), and declared Anglican orders "absolutely null and utterly void" (Apostolicae curae, 1896).5 For how Orthodox and Protestant Churches view papal infallibility, see IX.6 and the Part III matrix.

    Volume XV · 1900–2026

    Christianity in the Twentieth and Twenty-First Centuries

    The twentieth century saw more Christians killed for their faith, and more Christians converted, than any previous century. It also saw Christianity's centre move to the Global South, and the most sustained effort at reunion since the councils. This volume covers the world wars and totalitarian regimes, Pentecostalism, the ecumenical movement, Vatican II, Orthodoxy after communism, the Middle East, contemporary controversies, and the present-day distribution of Christians. All contemporary figures are dated and sourced.

    In this volume

    1. World wars, fascism, Nazism and the Holocaust
    2. Christianity under communism
    3. Pentecostal, charismatic, evangelical and independent Christianity
    4. The ecumenical movement
    5. Vatican II, Catholic social teaching and liberation theology
    6. Orthodoxy in the modern world
    7. Christians in the Middle East
    8. Contemporary controversies and the world Christian population

    Volume XV · Chapter 1

    World wars, fascism, Nazism and the Holocaust

    In 1914 Churches on both sides blessed the war. Benedict XV's peace proposals (1917) were ignored. The war's carnage shook liberal theology's optimism. Karl Barth's Epistle to the Romans (1919/1922) launched "dialectical theology".1

    The Churches and Nazism

    • Protestants. The pro-Nazi "German Christians" won church elections in 1933. In opposition, the Confessing Church adopted the Barmen Declaration (May 1934), drafted largely by Barth. It rejected the idea that the Church could recognise other sources of revelation besides Christ, but said little explicitly about the Jews. Dietrich Bonhoeffer joined the resistance and was executed on 9 April 1945. Most Protestants, however, accommodated the regime.2
    • Catholics. The Reichskonkordat (July 1933) sought to protect Catholic institutions. Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (1937) condemned Nazi violations and racial idolatry. Clergy and laity resisted in various ways, among them Bishop von Galen's 1941 sermons against euthanasia killings. Thousands of priests were imprisoned (Dachau).3
    • Pius XII (1939–1958). His public reticence about the Holocaust has been fiercely debated since Rolf Hochhuth's play The Deputy (1963). Some see diplomatic prudence and covert rescue efforts; others see moral failure. The Vatican archives of his pontificate opened in March 2020, and research based on them, for example by David Kertzer (2022), continues.4

    The Holocaust and Christian antisemitism

    Historians broadly agree that centuries of Christian anti-Judaism prepared the ground on which Nazi racial antisemitism grew, though Nazi ideology was itself anti-Christian in important respects. After 1945 Churches undertook major revisions:

    • the Seelisberg Theses (1947);
    • Vatican II's Nostra aetate 4 (1965), which rejected collective Jewish guilt for Christ's death and deplored antisemitism;
    • the Vatican's We Remember: A Reflection on the Shoah (1998);
    • Protestant declarations rejecting the idea that the Church has replaced Israel, such as the Rhineland synod (1980).

    See Part IV, study H.5

    Notes

    1. Karl Barth, Der Römerbrief (1919; 2nd ed. 1922). See Stanley 2018. ↩
    2. Bethge 2000; on the Barmen Declaration (1934), Barnett 1992. ↩
    3. Clemens August von Galen, sermons of July and August 1941. See Stanley 2018. ↩
    4. Kertzer 2022; on the Protestant churches, Barnett 1992. ↩
    5. Synod of the Evangelical Church in the Rhineland, resolution of January 1980; Vatican II, Nostra aetate 4. ↩

    Volume XV · Chapter 2

    Christianity under communism

    • Soviet Union. The Russian Church restored its patriarchate in 1917 and elected Tikhon. The Bolsheviks then confiscated church property and carried out mass arrests and executions of clergy, especially in 1918–22 and 1937–38. By 1939 only a few hundred parishes remained open. Stalin permitted a revival in 1943 for wartime reasons, under strict state control. Khrushchev's campaign (1959–64) closed thousands of churches again.1 The Russian Church has canonised over a thousand "New Martyrs and Confessors". Their exact number is not settled.2
    • Eastern Europe. Churches faced varied pressures. Albania declared itself an atheist state in 1967. The Greek Catholic Churches of Ukraine and Romania were suppressed (XIII.6). In Poland, the Catholic Church became a pillar of national resistance. Karol Wojtyła was elected pope (John Paul II) in 1978, and Solidarity emerged in 1980.
    • After 1989–91. Massive revival of church life in Russia, Ukraine, Romania and elsewhere. The Cathedral of Christ the Saviour in Moscow, demolished in 1931, was rebuilt and consecrated in 2000. Close relations between the Moscow Patriarchate and the Russian state have been criticised, especially Patriarch Kirill's support for the war against Ukraine from 2022, which led parts of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church to distance themselves from Moscow.3
    • China. After 1949 missionaries were expelled. The state organised the Protestant Three-Self Patriotic Movement (1954) and the Catholic Patriotic Association (1957). Churches were closed during the Cultural Revolution (1966–76). Christianity then grew rapidly, especially through unregistered "house churches". Estimates of the number of Christians vary greatly with method: Pew's 2025 report estimated roughly 25 million self-identifying Christians in 2020, while other estimates are far higher.4 A Holy See–China provisional agreement on the appointment of bishops was signed in 2018 and renewed in 2020, 2022 and, for four years, 2024.5

    Notes

    Volume XV · Chapter 3

    Pentecostal, charismatic, evangelical and independent Christianity

    Pentecostalism traces its origins to several centres. At Charles Parham's Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, students spoke in tongues in January 1901. The Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles (1906–c. 1909) was led by the African American preacher William J. Seymour and was notable for its interracial worship. Parallel revivals took place in Wales (1904–05), India (Mukti, 1905) and Korea (1907).1 Pentecostals teach a "baptism in the Holy Spirit" evidenced, in classical Pentecostalism, by speaking in tongues, along with healing and prophecy. They formed denominations such as the Church of God in Christ (Pentecostal from 1907) and the Assemblies of God (1914). A dispute over the Trinity produced "Oneness" Pentecostalism (from 1913–16), which baptises in Jesus' name only and rejects the Trinitarian formulation.2

    The charismatic movement brought Pentecostal experience into historic Churches: among Episcopalians (Dennis Bennett, 1960), Catholics (the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, from Duquesne University in 1967) and others. "Neo-charismatic" and independent churches, including many African Initiated Churches such as the Kimbanguist Church (Congo, 1921) and the Aladura churches (Nigeria), and Latin American and Asian megachurches, have made Pentecostal-charismatic Christianity the fastest-growing form of Christianity in the twentieth century.3 Estimates of its size, often cited at over 600 million, depend heavily on how it is defined.4

    Evangelicalism was reorganised after the fundamentalist–modernist controversies (1920s). Landmarks include the "new evangelicals", Billy Graham's crusades, the Lausanne Congress (1974) and its Covenant, and global evangelical networks. In the United States, evangelical identity became closely linked with politics from the 1970s. This shift is analysed in an extensive literature. Non-denominational churches have grown rapidly in the US and elsewhere.

    Notes

    1. Anderson 2014. ↩

    Volume XV · Chapter 4

    The ecumenical movement

    • 1910. The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh.
    • 1920. The Ecumenical Patriarchate's encyclical called for a "fellowship of Churches" on the model of the League of Nations.1
    • 1925 and 1927. Life and Work (Stockholm, 1925) and Faith and Order (Lausanne, 1927).
    • 1948. These merged to form the World Council of Churches (Amsterdam). Its Toronto Statement (1950) declared that membership does not imply recognising other members as Churches in the full sense. Orthodox Churches joined, mostly in 1961. The Catholic Church is not a member, but participates in Faith and Order.2
    • Church unions:
      • the Church of South India (1947), uniting Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches with episcopacy;
      • the United Church of Canada (1925);
      • the Uniting Church in Australia (1977);
      • the Leuenberg Agreement (1973), establishing church fellowship between Lutheran and Reformed churches in Europe;
      • the Porvoo Communion (1996), Anglican and Nordic and Baltic Lutheran churches.3
    • Bilateral dialogues. The Faith and Order convergence text Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (Lima, 1982). The Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) (XI.6). Catholic–Orthodox and Oriental dialogues (V.5, IX.5, VII.6). ARCIC (Anglican–Roman Catholic) since 1970.4
    • 2025. Commemorations of Nicaea's 1700th anniversary, including at İznik, brought together leaders of many traditions (IX.5).

    Assessments differ. Some speak of an "ecumenical winter" since the 1990s, caused by divergence over ethics and ordination. Others point to practical and "receptive" ecumenism and growing cooperation among Pentecostal and evangelical bodies (the Global Christian Forum, from 1998).

    Notes

    Volume XV · Chapter 5

    Vatican II, Catholic social teaching and liberation theology

    John XXIII announced a council in January 1959. The Second Vatican Council met in four sessions from 11 October 1962 to 8 December 1965, with about 2,400 bishops and Protestant and Orthodox observers. Its sixteen documents included four constitutions1 :

    • Sacrosanctum concilium (1963), liturgical reform and the vernacular;
    • Lumen gentium (1964), the Church as the people of God and episcopal collegiality. It says the Church of Christ "subsists in" the Catholic Church, a phrase whose interpretation is debated;
    • Dei verbum (1965), on revelation, Scripture and tradition;
    • Gaudium et spes (1965), on the Church in the modern world.

    Its decrees and declarations included:

    • Unitatis redintegratio (1964), on ecumenism;
    • Orientalium Ecclesiarum (1964), on the Eastern Catholic Churches;
    • Dignitatis humanae (1965), on religious freedom;
    • Nostra aetate (1965), on non-Christian religions and the Jews.

    Implementation brought the Mass of Paul VI (1969/70) and the vernacular. Interpretation has been contested: "hermeneutic of reform in continuity" (Benedict XVI, 2005) versus "rupture" readings, and the traditionalist rejection by Archbishop Lefebvre's Society of St Pius X, whose bishops were excommunicated in 1988 and the excommunications lifted in 2009. Rules2 on the pre-conciliar liturgy were liberalised (2007) and then restricted (Traditionis custodes, 2021).3

    Catholic social teaching and liberation theology

    From Rerum novarum (1891) through Quadragesimo anno (1931), Pacem in terris (1963), Populorum progressio (1967) and Centesimus annus (1991) to Laudato si' (2015), on the environment, popes developed teaching on the dignity of work, the common good, subsidiarity and solidarity.4 In Latin America, the bishops' conference at Medellín (1968) spoke of structural sin and a "preferential option for the poor". Gustavo Gutiérrez's Theology of Liberation (1971) used social analysis, including Marxist categories. The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith criticised aspects of it (1984) and affirmed others (1986). Archbishop Óscar Romero was murdered in 1980 and canonised in 2018.5 Pope Francis (2013–2025) emphasised mercy, synodality and the poor. He died on 21 April 2025, and Leo XIV (Robert Prevost) was elected on 8 May 2025.6

    Volume XV · Chapter 6

    Orthodoxy in the modern world

    • Diaspora theology. Russian émigrés in Paris (St Sergius Institute, 1925) and America (St Vladimir's Seminary) renewed Orthodox theology. Georges Florovsky's "neo-patristic synthesis", Vladimir Lossky, Alexander Schmemann (liturgy), John Meyendorff, and in Greece John Zizioulas (Being as Communion, 1985) shaped Orthodox thought and ecumenical dialogue. Sergei Bulgakov's sophiology was controversial.1
    • The calendar. Constantinople and Greece adopted the Revised Julian calendar for fixed feasts (1923–24), provoking "Old Calendarist" schisms. Russia, Serbia, Georgia, Jerusalem and Athos keep the Julian calendar. Easter remains on the Julian computation for almost all Orthodox. A common Easter date with Western Christians is under discussion (IX.5).
    • The Holy and Great Council (Crete, June 2016) was decades in preparation. Moscow, Antioch, Bulgaria and Georgia withdrew shortly before it met, so it was attended by ten of the fourteen generally recognised autocephalous Churches.2
    • Ukraine. Constantinople granted a tomos of autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine in January 2019. Moscow had broken communion with Constantinople in October 2018 in anticipation, and several Churches have not recognised the new Church. The dispute over primacy within Orthodoxy (the "Constantinople versus Moscow" question) has deepened since Russia's 2022 invasion.

    Volume XV · Chapter 7

    Christians in the Middle East

    The twentieth century began with catastrophe. The Armenian genocide, and the Sayfo massacres of Assyrians and Syriac Christians (1914–1924), killed hundreds of thousands, with estimates for Armenians alone commonly 600,000 to 1.5 million.1 The population exchange between Greece and Turkey (1923) ended the Christian presence in much of Anatolia. Since then the Christian share of the population across the region has fallen sharply, through emigration, lower birth rates, conflict and pressure.2

    • Iraq. Christians were often estimated at over a million before 2003. They were targeted in sectarian violence after 2003 and expelled from Mosul and the Nineveh Plain by the Islamic State in 2014. Current estimates are commonly a few hundred thousand; precise figures are uncertain.
    • Syria. The civil war since 2011 brought large-scale displacement. The fall of the Assad government in December 2024 left the future of Syria's Christian communities uncertain, and churches were attacked in 2025.
    • Lebanon. The only state in the region with a Christian head of state. The constitutional balance is under strain, and Christian emigration has increased since the 2019 financial collapse and the 2020 Beirut port explosion.
    • Egypt. Copts are the largest Christian community in the Middle East, perhaps around 10% of Egypt's population. Estimates differ between Church and state sources.3
    • Israel/Palestine. Palestinian Christian communities have declined as a share of the population. Christian holy sites remain governed by the Ottoman-era status quo arrangements.

    The Gulf states meanwhile host large migrant Christian populations from Asia and Africa, a reminder that the region's Christianity is changing in composition as well as size.

    Volume XV · Chapter 8

    Contemporary controversies and the world Christian population

    Where Christians are (2020 data)

    According to the Pew Research Center's June 2025 report, based on more than 2,700 censuses and surveys1 :

    • the number of Christians grew from 2.1 billion (2010) to 2.3 billion (2020);
    • their share of the world population fell from about 30.6% to 28.8%, largely because many people "switched" out of religion;
    • sub-Saharan Africa held 31% of the world's Christians, and Europe 22%;
    • sub-Saharan Africa was the only region where the Christian share rose (to 62%);
    • the United States had the largest Christian population of any country.

    Source: Pew Research Center, “How the Global Religious Landscape Changed From 2010 to 2020” (June 2025). Only the two figures the source states directly are charted, sub-Saharan Africa (31%) and Europe (22%); the remaining 47% is shown as a single “other regions” bar, since its breakdown was not verified during preparation.

    Other projects (e.g. the World Christian Database, Gordon-Conwell's Center for the Study of Global Christianity) use different definitions, such as counting baptised members rather than self-identification. They produce higher totals and should not be mixed with Pew's figures.

    Contemporary controversies

    • Clerical sexual abuse. Revelations in many countries include Ireland (Ryan and Murphy reports, 2009), the US (the Boston Globe, 2002; the Pennsylvania grand jury, 2018), Australia (Royal Commission, 2017), France (the CIASE report, 2021), and many Protestant and other bodies, including the Southern Baptist Convention's 2022 report and Church of England reviews. In November 2024 Archbishop Justin Welby resigned over failures in the Smyth case. These revelations have produced reforms (e.g. Vos estis lux mundi, 2019) and a profound loss of trust.2
    • Women's ordination. Most mainline Protestant Churches ordain women. Many Anglican provinces have women bishops (Church of England since 2014/15). The Catholic and Orthodox Churches do not ordain women as priests or bishops; the Catholic Church holds this to be definitive (Ordinatio sacerdotalis, 1994). The question of women deacons is under study in both.3
    • Sexuality and marriage. Divisions have reshaped denominations:
      • Anglican realignment, with GAFCON (2008) and, in 2023, the Global South Fellowship's rejection of the Archbishop of Canterbury's leadership after the Church of England's Prayers of Love and Faith;
      • the United Methodist disaffiliations, in which thousands of US congregations left (2019–2023), the Global Methodist Church was formed (2022), and the 2024 General Conference removed prohibitions on LGBTQ clergy;
      • Catholic debate after the declaration Fiducia supplicans (December 2023), on non-liturgical blessings of couples in irregular situations, which many African bishops declined to implement.
      4
    • Other debates. Bioethics and the beginning and end of life; Christian nationalism; creation and evolution; religious freedom and persecution, with watch lists compiled by groups such as Open Doors and Aid to the Church in Need, whose methods vary.

    For the structure of today's Christian traditions see Part III.

    Part III

    Comparative Theology and Ecclesiology

    This part describes the principal Christian traditions today: their origins, leadership, worship, doctrine, Scripture, sacraments or ordinances, and distribution. It then compares them on twenty-four topics in an interactive matrix. Positions are stated from each tradition's own authoritative documents where they exist. Every tradition contains internal variety, and the matrix summarises the official or majority position. Notes indicate where variation is important.

    In this part

    1. Profiles of the traditions
    2. Comparison matrix (24 topics)

    Membership figures are approximate. They come from the traditions' own world bodies or standard surveys, which count differently (baptised members vs. self-identification). They are marked and were not individually verified during preparation. The only global figure verified for this edition is Pew's total for all Christians (XV.8).

    Part III · Profiles

    Profiles of the traditions

    Roman Catholic Church

    Origins: claims continuity with the apostolic Church through the see of Rome; history in Vols II–XV. Leadership: the pope with the college of bishops; Code of Canon Law (1983). Worship: Roman Rite Mass (and other Latin rites); seven sacraments. Doctrine: 21 ecumenical councils; Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992). Scripture: 73 books. Distribution: 1.406 billion baptised members at the end of 2023 (Annuarium Statisticum 2023); largest communities in Latin America, Europe, Africa and the Philippines.

    Eastern Catholic Churches

    23 Churches sui iuris in full communion with Rome, following Byzantine, Alexandrian, Antiochene, Armenian and East Syriac traditions: for example the Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Syro-Malabar, Maronite, Melkite and Chaldean Churches. Law: Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990). See XIII.6. Together perhaps 18–20 million members.

    Eastern Orthodox Church

    Origins: the Byzantine imperial Church of the first millennium; separated from Rome over centuries (Vol. IX). Leadership: autocephalous Churches (14–17 depending on recognition), each with its synod; the Ecumenical Patriarch is "first among equals". Worship: the Byzantine Divine Liturgy; seven or more "mysteries" (the number is not dogmatically fixed). Doctrine: seven ecumenical councils; Holy Tradition. Distribution: commonly estimated at about 220–260 million; Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Serbia, Bulgaria, Georgia, the Middle East and the diaspora.1

    Oriental Orthodox Churches

    Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara Orthodox Churches. They accept three councils and confess miaphysite Christology (V.2). In communion with one another, each autocephalous. Ancient liturgies in Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ge'ez. Commonly estimated at about 60–80 million, of whom the Ethiopian Church forms the largest part.

    Assyrian Church of the East

    The historic Church of the East (V.1). Catholicos-Patriarch (Mar Awa III since 2021), seat in Erbil since 2015. East Syriac liturgy (Addai and Mari). Accepts the councils of 325 and 381. Members in Iraq, Iran, Syria, India and a large diaspora; total commonly given as several hundred thousand.

    Ancient Church of the East

    Separated from the Assyrian Church in 1968, over the calendar and hereditary succession. Seat in Baghdad. Reunion talks with the Assyrian Church have taken place at intervals; the most recent failed in 2022. Catholicos-Patriarch Gewargis III Younan was elected in November 2022 and consecrated in Baghdad on 9 June 2023.

    Lutheran Churches

    Origins: Wittenberg Reformation (XI.2). Confessions: Book of Concord (1580). Polity: varied; episcopal in Scandinavia and the Baltic (some in historic succession), synodal elsewhere. Worship: liturgical Divine Service; two sacraments, with confession valued. World bodies: Lutheran World Federation; the more conservative International Lutheran Council (incl. the Missouri Synod). Largest growth in Ethiopia (Mekane Yesus) and Tanzania.2

    Anglican Communion

    Origins: the English Reformation (XI.5). Instruments of unity: the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lambeth Conference, the Anglican Consultative Council and the Primates' Meeting. Provinces are autonomous. Formularies: Thirty-Nine Articles, Book of Common Prayer and Ordinal; the Chicago–Lambeth Quadrilateral (1886/88). Distribution: the largest provinces are in Africa (Nigeria, Uganda). Divided since 2003–08 over sexuality (XV.8).3

    Reformed and Presbyterian Churches

    Origins: Zurich and Geneva (XI.3). Confessions: Heidelberg, Belgic, Dort, Westminster and others. Polity: presbyterian, with ministers and elders in sessions, presbyteries and synods; Congregationalists are a related tradition. Worship: centred on preaching; two sacraments. World bodies: World Communion of Reformed Churches; also the more conservative World Reformed Fellowship. Large communities in Korea, Indonesia, southern Africa, Brazil and Hungary.

    Methodist / Wesleyan Churches

    Origins: the Wesleys' revival (XIV.3). Polity: connexional, governed by conferences; bishops in the US tradition. Doctrine: Arminian; assurance; sanctification; Wesley's Sermons and Notes; Articles of Religion (1784). Includes the Holiness churches, such as the Nazarenes. World body: World Methodist Council.4

    Baptist Churches

    Origins: English Separatists (1609–12) (XI.5). Distinctives: believers' baptism by immersion; congregational autonomy; religious liberty; "soul competency". There are General (Arminian) and Particular (Calvinist) streams. World body: Baptist World Alliance. The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest US Protestant denomination, left the BWA in 2004.

    Anabaptist Churches

    Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites and Brethren (XI.4). Believers' baptism, discipleship, nonviolence and the community of faith. World body: Mennonite World Conference; the largest national churches are now in Africa (DR Congo, Ethiopia) and India. Total about 2 million.

    Pentecostal Churches

    Origins: Topeka and Azusa Street (XV.3). Distinctives: baptism in the Holy Spirit, spiritual gifts, divine healing, expectation of Christ's return. Classical denominations (Assemblies of God, Church of God in Christ, Foursquare) plus many independent churches. Oneness Pentecostals are non-Trinitarian. Largest presence in Latin America, Africa and Asia.

    Seventh-day Adventist Church

    Origins: Millerite movement; organised 1863 (XIV.5). Distinctives: Saturday Sabbath; Christ's imminent return; the heavenly sanctuary and investigative judgement; conditional immortality (no conscious existence after death until the resurrection); health message; the prophetic ministry of Ellen G. White. Polity: General Conference. About 22–23 million baptised members (church statistics).5

    Independent and other movements

    African Initiated Churches (Kimbanguist, Aladura, Zion Christian Church); Chinese house churches; non-denominational and "network" churches; Quakers (Religious Society of Friends); Churches of Christ; Old Catholics; and others. Movements that reject Nicene Trinitarian doctrine, such as the Latter-day Saints and Jehovah's Witnesses, are noted in XIV.5.

    Part IV · Study E

    The history of Christian worship

    • Eucharist. The Eucharist moved from a meal in households (II.8) to set prayers led by a bishop or presbyter. The Didache and Justin (2nd c.) are the earliest witnesses (III.8). In the 4th century came great basilicas and fixed anaphoras: in Syria, the Liturgies of St James and of Addai and Mari; in Byzantium, those of St Basil and St John Chrysostom; in Alexandria, St Mark; in Rome, the Roman Canon. Latin became Rome's liturgical language in the 4th century. Medieval Western developments included private Masses, elevation of the host (c. 1200) and infrequent lay communion; Lateran IV required communion once a year (X.5). The reformers restored the vernacular and communion in both kinds. Trent and Pius V's Missal (1570) standardised the Roman Rite, until Vatican II's reform (1969/70).1
    • Initiation. Adult catechumenate and Easter baptism (3rd–4th c.). Later infant baptism became general, and the West separated confirmation from baptism. The Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults (1972) restored the catechumenate. Believers' baptism was revived by Anabaptists and Baptists (XI.4).
    • The liturgical year. Easter is the oldest feast; its date was disputed (Quartodecimans, VII.1; Nicaea, IV.6). Christmas on 25 December is attested at Rome by 336 (the Chronograph of 354). Epiphany is older in the East. Lent took shape in the 4th century. Saints' days grew from martyrs' anniversaries (III.2). The Gregorian calendar (1582) divided the dating of Easter between East and West.2
    • Daily prayer. The Liturgy of the Hours developed from monastic and cathedral offices. Cranmer simplified it into Morning and Evening Prayer.
    • Music. Psalmody; Ephrem's Syriac hymns; Byzantine chant; Gregorian chant (Carolingian standardisation, 9th c.); polyphony (Notre-Dame, 12th–13th c.); Luther's chorales; metrical psalms (Geneva); English hymnody (Watts, Wesley); spirituals and gospel music; Taizé; contemporary worship music.
    • Architecture and images. House-churches (Dura-Europos, III.8); basilicas; Byzantine domed churches; Romanesque and Gothic (X.8); Reformed meeting-houses; Baroque (XII.2); modern liturgical architecture. On images, see VIII.3 and VI.7.
    • Vestments. Vestments derive from late Roman secular dress, such as the alb (tunic) and the chasuble (from the cloak paenula), and became distinctive from about the 6th century. Colour sequences were standardised in the West in the medieval period. Reformed churches adopted the academic gown.

    Notes

    1. Pius V, Quo primum (1570); Vatican II, Sacrosanctum concilium (1963); Paul VI, Missale Romanum (1969). See O’Malley 2008. ↩
    2. Gregory XIII, Inter gravissimas (1582). ↩

    Part IV · Study G

    Christianity and Islam

    • Origins. Islam emerged in 7th-century Arabia, a region with Christian communities (Najran; Christian Arab tribes such as the Ghassanids) and Jewish communities. The Qur'an honours Jesus (ʿĪsā) as prophet and Messiah, born of the virgin Mary. It denies his divinity and, in the usual reading of 4:157, his crucifixion, and it rejects the Trinity as understood by its hearers. Scholars debate which Christian groups and texts were known in the Qur'an's milieu.
    • Early encounters. John of Damascus treated Islam as a Christian "heresy" (On Heresies 100). Arabic Christian theology developed (Theodore Abu Qurrah; ʿAmmār al-Baṣrī). The Catholicos Timothy I debated Caliph al-Mahdi (c. 782); the account of the dialogue survives.1
    • Life under Islamic rule. Dhimmī status (XIII.3). Conversion over centuries; historians debate its pace (Richard Bulliet's "conversion curve" models). Christians participated in the translation movement (V.1).2
    • Conflict and exchange. Crusades and Reconquista; the Ottoman advance and the sieges of Vienna (1529, 1683); Latin translations of Arabic science and philosophy (X.3); Francis and al-Kamil (X.4).
    • Modern relations. Colonialism and mission; Nostra aetate 3 (1965) on esteem for Muslims; A Common Word (2007), an open letter from Muslim scholars to Christian leaders; the Document on Human Fraternity (Abu Dhabi, 2019), signed by Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar. Persecution of Christians in some Muslim-majority states, and of Muslims in some Christian-majority contexts, remains a reality (XV.7).

    Notes

    1. Mingana 1928; Griffith 2008. ↩
    2. Griffith 2008. ↩

    Part IV · Study H

    Christianity and Judaism

    1. Jewish origins. Jesus, his disciples and Paul were Jews. Christianity's scriptures, worship and hope come from Second Temple Judaism (Vol. I; II.4).
    2. Differentiation. A long process of separation, not one event (II.7).
    3. The adversus Iudaeos tradition. From Barnabas, Justin and Melito, through John Chrysostom's sermons Against the Jews (386–87), to the medieval charge of "deicide". Augustine's "witness" doctrine both protected Jews and justified their subordination.1
    4. Medieval violence and legislation. The 1096 massacres; Lateran IV (X.4); blood libels, starting at Norwich in 1144; the Talmud burned in Paris (1242); expulsions; Spanish conversos and the Inquisition (X.5); ghettos (Venice, 1516; Rome, 1555).2
    5. Reformation. Luther's 1543 writings (XI.2). In the Dutch Republic and England (readmission in 1656) Jews were tolerated.
    6. Modern antisemitism and the Holocaust. Racial antisemitism; Church responses (XV.1).
    7. Reconciliation. Nostra aetate 4 (1965); John Paul II at the Rome synagogue (1986) and the Western Wall (2000); The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable (2015); Protestant rejections of supersessionism; Jewish responses such as Dabru Emet (2000).3

    Notes

    1. Augustine, City of God 18.46 (NPNF I/2). See Cohen 1999. ↩
    2. Lateran IV, canons 67–70 (Tanner 1990, vol. 1); Paul IV, Cum nimis absurdum (1555). See Cohen 1999. ↩
    3. Vatican II, Nostra aetate 4 (1965); Dabru Emet (2000). ↩

    Part IV · Study J

    Church and state

    1. A persecuted or tolerated minority (to 311/313): "Render unto Caesar" (Mark 12:17); Romans 13; prayers for the emperor; refusal of the imperial cult1 (III.2).
    2. Imperial Church (313–6th c.): the emperor as convener of councils; Cunctos populos (380)2; Gelasius' two powers3; Justinian's symphōnia (IV.9, VII.4).
    3. Divergence. Byzantine emperor-and-patriarch models (Dagron); the Latin papal monarchy and investiture conflict (X.1, X.6); Islamic dhimma (XIII.3); Persian Christians (V.1).
    4. Confessional states (16th–18th c.): cuius regio, eius religio (1555); royal supremacy (England, 1534); the Russian Holy Synod (1721) (XI.2, XIII.2).
    5. Toleration, disestablishment and secular states: the First Amendment (1791); the French Revolution and laïcité (1905) (XIV.2); concordats (1801, 1929, 1933).
    6. Totalitarianism and resistance (20th c.) (XV.1–2).
    7. Religious freedom as Christian teaching: Dignitatis humanae (1965); the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), whose drafting involved Christian contributors (e.g. Charles Malik). Debates continue about established churches, Christian nationalism and secularity.4

    Notes

    1. 1 Timothy 2:1–2; 1 Clement 61 (Holmes 2007); Tertullian, Apology 30–33 (ANF, vol. 3). ↩
    2. Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2 (Pharr 1952). ↩
    3. Gelasius I to Emperor Anastasius (494): DH 347 (DH). ↩
    4. Vatican II, Dignitatis humanae (1965); Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), article 18. ↩

    Part IV · Study K

    Transmission and preservation

    • The codex. Christians adopted the codex (book) rather than the scroll unusually early. Most 2nd–4th century Christian manuscripts are codices.1
    • Translations. Each major translation carried Christianity into a new culture:
      • Old Latin and the Vulgate (Jerome, late 4th c.);
      • Syriac (the Peshitta) and Coptic;
      • Gothic (Ulfila, 4th c.);
      • Armenian (5th c.) and Ge'ez;
      • Georgian;
      • Old Church Slavonic (9th c.);
      • Arabic (from the 8th–9th c.);
      • later the vernacular Bibles of the Reformation and modern missions. Scripture has been translated in full into over 700 languages. That figure is reported annually by Bible societies and was not verified for this edition.
    • Libraries and monasteries. Caesarea (Origen, Pamphilus, Eusebius); Constantinople; Irish and Anglo-Saxon monasteries; the Carolingian scriptoria and minuscule script (most surviving classical Latin texts depend on Carolingian copies); St Catherine's, Sinai; Mount Athos; the Ethiopian monasteries; the Syriac manuscripts of Deir al-Surian (Egypt).
    • Movement between cultures. Greek philosophy passed through Syriac and Arabic into Latin (X.3). Byzantine scholars brought Greek texts to Italy (15th c.). Printing (from the 1450s; XI.1).
    • Rediscoveries. The Didache (1873); Nag Hammadi (1945); the Dead Sea Scrolls (1947) (I.4); the Sinai "new finds" (1975). Digitisation projects, such as the Codex Sinaiticus Project (2009) and the Vatican Library, make manuscripts widely available today.2
    • Losses. Destruction in wars and conquests: Constantinople 1204 and 1453, Baghdad 1258; deliberate burnings, such as Diamper (1599) and Lollard books; and destruction in 20th-century conflicts, including Iraq and Syria since 2003.

    Notes

    1. Hurtado 2006; Metzger & Ehrman 2005. ↩
    2. Codex Sinaiticus Project (2009), codexsinaiticus.org; Metzger & Ehrman 2005. ↩

      Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo ChurchOriental OrthodoxPatriarch (Asmara)Autocephalous since the 1990s. →
